items.subtitle: A wall and a solid stone tower with an internal staircase, built by people who had no metal and no pottery.
items.reveal: Jericho, in the Jordan Valley, has one of the oldest town walls ever found, built roughly ten thousand years ago by people who had no metal tools and had not yet learned to make pottery. Beside the wall stands a round stone tower more than twenty-six feet high, with a staircase built inside it — a huge project for a community farming with tools of stone and bone. Archaeologists still argue about what the wall and tower were for: some think they defended the town from raiders, others that they held back floodwater or mudslides. Radiocarbon dating actually puts the tower closer to 8000 BC than the traditional estimate of 6800 BC.

items.prompt: The first nomads of the Fertile Crescent
items.subtitle: Following the herds and the ripening grain, carrying everything, and staying nowhere.

place.label: The Fertile Crescent, from the Levant round to the Gulf

items.reveal: Long before people settled into permanent villages, the earliest inhabitants of the Fertile Crescent — the arc of land curving from the eastern Mediterranean through Mesopotamia to the Persian Gulf — lived by following wild herds and gathering wild grain as it ripened each season, carrying their belongings and never staying anywhere for long. Over thousands of years, some of these groups began instead to plant grain on purpose and keep animals penned rather than hunting them; wheat, barley, sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle were all first domesticated in this region. That shift, from finding food to growing it, is considered the single biggest change in the whole span of ancient history, since it made permanent towns, larger populations, and eventually writing and government all possible.

items.prompt: The drying of the Green Sahara
items.subtitle: Rock paintings of swimmers, hippos, and cattle herds, in a place where it now never rains.

time.label: Desiccation of the African Humid Period

items.reveal: Thousands of years ago the Sahara Desert was not a desert at all: it held lakes, rivers, and grassland where hippos, giraffes, and cattle grazed, and the people who lived there left paintings of swimmers and herders on rock walls that survive today in the middle of what is now bone-dry desert. Gradually, a shift in Earth's tilt changed the rain patterns that had watered the region, and the grassland dried into the sand sea we know now. The drying of the Sahara pushed farming peoples toward the Nile valley, helping fill it with the population that would build Egypt, while it also cut West Africa off from the Mediterranean world, so it developed largely along its own path.

items.subtitle: City of the falcon god, seat of the kings of the valley before there was one Egypt.
items.reveal: Hierakonpolis — Greek for "city of the hawk" — was one of the largest towns in Egypt before the country was unified into a single kingdom, and it served as a center of power for the rulers of Upper Egypt, the southern stretch of the Nile valley. Its Egyptian name was Nekhen, and it was sacred to the falcon god Horus, whose image later stood for kingship itself. Excavations there have turned up the oldest painted tomb yet found in Egypt, along with the earliest known walled animal enclosure, sometimes called the world's oldest zoo.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The falcon who avenged his murdered father, lost an eye doing it, and whose living image every pharaoh claimed to be.
items.reveal: Horus was the falcon-headed god of the sky and of kingship, worshipped throughout ancient Egyptian history. In the central myth about him, his father, King Osiris, is murdered by his jealous brother Seth; Horus fights Seth to avenge his father, losing one eye in the battle before finally winning back the throne. Because of this story, every living pharaoh was considered a living Horus, while a dead pharaoh became Osiris, so each change of ruler was thought of as a re-enactment of the myth. Horus's restored eye, called the wedjat, became one of the most common protective symbols in Egyptian art.

items.subtitle: The White Walls, capital where the valley opens into the delta.

time.label: Capital from unification to the Late Period

items.reveal: Memphis stood at the point where the Nile valley opens out into its wide delta, making it a natural capital for a kingdom that needed to control both regions; the Egyptians called it "the White Walls" after its fortifications. It served as Egypt's capital from the unification of the country around 3100 BC until well into the first millennium BC, and remained an important city long after it stopped being the seat of government. Its ruins lie near the modern town of Mit Rahina, about 20 km south of Cairo.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The king remembered as the first to wear both crowns.

place.label: Memphis and the lower Nile valley

items.reveal: Narmer was a king of Upper Egypt, credited with uniting the separate kingdoms of the Nile valley and the delta into a single Egypt around 3100 BC — traditionally the starting point of Egyptian history. Ancient Egyptian king-lists remember the unifier under the name Menes, and scholars have long debated whether Menes and Narmer were the same king known by two names, or two different men. Because writing had barely begun and no dated document survives from this period, even the date of 3100 BC is a rough marker built from later king-lists and radiocarbon science, not a measurement anyone can be fully certain of.

items.subtitle: A slab of green stone showing a king clubbing an enemy, and the same king wearing the other crown on the reverse.
items.reveal: The Narmer Palette is a shield-shaped slab of gray-green stone, carved on both faces with images of the same king. On one side he wears the crown of Upper Egypt and clubs a kneeling enemy; on the other he wears the crown of Lower Egypt, reviewing rows of defeated foes — many historians read the two scenes together as marking Egypt's unification. It was carved around 3100 BC for use in temple ritual, not as a public monument, and was found in 1898 buried in a temple deposit at Hierakonpolis, some 500 km up the Nile from Memphis — a reminder that where an object was made, used, and later buried can be three different places.

items.subtitle: A murdered king becomes lord of the dead; his wife gathers the pieces.

time.label: First attested in the Pyramid Texts; worshipped for two millennia after

items.reveal: Osiris was an Egyptian king-god murdered by his jealous brother Seth, who cut his body into pieces and scattered them; his wife and sister, the goddess Isis, gathered the pieces back together and used her magic to bring him briefly back to life, long enough to conceive their son Horus. Afterward, Osiris ruled not the living but the dead, judging souls in the underworld, while Isis became honored as a devoted wife and a powerful protector. The fullest surviving version of this story was written down by the Greek author Plutarch around AD 100 — nearly 2,500 years after Egyptians first mention Osiris — so the wide time window given here reflects a cult that was worshipped continuously across the centuries rather than one dateable event.

items.subtitle: The sun, sailing a boat across the sky by day and through the underworld by night, fighting a serpent on the way.

place.label: Heliopolis, at the head of the delta

time.label: From the Old Kingdom solar cult onward

items.reveal: Ra was the Egyptian sun god, imagined as sailing a boat across the sky each day and then through the dangerous underworld each night, where he had to fight off a giant serpent named Apep before rising again at dawn. His main temple stood at Heliopolis, near the head of the Nile delta — a name the Greeks gave the city, meaning "sun city," since it was Egypt's chief center of sun worship. Many of the tall stone obelisks that once stood at Heliopolis's temples were later moved abroad, and now stand in London, Paris, and New York.

items.prompt: Upper and Lower Egypt become one kingdom
items.subtitle: The white crown of the valley and the red crown of the delta are joined.

place.label: Memphis, at the junction of valley and delta

items.reveal: For centuries, Egypt was divided into two separate kingdoms: one ruling the narrow Nile valley to the south, symbolized by a white crown, and one ruling the marshy delta to the north, symbolized by a red crown. Around 3100 BC these two kingdoms were joined into a single Egypt, whose kings from then on wore a double crown combining both, with a new capital built at Memphis, right at the point where valley meets delta. The event is often shown compressed into a single dramatic image, such as the Narmer Palette, but historians think unification was more likely a gradual process across several generations than one decisive conquest.

items.subtitle: Wedges pressed into wet clay with a cut reed — the world's first writing.
items.reveal: Cuneiform was the world's first system of writing, developed in the Sumerian city of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia. Scribes pressed a cut reed into soft clay tablets to make wedge-shaped marks — the name comes from Latin for "wedge-shaped." It began purely as a bookkeeping tool, used to track grain, beer, and livestock, and it would be nearly a thousand years before anyone used it to write down stories or literature.

items.subtitle: Sacred carvings: pictures that stand for sounds as well as things.
items.reveal: Egyptian hieroglyphs were a writing system that combined pictures standing for whole words with signs standing for individual sounds; the name comes from Greek for "sacred carving," since the Greeks first saw them on temple walls. The oldest known examples are small labels made of bone and ivory, found among grave goods in a royal tomb at Abydos. Historians still debate whether Egyptians invented writing on their own or were inspired after hearing that the Mesopotamians nearby had already invented cuneiform.

items.subtitle: One decree in three scripts — the key that reopened hieroglyphs.
items.reveal: The Rosetta Stone is a large slab of stone carved in 196 BC with a single decree honoring the pharaoh Ptolemy V, written out three times: once in Egyptian hieroglyphs, once in an everyday Egyptian script called demotic, and once in Greek. Because scholars could already read Greek, the stone let them work out what the hieroglyphs meant for the first time in centuries; the French scholar Jean-François Champollion finally cracked the code in 1822, more than two thousand years after hieroglyphic writing had gone out of use. It was found in 1799 by French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rosetta (Rashid) in the Nile delta. The stone itself dates from a fairly late period of Egyptian history, so it is scored here as a marker for the much older writing system it unlocked, not for its own moment.

items.subtitle: The black-headed people of the marshes between two rivers.

time.label: From the first cities to absorption into Babylonia

items.reveal: The Sumerians were the people who built the earliest cities in southern Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, and are generally credited with inventing writing. They called themselves "the black-headed people," and their language, Sumerian, is a rare case of a language with no known relatives in any larger family. Even after Sumerian stopped being anyone's everyday spoken language, it kept being written and studied for religious and scholarly purposes for well over a thousand years afterward, much as Latin was long after Rome fell.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Arguably the first city on earth, and later the city Gilgamesh was said to rule.
items.reveal: Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, is one of the strongest candidates for the first true city in human history, growing to hold as many as forty thousand people behind a wall nearly six miles long at its peak. It was also the legendary home of Gilgamesh, the hero-king of the oldest surviving epic poem, though that poem was written down long after Uruk's height. Today the site lies in dry desert, since the Euphrates River has since shifted its course away from the ancient city.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The jackal who guards the cemetery and weighs the heart against a feather.
items.reveal: Anubis was the Egyptian god of embalming and the dead, shown with the head of a jackal or wild desert dog. He was believed to guide dead souls to judgment, where their heart was weighed on a scale against a feather representing truth — a heart heavier than the feather meant the soul would be destroyed. Egyptians gave their god of the dead this shape because real jackals were a familiar, unwelcome sight scavenging around desert cemeteries, so giving the animal to a god who protected graves turned a threat into a guardian.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Four stoppered jars for the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines — and nothing at all for the brain.
items.reveal: Canopic jars were sets of four stone or pottery containers used in Egyptian burial to hold organs removed from a body during mummification: the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines each went into its own jar, often topped with the carved head of a protective god. The heart was deliberately left inside the body, since Egyptians believed it, not the brain, was the source of thought and feeling. The brain itself was considered unimportant, and embalmers pulled it out through the nose with a hook and threw it away.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The king who wanted a tomb no one had built before.
items.reveal: Djoser was an early pharaoh of Egypt's Old Kingdom, remembered chiefly for commissioning the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental building in the world made almost entirely of cut stone rather than mud brick. Earlier Egyptian tombs had been simple flat-roofed mounds; Djoser's architect stacked six of these, each smaller than the one beneath it, into a stepped pyramid rising over 200 feet. Later Egyptians looked back on his reign as the moment large-scale stone architecture began.

items.subtitle: 2.3 million blocks, aligned to true north, tallest building on earth for 3,800 years.
items.reveal: The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the pharaoh Khufu, is made of roughly 2.3 million cut stone blocks and was, at about 480 feet tall, the tallest building on Earth for more than 3,800 years — a record unbroken until modern towers surpassed it. Its sides are aligned to true north with remarkable precision for a structure raised without any modern surveying instruments. In 2013, papyrus logbooks were discovered at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, written by a work-gang overseer named Merer, who describes hauling limestone blocks by boat for the pyramid's outer casing — the only firsthand written account of the construction ever found.

items.subtitle: Architect, physician, and vizier — later worshipped as a god.
items.reveal: Imhotep served as a top official, architect, and physician under the pharaoh Djoser, and is credited with designing the Step Pyramid, the world's first great stone monument. He was remembered so highly by later Egyptians that, over a thousand years after his death, he came to be worshipped as a god of wisdom, medicine, and healing — one of the very few non-royal Egyptians ever given that honor. No record survives of when he was born or died; everything known about him comes from evidence of his work and his later reputation, not from any biography.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A lion with a king's face, carved from the bedrock left by a quarry.
items.reveal: The Great Sphinx is a giant statue of a reclining lion with a human king's face, carved directly from a mound of bedrock left over after stone was quarried nearby to build the pyramids at Giza. It is usually credited to the pharaoh Khafre, since it lines up with his pyramid and causeway and its face resembles his other statues, though no inscription actually names its builder. Sand buried the statue up to its neck more than once over the centuries; a story carved much later claims a young prince, the future Thutmose IV, had it dug free after the Sphinx promised him the throne in a dream. Because the link to Khafre rests on inference rather than any inscription, a minority of researchers argue the Sphinx may be considerably older.

items.subtitle: Builder of the largest tomb ever raised; the Greeks called him a tyrant.
items.reveal: Khufu was the pharaoh who commissioned the Great Pyramid at Giza, the largest tomb ever built, ruling Egypt during the Old Kingdom. Later Greek writers, including the historian Herodotus, described him as a cruel tyrant who forced his people into hard labor to build his monument, though this reputation may say more about how the Greeks imagined Egypt than about Khufu's actual rule. Strangely, given the size of his monument, the only surviving portrait of Khufu is a tiny ivory statuette just three inches tall.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Low mud-brick rectangles with sloping sides over a burial shaft — the word is Arabic for bench.
items.reveal: A mastaba is a type of ancient Egyptian tomb: a low, flat-topped rectangular structure with sloping sides, built of mud brick over a burial shaft cut into the ground. The name comes from the Arabic word for "bench," since later visitors thought the low, flat shape resembled one. Egypt's first great stone pyramid, the Step Pyramid, was essentially created by stacking six mastabas of shrinking size on top of one another, so the mastaba can be thought of as the shape pyramids grew out of.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Seventy days of natron, linen, and canopic jars — the brain discarded, the heart left in place.

time.label: Old Kingdom through New Kingdom, at its most elaborate

items.reveal: Mummification was the Egyptian process of preserving a dead body so it would last for the afterlife, taking about seventy days from start to finish. Embalmers removed the internal organs, storing several of them in canopic jars, but left the heart in place since it was thought to hold a person's thoughts and character; they then packed the body with a drying salt called natron and wrapped it in many layers of linen bandages. Deliberate embalming like this had already begun in Egypt earlier than this period and continued long afterward, including into the centuries when Rome ruled Egypt, so this window marks when the practice was at its most elaborate and widespread rather than when it started or ended.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The age of pyramid-building, ended by drought and a collapse of royal power.
items.reveal: The Old Kingdom was the period when Egypt's pharaohs, ruling from the capital at Memphis, built the great pyramids, including those at Giza and Saqqara. It lasted for roughly nine centuries, spanning several dynasties of kings, before ending when royal authority collapsed and Egypt broke apart into rival regional territories. Its collapse roughly coincides with a severe, long-lasting drought that affected the whole eastern Mediterranean region, though historians still debate how much changing climate versus internal political weakness was to blame. The start and end dates given here are conventional round numbers; different Egyptologists shift them by up to a century in either direction.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Six stone platforms stacked smallest on top — the first pyramid.
items.reveal: The Step Pyramid of Djoser, at Saqqara, was ancient Egypt's first pyramid and its first large building made almost entirely of cut stone. It gets its stepped shape from six mastaba-style platforms of shrinking size, stacked directly on top of one another, rising to about 200 feet. Archaeologists can tell from the structure itself that its design changed as work went on: it started as a single flat mastaba tomb and was enlarged upward at least five separate times before reaching its final form.

items.subtitle: Sargon's capital, which gave its name to an empire and a language — and has never been found.

place.label: Somewhere on the Euphrates near modern Baghdad

items.reveal: Akkad, also spelled Agade, was the capital city of Sargon, the king who built the world's first known empire, and it gave its name to both that empire and to Akkadian, one of the most important languages of the ancient Near East. Yet despite constant mentions in ancient texts, no archaeologist has ever found the actual site of the city: its location is only guessed at from travel times and distances recorded in surviving documents, somewhere along the Euphrates near modern Baghdad. It remains one of the very few major capital cities of the ancient world that has genuinely vanished without a trace.

items.subtitle: The first state to rule Sumer, Akkad, and the lands beyond as one.

place.label: Mesopotamia from the Gulf toward the Levant

time.label: Sargon to the fall to the Gutians

items.reveal: The Akkadian Empire, founded by Sargon of Akkad, was the first state in history to rule the separate city-states of Sumer and Akkad together as a single empire, and its influence reached from the Persian Gulf toward the Mediterranean. It lasted less than two centuries before collapsing. That collapse is often linked to a sharp, sudden drought around 2200 BC, evidence for which shows up in soil and lake-sediment samples taken across the wider region, though historians also point to rebellion and invasion as contributing causes.

items.subtitle: Sargon's daughter, high priestess of the moon god, and the first author in history to sign her name.
items.reveal: Enheduanna was the daughter of Sargon of Akkad, appointed high priestess of the moon god Nanna in the city of Ur. She wrote hymns and poems addressed to the goddess Inanna and signed her own name to them, making her the earliest author in world history known to us by name, male or female. Her works survive only in copies made by scribes centuries after she lived; while most scholars accept that she was a real person and genuine author, a few argue the poems may have been credited to her name later rather than written by her personally.

items.subtitle: Mountain people out of the Zagros who finished off the Akkadian empire, and whom Sumerian scribes called a people who know no restraint.

place.label: The Zagros mountains and central Mesopotamia

items.reveal: The Gutians were a people from the Zagros Mountains, east of Mesopotamia, who swept down and helped bring about the final collapse of the Akkadian Empire, ruling parts of Mesopotamia loosely for roughly a century afterward. Nearly everything known about them comes from Sumerian scribes they had conquered, who described them in starkly unflattering terms, once calling them "a people who know no restraint" — leaving a thin and one-sided picture of who they actually were. Modern historians think a severe regional drought did at least as much damage to Akkad's power as any Gutian invasion did.

items.subtitle: The city whose king Sargon served as cupbearer before he served nobody.
items.reveal: Kish was one of the oldest and most respected cities of ancient Sumer, and according to the Sumerian King List, it was the city where kingship was restored to earth after a great flood swept the world clean. Because of this legendary status, "King of Kish" became a prestigious royal title that later rulers claimed as a mark of supreme authority, even when they had no real connection to the city itself. Sargon of Akkad is said to have started his career humbly, serving as a cupbearer to the king of Kish, before eventually building an empire that swallowed Kish along with everywhere else.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Sargon's grandson, the first Mesopotamian king to call himself a god.
items.reveal: Naram-Sin, grandson of Sargon of Akkad, ruled the Akkadian Empire at the height of its power, and was the first Mesopotamian king known to have declared himself a god during his own lifetime rather than waiting to be honored as one after death. A stone monument celebrating one of his victories, the Victory Stele, shows him larger than his soldiers, climbing a mountain over the bodies of defeated enemies while wearing the horned helmet that marked divinity in Mesopotamian art. That stele was carried off as war booty roughly a thousand years later by Elamite raiders, who took it to their own capital, Susa, where archaeologists eventually found it.

items.subtitle: A cupbearer's son, set adrift in a reed basket, who took the throne and then took everything else.
items.reveal: Sargon of Akkad rose from humble origins, said in legend to have been the son of a cupbearer, set adrift as a baby in a reed basket on a river before being found and raised by a gardener. He grew up to become cupbearer to the king of Kish himself, then seized power and went on to conquer the independent city-states of Sumer, building the first empire in world history to rule Mesopotamia as one state. The basket story survives only in a text written more than a thousand years after Sargon actually lived, and a very similar story is later told about the infant Moses in the Bible — a shared folktale pattern found across the ancient Near East, rather than proof that either story copied the other.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Great ziggurat, royal tombs full of harps and headdresses, and the city Abraham left.
items.reveal: Ur was one of the great cities of ancient Sumer, home to a massive stepped temple tower called a ziggurat and to a set of royal tombs whose occupants were buried with astonishing wealth, including golden headdresses and lyres and harps decorated with gold and lapis lazuli. It reached its political peak around 2100-2000 BC, when kings of Ur ruled much of Mesopotamia, though the site was inhabited for thousands of years both before and after that. Ur is also identified in the Bible as the hometown Abraham's family left behind, though some scholars argue the biblical "Ur of the Chaldees" actually refers to a different, more northerly town near Harran, which would make Abraham's journey to Canaan considerably shorter than the traditional route.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Told to leave his country for a land he would be shown.
items.reveal: Abraham is remembered in the Bible as the patriarch chosen by God to found a new nation, leaving his home in Mesopotamia and traveling first to Harran and then on to Canaan, in a journey undertaken on the promise of a land he had not yet seen. His story is foundational to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam alike, each of which traces its origins back to him. No source outside the Bible mentions Abraham, and the dates usually given for him come from adding up generations listed in biblical genealogies rather than from any independent record; scholars who think a historical patriarch lies behind the stories generally place such a figure sometime in the Middle Bronze Age, roughly 2000 to 1500 BC.

items.subtitle: A family packs up and walks northwest along the Euphrates.
items.reveal: According to Genesis, Abraham's family first migrated from Ur to the town of Harran, and it was from Harran that Abraham himself set out for Canaan after receiving God's call and promise, traveling with his wife, his nephew Lot, and their household along a route roughly following the Euphrates River northwest before turning south. Genesis says he was seventy-five years old when he made this second leg of the journey. As with the rest of the patriarchal stories, the dates given here follow traditional biblical chronology rather than any independent historical record.

items.prompt: Jacob's family goes down to Egypt
items.subtitle: Seventy people leave a famine in Canaan for grain and pasture in the delta, and stay for centuries.

place.label: From Canaan to Goshen in the eastern delta

time.label: Kitchen scheme: 430 years before the Exodus

items.reveal: According to Genesis, a severe famine in Canaan drove Jacob and his large extended family, about seventy people in all, to migrate to Egypt, where his son Joseph had risen to power and could offer them grain and pastureland in the delta region called Goshen. What began as a temporary move became permanent, and the family's descendants remained in Egypt for centuries afterward. Interestingly, this lines up with a real historical pattern: in exactly this period, the eastern Nile delta was genuinely filling up with Semitic-speaking settlers from Canaan, the same population that would soon rule Egypt as the Hyksos, making this one of the few points where the patriarchal narrative and outside archaeological evidence appear to touch, even though the connection falls out of the chronology rather than being something historians set out to prove.

items.subtitle: A caravan town on the road between the rivers and the sea, where Abraham's father stopped and stayed.
items.reveal: Harran was a busy caravan town in what is now southern Turkey, sitting on a trade route that connected Mesopotamia to the Mediterranean coast. According to Genesis, it was here that Abraham's father, Terah, settled the family after leaving Ur, and where Abraham himself lived for a time before continuing on to Canaan. Harran was also a major center of worship for the moon god — the same god whose priestess, Enheduanna, served at Ur, at the opposite end of the very same trade road.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The son promised to a hundred-year-old man, and nearly given back.
items.reveal: Isaac was the son promised to Abraham and his wife Sarah in their old age, born when Abraham was said to be a hundred years old. In one of the Bible's most dramatic stories, God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac, only to stop him at the last moment and provide a ram instead. Isaac went on to become the second of the three biblical patriarchs, living mainly around Beersheba and Hebron in Canaan; as with the rest of these figures, his traditional dates come from biblical genealogy rather than any outside record.

items.subtitle: Bought a birthright with lentil stew, wrestled all night, and got a new name out of it.
items.reveal: Jacob, later renamed Israel, was the son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham, remembered for tricking his older twin brother Esau out of his birthright with a bowl of lentil stew and later wrestling all night with a mysterious figure, after which he received the new name Israel. He fled to Harran to escape his brother's anger, working there for years for his uncle Laban before returning to Canaan with two wives, many children, and great flocks. His twelve sons became the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel, making Jacob the hinge figure connecting the patriarchal stories to the rest of the Hebrew Bible.

items.subtitle: Sold by his brothers, jailed on a lie, and made second in Egypt for reading a dream about cows.
items.reveal: Joseph was Jacob's favorite son, sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous older brothers after he described dreams suggesting he would one day rule over them. In Egypt he was falsely accused and imprisoned, but gained his freedom by correctly interpreting the pharaoh's dream about seven fat cows and seven starving ones as a warning of coming famine, and was rewarded with the position of chief minister. No Egyptian record names Joseph, but the general picture — a Semitic-speaking foreigner rising to high office in Egypt — fits well with the Second Intermediate Period, when Semitic-speaking Hyksos rulers actually controlled the Nile delta.

items.subtitle: Seven fat years to store grain against seven lean ones.
items.reveal: After correctly predicting seven years of plentiful harvests followed by seven years of famine, Joseph was placed in charge of storing Egypt's surplus grain during the good years, so there would be enough food to survive the lean ones that followed. The plan worked, and it was this stockpiled grain that later drew his starving brothers to Egypt to buy food, not knowing that the official they were dealing with was the brother they had sold into slavery. The biblical account never names which pharaoh Joseph served, calling him only "Pharaoh," so his identity, if he existed as a specific historical person, remains unresolved.

items.subtitle: Childless into old age, she laughed at the promise of a son and then had one.
items.reveal: Sarah, originally named Sarai, was Abraham's wife, who traveled with him from Ur through Harran and into Canaan but remained childless well into old age. When told she would finally bear a son in her nineties, she laughed at the idea, and the resulting child was named Isaac, meaning "he laughs," in honor of that moment. Both her name and her husband's changed at the same time, as a sign of a covenant with God: Abram became Abraham, and Sarai became Sarah. She died at Hebron and was buried in a cave Abraham purchased there, remembered as the first piece of land the family ever owned in Canaan.

items.subtitle: A minor town on the Euphrates, until Hammurabi made it an empire's capital.

time.label: The Old Babylonian dynasty, from its founding to its fall to a Hittite raid

items.reveal: Babylon began as a fairly minor town on the Euphrates River, but rose to become one of the most powerful cities in the ancient world under King Hammurabi in the 18th century BC, who made it the capital of an empire covering much of Mesopotamia and gave it the law code he is remembered for today. His descendants continued ruling the city for about a century and a half after his death, though the empire gradually weakened, until a raiding Hittite army arrived all the way from Anatolia, sacked Babylon, and ended the dynasty around 1595 BC. The city survived the collapse but faded in importance for the next thousand years, until it was rebuilt on a far grander scale under the later Neo-Babylonian dynasty.

items.subtitle: 282 laws cut into a black pillar, so that the strong might not oppress the weak.
items.reveal: The Code of Hammurabi is a set of 282 laws, covering everything from theft and property to marriage and injury, carved into a tall black stone pillar by order of the Babylonian king Hammurabi, who said its purpose was so "the strong might not oppress the weak." It was not the first Mesopotamian law code — an earlier one issued by King Ur-Nammu survives from roughly three centuries before — but it is by far the most complete and famous to survive. The pillar itself was found not in Babylon but far away in Susa, in what is now Iran, where Elamite raiders had carried it off as plunder roughly six centuries after it was originally carved.

items.subtitle: Inherited one city and left an empire, and wanted to be remembered for his laws.
items.reveal: Hammurabi inherited the throne of Babylon when it was just one modest city-state among many rivals in Mesopotamia, and through a mix of alliances and military conquest, transformed it into the capital of a large empire before his death. He is remembered above all for his law code, a long list of specific rulings he clearly wanted future generations to remember him by, since he had it carved onto a stone pillar for public display. Historians actually disagree by as much as 140 years over exactly when Hammurabi reigned, since Mesopotamian chronology this far back is pieced together from later king-lists cross-checked against ancient records of when the planet Venus was visible, and different ways of anchoring those records to a fixed calendar produce different results.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A local city god promoted to king of the gods when his city was promoted too.

time.label: From Hammurabi's elevation of the cult to the Hellenistic period

items.reveal: Marduk began as a relatively minor local god of the city of Babylon. As Babylon itself grew from an unimportant town into the capital of a powerful empire under Hammurabi, Marduk's status rose right along with it, until he was eventually elevated to king of all the Mesopotamian gods. The Babylonian creation myth, the Enuma Elish, was rewritten to make Marduk the hero who defeats the chaos-monster Tiamat and creates the world — a clear case of religious belief being reshaped to match political power.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Hammurabi's dynasty, which outlived him by a century and a half and then fell to raiders from the north.
items.reveal: The Old Babylonian Empire was the state built by Hammurabi, centered on his capital city of Babylon and covering much of southern and central Mesopotamia at its height. His descendants continued to rule it for about a century and a half after his death, though the empire gradually shrank and weakened over that time. It finally came to an end when a Hittite army, arriving all the way from Anatolia (modern Turkey), raided down the Euphrates River, sacked the city of Babylon itself, and then withdrew home without staying to rule.

items.prompt: Dividing the hour into sixty minutes
items.subtitle: Counting by sixties, from people who watched the sky for a living.
items.reveal: Ancient Mesopotamian scholars, especially astronomers who spent their careers tracking the movements of the sun, moon, and stars, used a counting system based on sixty rather than the ten most people count by today. That system is why, to this day, an hour is divided into sixty minutes, a minute into sixty seconds, and a circle into 360 degrees. The base-sixty system is actually older than Babylon itself, going back to the Sumerians before it, meaning that every time a clock or a compass is read, an idea invented in ancient Mesopotamia is still quietly in use.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A city, a god, and a people, all wearing the same name.

time.label: Occupied until destroyed by the Medes

items.reveal: Ashur was the great religious and ancestral capital of the Assyrian people, sitting on the Tigris River in northern Mesopotamia — the city, its patron god, and the people themselves were all called by the very same name. Even after Assyria's kings moved their political capital elsewhere, first to Nimrud and later to Nineveh, Ashur remained the empire's sacred heart, and no Assyrian king could be properly crowned anywhere else. The city was finally destroyed in 614 BC by the Medes, an Iranian people allied with Babylon against a weakening Assyrian empire.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Made from clay to be the king's equal, he lives with the animals until a woman civilises him, and then the animals will not have him back.

place.label: Uruk and the steppe beyond it

items.reveal: Enkidu is a character in the Epic of Gilgamesh, described as a wild man created by the gods out of clay to be a match for the too-powerful King Gilgamesh of Uruk. In the story, Enkidu starts out living among wild animals on the open steppe, until a woman is sent to introduce him to human ways of life, after which, strangely, the animals he once ran with no longer accept him as one of their own. He becomes Gilgamesh's closest companion, and it is Enkidu's death partway through the epic that sends the grieving Gilgamesh on a desperate quest for immortality, making their friendship one of the oldest deep friendships recorded in world literature.

items.subtitle: Two parts god and one part man, king of a walled city, and very bad at accepting death.

time.label: Traditional reign in the Sumerian King List

items.reveal: Gilgamesh is the legendary king of the Sumerian city of Uruk at the center of the oldest great work of literature to survive, the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which he is described as two-thirds god and one-third human, immensely strong, and utterly unwilling to accept that he, too, must eventually die. A king of Uruk by that name probably really existed — a contemporary ruler's inscription mentions him — but almost everything memorable about him comes from legend rather than history. The ancient Sumerian King List, which credits many early kings with implausibly long reigns, gives Gilgamesh a reign of 126 years.

items.subtitle: Five separate short tales about a king of Uruk — the cedar forest, the bull of heaven, the death — with no single story joining them.

place.label: Nippur and the Sumerian scribal schools

items.reveal: Long before the famous single Epic of Gilgamesh was assembled, Sumerian scribes wrote and copied out five separate shorter poems about the legendary king of Uruk — stories like his journey to a distant cedar forest, his fight against the monstrous Bull of Heaven, and his grief at Enkidu's death — with no single narrative yet tying them together. These are the oldest surviving layer of the Gilgamesh tradition, roughly 4,000 years old, and most surviving copies were written out by trainee scribes as writing exercises in the scribal schools of the city of Nippur. It would be many centuries before a later editor combined material like this into the unified epic read today.

items.subtitle: Goddess of love and of war at once, and of the planet Venus — Gilgamesh refuses to marry her and lists what happened to the others.

time.label: From Sumerian Inanna to the Hellenistic period

items.reveal: Ishtar was one of the most important goddesses of ancient Mesopotamia, associated at once with love and with war, and identified with the planet Venus. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, when Ishtar proposes marriage to the hero, he refuses her bluntly, listing all her previous lovers and the terrible fates that befell each one. Ishtar was actually the same goddess worshipped across many cultures under different names over three thousand years: she was called Inanna by the Sumerians, Ishtar by the Akkadians and Babylonians, and Astarte by the Canaanites, and she is probably an ancestor of the Greek goddess Aphrodite.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.prompt: The Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh
items.subtitle: A donkey caravan of tin and cloth left Ashur; forty days later it arrived here, and somebody wrote it all down.

time.label: Height of the Old Assyrian trade network

items.reveal: Kanesh was a trading colony in central Anatolia (modern Turkey) where merchants from the Assyrian city of Ashur set up a permanent settlement to run a long-distance trade in tin and textiles, carried back and forth by donkey caravan over a journey of roughly forty days. More than 20,000 clay tablets have been recovered from the houses of these merchant families, recording everything from business contracts and shipment invoices to personal letters, including wives writing home to complain about money. It is, as a result, the best-documented commercial economy anywhere in the Bronze Age world.
items.outsideBook: Not in the book's pronunciation guide; enrichment only.

items.subtitle: A palace of 300 rooms on the middle Euphrates, and an archive its conqueror forgot to burn.
items.reveal: Mari was a wealthy city-state on the middle Euphrates River, home to a royal palace of some 300 rooms that was, for its time, one of the grandest buildings in the ancient Near East. The city changed hands violently more than once: the Assyrian king Shamshi-Adad seized it and installed his son as ruler, the local prince Zimri-Lim later won it back, and finally the Babylonian king Hammurabi conquered and destroyed it for good. When Hammurabi's forces sacked Mari, they left behind roughly 25,000 clay tablets in the ruins, an archive that has become one of historians' main sources for piecing together the politics of this whole period.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Assyria's first turn at empire — traders first, conquerors second.

time.label: Old Assyrian period, ending with Hammurabi's ascendancy

items.reveal: The Old Assyrian kingdom was the first period in which the city of Ashur, in northern Mesopotamia, built real regional power and influence, though it did so mainly through trade rather than conquest, establishing merchant colonies like the one at Kanesh in Anatolia. Its most independently powerful ruler was Shamshi-Adad I, who briefly built a substantial territorial kingdom of his own. Assyrian independence collapsed after Shamshi-Adad's death, as Hammurabi of Babylon rose to dominate the region instead, though the broader "Old Assyrian" period as a cultural label is sometimes stretched later, to around 1360 BC.

items.subtitle: An exiled prince who came back, took the north, and styled himself King of the Whole World.
items.reveal: Shamshi-Adad I was an Amorite prince who spent time in exile before returning to seize control of northern Mesopotamia, eventually building a substantial kingdom and giving himself the grand title "King of the Whole World." He ruled as an older, rival contemporary of Hammurabi of Babylon, who paid him a wary respect while he lived but expanded north into his territory almost immediately after his death. His impressive title was not really a boast about his own conquests so much as inherited ceremonial language, first used centuries earlier by Sargon of Akkad.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The old tales rewritten as one poem on twelve tablets, framed around a friend's death and the refusal to accept it.
items.reveal: The Epic of Gilgamesh, as it is most commonly read today, is a unified poem spread across twelve clay tablets that combines and reshapes the older, separate Sumerian tales about Gilgamesh into one continuous story, built around his grief at the death of his friend Enkidu and his refusal to accept his own mortality. Babylonian tradition credits its compilation to a scribe named Sin-leqi-unninni, one of the earliest editors in history known to us by name. This standard version — the one that includes a famous flood story and Gilgamesh's search for eternal life — was composed roughly eight hundred years after the original Sumerian poems it draws on, and the copy modern readers actually rely on was recovered from the ruined library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, centuries later still.

items.subtitle: Warned by a god to pull down his house and build a boat, he survives the flood and releases a dove, a swallow, and a raven.

place.label: Shuruppak, his city in the story

items.reveal: Utnapishtim is a character in the Epic of Gilgamesh who survived a great flood sent by the gods to destroy humanity, after being warned in advance by a god to tear down his house and build a boat instead. Once the flood receded, he released a dove, a swallow, and finally a raven to check whether dry land had reappeared, and as a reward for surviving, the gods granted him eternal life. When the British scholar George Smith first translated this flood story at the British Museum in 1872 and realized it closely resembled the biblical flood of Noah but was clearly older, it caused a public sensation, and historians still debate today whether the two accounts share a common source, a shared cultural memory, or a direct borrowing from one to the other.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A watertight brick tank forty feet long, sealed with tar, on the highest ground in the city.

time.label: Built early in the city's life

items.reveal: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is a large, carefully built brick tank, about forty feet long, waterproofed with a layer of natural tar and positioned on the highest, most prominent ground in the whole city. It sat within a larger complex of small rooms and what may have been a nearby granary, suggesting it was part of a bigger ceremonial or administrative center at the heart of the city. Its size, careful construction, and central location strongly suggest it was used for ritual bathing rather than everyday washing, though this is really an educated guess based on design and placement rather than something any surviving text confirms, since no writing from the Indus civilization has ever been deciphered.

items.subtitle: The first of these cities to be dug up, and so the one that named the whole civilization.
items.reveal: Harappa was a major city of the ancient Indus Valley civilization, built like its sister cities with carefully planned street grids, standardized brick sizes, and covered drains. It was also the first Indus site excavated by archaeologists, and as a result the entire civilization came to be named after it, the "Harappan civilization." Unfortunately, much of the ancient city was destroyed before serious archaeology even began: in the 1850s, British engineers building the Lahore-Multan railway dug up and carted away huge quantities of its ancient fired brick to use as track ballast, so that roughly a hundred miles of railway line now sit atop material quarried straight from the ruins.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Grid-planned cities with brick drains, standard weights, and no palaces or royal tombs anyone has found.

place.label: The Indus basin and northwest India

items.reveal: The Indus Valley civilization was a Bronze Age society spread across what is now Pakistan and northwest India, with cities built to careful grid plans, sophisticated brick-lined drains running beneath their streets, and a set of standardized weights used consistently across hundreds of miles. At its height it covered a larger area than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, yet it remained almost completely unknown to modern archaeology until excavations first uncovered it in 1921. Strikingly, unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, no palace, royal tomb, or clear image of a king has ever been found anywhere in the civilization, an absence considered a real and still-unexplained feature of Indus society, not simply a gap in digging.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.prompt: The abandonment of the Indus cities
items.subtitle: The drains stop being cleaned, the weights stop matching, and people drift east.
items.reveal: Toward the end of its mature period, the great cities of the Indus Valley civilization gradually stopped being maintained in the careful way they once were — street drains went uncleaned, and the standardized weights used in trade became less consistent — and much of the population appears to have drifted away, resettling further east. Older explanations blaming this decline on an invasion by Aryan peoples destroying the cities are no longer accepted by most historians, since no layer of destruction from warfare has ever been found at Indus sites. The leading explanations today point instead to environmental causes, especially the drying up of the Ghaggar-Hakra river system and a weakening of the seasonal monsoon rains the civilization depended on.

items.subtitle: Four hundred signs, mostly on stamp seals, mostly in strings of five, and still unread.
items.reveal: The Indus script consists of around four hundred distinct symbols, found mostly stamped on small carved seals, usually arranged in short strings averaging about five signs each. Despite more than a century of study, nobody has ever managed to read it: unlike the Rosetta Stone, no bilingual inscription pairing the Indus script with a known language has ever been found to provide a way in. A serious minority of researchers even argue the symbols may not represent language at all, but were instead a system of non-linguistic symbols, such as clan or trade marks.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A port town with what may be the world's oldest dock, and a bead factory.
items.reveal: Lothal was a port town of the Indus Valley civilization, built around a large brick-lined basin that may be the oldest known dock in the world, connecting the settlement to a nearby tidal channel and the sea beyond, alongside a substantial workshop for making beads. Archaeologists have found Harappan seals as far away as Mesopotamia and Mesopotamian-style goods within the Indus region, and Lothal, sitting on the coast, looks like one of the key points where these two distant trading worlds actually met. Whether its famous brick basin was truly a working dock or simply a large reservoir for irrigation and water storage remains disputed among archaeologists.

items.subtitle: The Mound of the Dead — a city of 40,000 with covered sewers, abandoned without a battle.
items.reveal: Mohenjo-daro — whose modern name, in the local Sindhi language, means "Mound of the Dead," since nobody knows what its own inhabitants called it — was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley civilization, home to as many as 40,000 people at its height. It was built with remarkably advanced sanitation for its time: nearly every house had its own private bathroom connected to a covered street drain, a level of household plumbing that even the city of Rome, two thousand years later, could not match. Unlike many ancient cities, Mohenjo-daro shows no clear signs of having been destroyed in war; it appears instead to have been gradually abandoned.

items.subtitle: An empress drinking tea under a mulberry tree when a cocoon falls into her cup and starts to unwind.

time.label: Traditional date, as consort of the Yellow Emperor

items.reveal: According to Chinese legend, Lei Zu was an empress who discovered how to make silk after a silkworm cocoon accidentally fell from a mulberry tree into her cup of hot tea, and as she watched, the heat began unwinding it into a single continuous thread. She was said to be the wife of the legendary Yellow Emperor, one of the mythical founding rulers of Chinese civilization. Like much of the earliest Chinese tradition, this story was written down long after the events it describes are supposed to have happened, and the actual archaeological evidence for silk-making in China is considerably older than the legend that explains its invention.

items.subtitle: Ox shoulder blades and turtle shells, drilled, heated until they crack, and the answer read off the cracks.

time.label: Late Shang, from the reign of Wu Ding

items.reveal: Oracle bones were ox shoulder blades and turtle shells used by kings of China's late Shang dynasty to ask questions of their ancestors and gods, usually about matters like harvests, illness, or warfare. Diviners drilled small hollows into the bone or shell, applied intense heat until it cracked, and then read the pattern of cracks as an answer, sometimes carving the question and result directly onto the surface in early Chinese writing. The bones were rediscovered by accident in 1899, when a Chinese scholar noticed that "dragon bones" being sold as a traditional medicine ingredient in Beijing pharmacies were covered with ancient writing; that writing turned out to be the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, making it the only one of the world's earliest writing systems still in everyday use today.

items.subtitle: Bronze vessels, chariots, human sacrifice, and kings who asked the future questions in writing.
items.reveal: The Shang dynasty was an early Chinese royal dynasty centered on the North China Plain, known for elaborate cast-bronze ritual vessels, the use of war chariots, the practice of human sacrifice at royal tombs, and kings who had questions about the future carved onto bone and shell to be answered by their ancestors. Unlike the legendary Xia dynasty said to have come before it, the Shang is confirmed as historically real by its own surviving written records, especially the oracle-bone inscriptions found at its last capital. The dynasty's precise end date, usually given as 1046 BC, actually rests on a reconstructed astronomical record connected to its conquest by the following Zhou dynasty, and remains disputed by scholars by up to a century in either direction.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Wine vessels and cauldrons cast in piece-moulds, covered in a staring animal face nobody can name.
items.reveal: Shang ritual bronzes were elaborate wine vessels, cooking cauldrons, and other ceremonial containers, cast in bronze and used in ceremonies honoring royal ancestors. Chinese bronze-workers made them using a technique called piece-mold casting, building a mold out of several separate carved sections, rather than the lost-wax method used almost everywhere else in the ancient world, which is part of why Shang bronze decoration tends to look so sharp-edged and geometric. Many of these bronzes are covered in a staring animal-like face design known as the taotie, whose exact meaning is still debated; the tomb of the royal consort Fu Hao alone contained around 200 such bronze vessels.

items.subtitle: Boil the cocoon, kill the moth inside, and reel off a single thread half a mile long.

time.label: From the earliest silk finds through the Shang

items.reveal: Making silk starts with silkworms, the caterpillars of a particular moth, which spin cocoons out of a single continuous thread; to harvest it, the cocoons are boiled, which kills the developing moth inside and loosens the thread so it can be carefully unwound in one piece, sometimes stretching half a mile long from a single cocoon. Actual surviving fragments of woven silk fabric date back to around 2700 BC, found at the site of Qianshanyang in China, while some archaeologists claim even earlier chemical traces of silk protein from as far back as 3600 BC. China guarded the secret of silk-making so successfully that it held a near-total monopoly on its production for roughly three thousand years.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Overthrew a tyrant and founded a dynasty, and is said to have offered himself as the sacrifice to end a seven-year drought.

place.label: Bo, the first Shang capital, on the eastern plain

time.label: Union of the traditional and reconstructed dates

items.reveal: T'ang is remembered as the founder of the Shang dynasty, who overthrew the last, tyrannical ruler of the legendary Xia dynasty before him and established Shang rule from his capital at Bo, on China's eastern plain. According to legend, when a severe drought gripped his kingdom for seven years, T'ang offered to sacrifice himself to end the suffering of his people, a story meant to illustrate his selfless virtue as a ruler. Traditional Chinese chronology dates his reign to 1766 BC, while modern reconstructed chronology places it closer to 1600 BC; interestingly, the Shang's own account of its history, as preserved in tradition, never actually mentions the Xia dynasty T'ang is said to have replaced.

items.subtitle: Credited with the compass, the calendar, medicine, boats, and writing — which is one clue about how historical he is.
items.reveal: The Yellow Emperor, or Huangdi, is a legendary early ruler credited by Chinese tradition with inventing an extraordinary range of things at once, including the compass, the calendar, medicine, boats, and writing — a suspiciously long list that is itself one clue that he is a legendary culture hero rather than a single historical person. The precise-looking dates traditionally given for his reign were actually worked out by historians of the later Han dynasty, calculating backward roughly 2,500 years after the events he is supposed to represent were said to have happened. He is best understood as a symbolic founding figure for Chinese civilization, similar to how other cultures credit a single legendary ancestor with inventing agriculture or fire.

items.subtitle: Farmers with iron tools and yams spreading south and east across a continent over fifteen centuries.

place.label: From the Nigeria-Cameroon border across central and southern Africa

items.reveal: Starting from a homeland near the modern border of Nigeria and Cameroon, farming peoples speaking early Bantu languages gradually spread out across central, eastern, and southern Africa over roughly fifteen centuries, bringing with them iron tools and crops like yams. This was not a single organized migration but countless separate movements of small farming communities settling new land generation after generation. Historians have pieced the story together mainly from patterns in how related Bantu languages differ from each other today, combined with archaeological finds of pottery and iron tools, rather than from any written record; the scale of the spread was enormous, and roughly a third of Africa's population speaks a Bantu language today.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The oldest known city south of the Sahara, built of mud brick on an island in the Niger flood plain.

time.label: Occupation of the site (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: Djenné-Djenno, on an island in the flood plain of the Niger River in what is now Mali, is the oldest known city south of the Sahara, built up almost entirely from mud brick. Excavations beginning in 1977 showed that the city grew into a substantial settlement well before any Arab or trans-Saharan trade routes reached it, meaning it developed as an independent African urban center rather than as a product of outside contact. Unlike most ancient capitals, it shows no sign of ever having had a royal palace or a fortified citadel at its center.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Life-size terracotta heads with triangular eyes, found in tin-mining spoil heaps, made by people who were already smelting iron.
items.reveal: The Nok culture, centered on the Jos Plateau in what is now central Nigeria, is known chiefly for life-size terracotta sculpted heads and figures with distinctive triangular-shaped eyes, among the earliest figurative sculpture found anywhere in sub-Saharan Africa. The people who made them were already smelting iron, and many of the surviving terracotta pieces were actually discovered by chance in the waste heaps left behind by later tin-mining operations. Because so many pieces have been dug up by looters rather than recovered through careful archaeological excavation, much of the original context has been lost, which is part of why dating the culture precisely remains difficult.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Furnaces in the forest, with no Bronze Age in between.

place.label: Nigeria, Niger, and the Central African fringe

items.reveal: In much of West Africa, ironworking appears in the archaeological record with no earlier stage of bronze or copper metalworking coming before it; communities went directly from working stone tools to smelting iron. Whether the knowledge of ironworking spread south across the Sahara from Carthage and the Mediterranean world, or was invented independently within West Africa itself, remains genuinely unresolved among historians, and some claimed dates from the site of Termit in Niger would push the origins of West African iron even earlier, though these are disputed. What is fairly clear is that skipping a separate "Bronze Age" stage entirely was common across much of the African continent.

items.subtitle: A town buried under volcanic ash with its frescoes intact, its pots stacked — and no bodies.
items.reveal: Akrotiri was a Bronze Age Minoan town on the island of Thera (modern Santorini), buried and preserved under a thick layer of volcanic ash when the island's volcano erupted catastrophically. Excavations have found the town remarkably intact, with detailed wall paintings, or frescoes, still on the walls and pottery still neatly stacked in storage, yet almost no human remains have been found. This suggests that, unlike the more famous Roman town of Pompeii, Akrotiri's residents had enough advance warning, probably from earthquakes before the eruption, to escape with their lives; the exact date of the eruption is tied to one of the sharpest ongoing arguments in ancient chronology.
items.outsideBook: Not in the book's pronunciation guide; enrichment only.

items.subtitle: Three figures, one bull, and a vault over the horns that may or may not be physically possible.
items.reveal: This wall painting from the palace of Knossos on Crete shows a scene repeated often in Minoan art: a bull charging with lowered horns while human figures interact with it, in this case appearing to vault directly over its back. Bulls appear constantly throughout Minoan art and architecture, from horn-shaped decorations on rooftops to cups shaped like bulls' heads, suggesting the animal held deep religious or symbolic importance for Minoan society. Whether the leap shown here depicts an actual dangerous sport people really performed, a purely religious ritual, or simply an artistic convention that was never meant to be physically real, is still debated by historians.

items.subtitle: Twelve hundred rooms on five storeys around a central court, with light wells and flushing drains.
items.reveal: The palace at Knossos, on the island of Crete, was an enormous complex of some 1,200 rooms spread across five stories, arranged around a large central courtyard and featuring advanced engineering for its time, including light wells that let sunlight reach interior rooms and drains that could flush away waste. An earlier version of the palace was destroyed, probably by an earthquake, around 1700 BC, and was then rebuilt on an even grander scale. Much of what visitors see and photograph at the site today is actually a modern reconstruction in reinforced concrete, built in the 1920s by the archaeologist Arthur Evans based on his own interpretation of the ruins.

items.subtitle: The Minoan script — we can pronounce many of the signs and still understand nothing.
items.reveal: Linear A was the writing system used by the Minoan civilization of Bronze Age Crete. Because a later script called Linear B, used to write an early form of Greek, borrowed many of the same symbols and was successfully deciphered in 1952, scholars can confidently sound out how most Linear A signs were pronounced. The problem is that the language those sounds spell out simply isn't Greek, or any other language anyone has been able to identify, making Linear A one of the rare cases in archaeology of a decipherment that stalls at the very last step: readable sounds attached to an unknown language.
items.outsideBook: Not in the book's pronunciation guide; enrichment only.

items.subtitle: The palaces burn, and the next records from Knossos are written in Greek.

time.label: Destruction of the palaces and Mycenaean takeover

items.reveal: Sometime in the fifteenth century BC, the great palaces of Minoan Crete, including the one at Knossos, were destroyed by fire, marking the effective end of Minoan civilization as an independent power. Historians have blamed the destruction on a volcanic eruption, an earthquake, and an invasion by the mainland Greek Mycenaeans, though the volcanic eruption of Thera is now generally considered too early to have been the direct cause. What is certain is that afterward, the records kept at Knossos switch from the undeciphered Minoan script, Linear A, to Linear B, an early form of Greek, showing that Greek-speaking Mycenaeans had taken control of the island.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Europe's first civilization: sailors, frescoes full of dolphins and octopuses, and towns without walls.
items.reveal: The Minoans were the Bronze Age civilization centered on the island of Crete, generally considered Europe's first advanced civilization, known for skilled seafaring, vivid wall paintings full of dolphins, octopuses, and other sea life, and towns that, unlike most ancient settlements, were often built without defensive walls. Their grandest palaces, including the one at Knossos, were built starting around 1950 BC. The name "Minoan" itself is not what these people called themselves; it was coined in 1900 by the archaeologist Arthur Evans, based on the legendary King Minos, since their own writing has never been deciphered and their real name for themselves is unknown.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A tribute of fourteen Athenian children, a maze nobody escapes, and a ball of thread.

time.label: The Bronze Age setting the Greeks assigned to the story

items.reveal: According to Greek legend, King Minos of Crete kept a monstrous creature called the Minotaur, half man and half bull, imprisoned within an inescapable maze called the Labyrinth beneath his palace at Knossos, and forced the city of Athens to send a tribute of fourteen young men and women every so often to be fed to it. The hero Theseus finally killed the Minotaur and found his way back out of the maze using a ball of thread given to him by the princess Ariadne. The story survives only in Greek sources written roughly a thousand years after the Bronze Age setting it describes, but many historians think it may preserve a folk memory of a real period when mainland Greeks paid tribute to a more powerful Crete, and the actual palace at Knossos really was a maze-like, confusing complex of rooms.

items.subtitle: An island blows its centre out, drops ash across the eastern Mediterranean, and sends a wave at Crete.
items.reveal: The volcanic island of Thera, now called Santorini, erupted catastrophically sometime in the Bronze Age, blasting out the center of the island, scattering volcanic ash across much of the eastern Mediterranean, and very likely sending a destructive wave toward the nearby coast of Crete. Exactly when this happened is one of the sharpest, most heavily argued dating disputes in all of archaeology: radiocarbon dating of a tree branch buried in the ash points to around 1610 BC, while comparisons with dated Egyptian pottery found nearby suggest a date almost a century later, closer to 1500 BC. Because so many other Aegean Bronze Age dates are calculated relative to this one eruption, resolving the dispute would reshape the timeline of the whole region.

items.subtitle: A vizier who took the throne, moved the capital, and left his son a warning that the men who eat your bread are the ones who plot against you.

place.label: Itjtawy, near Lisht, at the mouth of the Faiyum

items.reveal: Amenemhet I began his career as a vizier, one of the pharaoh's chief officials, before seizing the Egyptian throne himself and founding a new dynasty. He moved Egypt's capital to a new city called Itjtawy, near the entrance to the Faiyum region, positioning it more centrally between Upper and Lower Egypt. He was assassinated in a palace conspiracy, the very event that opens one of ancient Egypt's most famous stories, the Tale of Sinuhe, but not before advising his son and successor, in writing, to trust no one, warning that even the men who share your bread may be plotting against you.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A delta port full of Canaanite houses, Canaanite burials, and one wall of Minoan frescoes.

time.label: Levantine settlement through the Hyksos capital

items.reveal: Avaris was a bustling port city in Egypt's eastern Nile delta, where archaeologists have found houses, burial customs, and pottery styles typical of Canaan rather than Egypt, showing a large community of Semitic-speaking settlers living there. It eventually became the capital of the Hyksos, foreign kings who ruled northern Egypt for roughly a century. Surprisingly, one part of the site has also turned up wall paintings in a clearly Minoan artistic style, similar to those on Crete far across the Mediterranean, a discovery made in the 1990s that historians still have not fully explained; centuries later, the pharaoh Ramesses II would build his own great capital on this same ground.

items.prompt: The war chariot comes to Egypt
items.subtitle: A light spoked-wheel platform pulled by two horses, with a bow that shoots through armour.
items.reveal: The war chariot, a lightweight platform on two spoked wheels pulled by a team of horses, was introduced into Egypt during the period when foreign Hyksos rulers controlled the delta, along with a powerful new weapon, the composite bow, capable of shooting through armor that had previously offered good protection. Egyptian forces initially lost battles to this superior technology, but they went on to adopt and master it themselves. The chariot-based army that later Egyptian pharaohs used to build an empire across Syria and the Levant was directly built around the very technology the Hyksos had brought with them.

items.subtitle: Rulers of foreign lands — Semitic-speaking kings who took the delta while Egypt was divided.

place.label: The eastern Nile delta, ruled from Avaris

time.label: Fifteenth Dynasty rule in the delta

items.reveal: The Hyksos, whose name means roughly "rulers of foreign lands," were a group of Semitic-speaking kings who took control of Egypt's Nile delta while the country was politically divided and weak, ruling from their capital at Avaris for about a century. The ancient Egyptian historian Manetho later described their arrival as a sudden, violent invasion, but modern archaeology tells a different story: it shows Semitic-speaking Levantine peoples settling gradually in the delta over several generations, building up in numbers and influence long before any Hyksos king actually took power. Their rule was eventually ended when Egyptian kings based in Thebes, in the south, drove them out and reunified the country.

items.subtitle: The capital of Kush, with a mud-brick temple the size of a cathedral and royal tombs ringed by hundreds of sacrificed retainers.

time.label: Kingdom of Kerma, until conquered by Thutmose I

items.reveal: Kerma, in what is now northern Sudan, was the capital of the kingdom of Kush, an African state that at times rivaled Egypt itself in power. Its most impressive structure was a massive mud-brick temple, called a deffufa, roughly the size of a cathedral, which still stands today, while its royal tombs were surrounded by the burials of hundreds of retainers apparently sacrificed to accompany the king into the afterlife. Kush was no minor backwater: during periods when Egypt was weak and divided, Kerma's kings took back territory in Lower Nubia and even allied with the Hyksos rulers of the delta against Thebes, before the kingdom was eventually conquered by the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose I.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Egypt put back together after a century of famine and warlords — later Egyptians called it the classical age.
items.reveal: The Middle Kingdom was the period when Egypt was reunified and stabilized after roughly a century of famine, weak central authority, and competing local rulers that followed the collapse of the Old Kingdom. Later Egyptians looked back on this era as a golden age, and its literature, including famous works like the Tale of Sinuhe and the Eloquent Peasant, became standard schoolroom texts that Egyptian scribes kept copying out for a thousand years afterward. Politically, the Middle Kingdom also saw Egypt expand its control southward, building fortresses to secure the valuable Nubian gold trade.

items.prompt: The Egyptian forts at the Second Cataract
items.subtitle: Mud-brick walls forty feet thick strung along the river, to hold the gold road and stop Nubians coming north.

place.label: Buhen, Semna, and the Second Cataract, Lower Nubia

items.reveal: Along the Nile's Second Cataract in Lower Nubia, Egyptian kings of the Middle Kingdom built a chain of massive fortresses, with mud-brick walls up to forty feet thick, to control the valuable trade route bringing gold north from the south and to keep Nubian peoples from moving into Egyptian territory. These forts, at sites including Buhen and Semna, represented some of the most sophisticated military engineering anywhere in the ancient world at the time. Most of these sites are now permanently underwater, flooded by Lake Nasser after Egypt built the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s, though archaeologists carried out emergency excavations beforehand to record what they could.

items.subtitle: A bucket on one end of a pole and a lump of clay on the other, so that one man can lift water all day without breaking his back.

time.label: In use from the Middle Kingdom onward

items.reveal: A shaduf is a simple but effective machine for lifting water: a long wooden pole balanced on a post, with a bucket hanging from one end and a heavy counterweight, often a lump of dried clay, on the other, letting one person raise and pour water using far less effort than lifting a full bucket by hand. Along the Nile, this device let farming families irrigate land that the yearly flood didn't naturally reach, extending the amount of usable farmland well beyond the riverbanks. It came into use during Egypt's Middle Kingdom and remained a normal sight along the Nile within living memory, essentially unchanged for thousands of years.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The southern capital, with the living on the east bank where the sun rises and the dead on the west where it sets.

time.label: As capital and as religious centre

items.reveal: Thebes, known today by its modern name Luxor, served as Egypt's southern capital and, at various points, its chief religious center as well. Like other Egyptian cities on the Nile, it was laid out with the living world on the east bank, where the sun rises, and the realm of the dead, including its famous royal tombs, on the west bank, where the sun sets. Ancient Greek writers, including Homer, gave this Egyptian Thebes the same name as an entirely separate city in Greece, the Thebes of the Oedipus legend, and even called it "the city of a hundred gates" for its grand scale, a name it shares only by coincidence with its unrelated Greek namesake.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The Theban king who drove the foreign rulers out of the delta and started Egypt's greatest age.

place.label: Egypt, from Thebes to the delta

items.reveal: Ahmose was a king based in Thebes, in southern Egypt, who led the campaign that finally drove the foreign Hyksos rulers out of the Nile delta and reunified Egypt under native rule. His victory marked the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and launched what would become ancient Egypt's most powerful and prosperous era, the New Kingdom. Traditional chronology places the expulsion of the Hyksos in 1567 BC, while most modern Egyptologists date Ahmose's actual reign to roughly twenty years later than that.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A capital built from nothing on virgin desert in about five years, and abandoned within twenty.
items.reveal: Akhetaten, known today by the modern name Amarna, was an entirely new Egyptian capital city, built essentially from nothing on empty desert land in only about five years. It was abandoned again within roughly twenty years of being built, once the religious and political changes that had led to its founding were reversed. Because no one built over the site afterward, unlike almost every other Egyptian city that has been continuously lived in and rebuilt for millennia, Amarna survives as the best-preserved ancient Egyptian city known, essentially a whole society frozen at one particular moment in time.
