items.subtitle: A pharaoh who shut the old temples, changed his own name, and built a new capital on empty ground.
items.reveal: Amenhotep IV was an Egyptian pharaoh who carried out one of the most dramatic religious upheavals in ancient history: he shut down worship of Egypt's traditional gods, changed his own name to Akhenaten in honor of a single sun-disc god called the Aten, and built an entirely new capital city, Akhetaten, on land that had never been used for any other purpose. His religious revolution largely collapsed after his death, and Egypt returned to its old gods under his successors. Because a large surviving archive of diplomatic letters, called the Amarna letters, was written and stored during his reign, his exact dates are unusually well established compared to most Egyptian rulers this far back in time.

items.subtitle: A local Theban god fused with the sun god, whose priests grew rich enough to frighten pharaohs.

time.label: From the Middle Kingdom through the New Kingdom

items.reveal: Amun-Ra began as two separate gods that were merged into one: Amun, a local god of the city of Thebes, and Ra, the older and more widely worshipped Egyptian sun god. As Thebes grew from a regional city into the capital of a powerful empire, Amun-Ra's temples, especially the great complex at Karnak, grew wealthier and more powerful along with it, until the god's priesthood controlled enough land and treasure to rival the pharaoh's own power. The pharaoh Akhenaten's religious revolution, which briefly banned worship of Amun-Ra in favor of a single sun-disc god, is best understood as an attempt by one pharaoh to break the grip of this overly powerful priesthood, an attempt that ultimately failed.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The sun's disk with rays ending in little hands, worshipped as the only god worth worshipping.
items.reveal: The Aten was the visible disc of the sun itself, worshipped during the reign of the pharaoh Akhenaten as the one and only god deserving worship, shown in Egyptian art as a sun disc with rays of light ending in small hands reaching down toward the royal family below. This represented a radical break from traditional Egyptian religion, which recognized many gods, each responsible for a different part of life and nature. Historians still debate whether this counted as true monotheism, belief in only one god, or whether it was really a case of one god being promoted so far above all the others that, for practical purposes, they stopped mattering.

items.subtitle: Three colonnaded terraces cut into a cliff, with a wall showing a whole expedition to Punt — ships, monkeys, and a very fat foreign queen.
items.reveal: Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes, was built into the base of a dramatic cliff face, with three tall colonnaded terraces rising one above another. Its walls are carved with detailed scenes recording a trading expedition Hatshepsut sent to a distant land called Punt, showing ships, exotic goods, monkeys, and even a portrait of a foreign queen depicted with an unusually large body. The temple was deliberately built right beside, and closely modeled on, an earlier temple built five hundred years before by the pharaoh Mentuhotep II, a clear case of one ruler intentionally echoing an earlier monument to link herself to Egypt's past.

items.subtitle: A woman who ruled as pharaoh, wore the false beard in her statues, and sent a fleet to a land of incense trees.
items.reveal: Hatshepsut was one of the few women in Egyptian history to rule as pharaoh in her own right, rather than merely as a queen or regent, and she had herself shown in statues wearing the traditional false beard that symbolized pharaonic authority. During her reign she sent a major trading expedition by sea to the distant land of Punt, returning with incense trees, gold, and exotic goods. Decades after her death, her stepson and successor Thutmose III had her name and image chiseled off many of her monuments; because this happened so long after she died, historians think it was more likely a move connected to securing his own son's succession than an act of simple spite.

items.subtitle: Great royal wife, shown offering to the sun alongside her husband as an equal — and known chiefly from one unfinished bust.
items.reveal: Nefertiti was the "Great Royal Wife," or chief queen, of the pharaoh Akhenaten, and Egyptian art from his reign shows her standing alongside her husband as an equal, both of them making offerings directly to the sun god Aten, an unusually prominent role for a queen. Today she is known mainly through a single famous, but unfinished, painted limestone bust discovered in an artist's workshop at Amarna. She disappears from the historical record around the twelfth year of Akhenaten's reign, and one serious theory among historians is that she did not die at that point but instead took on a new name and ruled afterward as pharaoh in her own right.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Egypt at its largest and richest — an empire reaching into Syria and deep into Nubia.

place.label: From the Euphrates bend to the Fourth Cataract

items.reveal: The New Kingdom was ancient Egypt's most powerful and wealthy era, when its empire stretched from deep in Nubia, to the south, all the way north into Syria, near the bend of the Euphrates River. This era included some of Egypt's most famous rulers, among them Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamen, and Ramesses II. It was also the first period in Egyptian history when pharaohs stopped being buried in pyramids and instead chose hidden tombs cut directly into rock, most famously in the Valley of the Kings, a change driven by two thousand years of pyramids being broken into and robbed of their treasure.

items.subtitle: A general, not a prince, who took the throne and marched an army to the Euphrates.
items.reveal: Thutmose I became pharaoh despite not being born a prince, likely rising to power through his career as a military general rather than through royal birth. Once on the throne, he led Egyptian armies further than any pharaoh before him, marching all the way to the Euphrates River in Syria. He was also the first pharaoh known to have been buried in the Valley of the Kings, the hidden desert valley that would become the standard royal burial ground for the rest of the New Kingdom, and he was the father of the future pharaoh Hatshepsut.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A boy king who undid his father's religion, died at eighteen, and mattered to nobody until 1922.
items.reveal: Tutankhamen became pharaoh of Egypt as a young boy and died at only about eighteen years old, but during his short reign he reversed the religious revolution of his predecessor Akhenaten, restoring worship of Egypt's traditional gods and changing his own name from Tutankhaten, which honored the god Aten, to Tutankhamen, honoring the god Amun instead. For most of history he was a minor, largely forgotten pharaoh, until 1922, when the archaeologist Howard Carter discovered his tomb almost completely intact, filled with treasures that made Tutankhamen the most famous pharaoh in the modern world. Scholars still disagree by roughly sixteen years over the exact dates of his short eighteen-year life.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A dry desert wadi behind the cliffs where sixty-odd pharaohs were hidden instead of monumentalised.

time.label: In use through the New Kingdom

items.reveal: The Valley of the Kings is a dry, remote desert ravine on the west bank of the Nile near Thebes, chosen by New Kingdom pharaohs as a hidden burial ground specifically because its narrow, easily guarded entrance made it harder for robbers to find and plunder their tombs, unlike the highly visible pyramids of earlier Egyptian rulers. More than sixty tombs have been found there, belonging to pharaohs and other members of the royal family. The strategy of hiding the tombs mostly failed anyway: nearly every tomb in the valley was broken into and robbed at some point in antiquity, and Tutankhamen's is the only one ever found still largely intact.

items.subtitle: A gilded acacia chest with carrying poles and two winged figures facing each other over the lid.

place.label: The Sinai and the wilderness camp

items.reveal: The Ark of the Covenant, as described in the Bible, was a wooden chest made of acacia wood, covered in gold, fitted with carrying poles so it could be transported without being touched directly, and topped with two facing winged figures called cherubim. According to the biblical account, it was built in the wilderness after the Exodus from Egypt to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, and carried at the center of the Israelite camp as a sign of God's presence among them. The kind of object described — a portable, poles-carried shrine kept inside a tent — closely resembles similar sacred items known from ancient Egyptian religious practice, roughly what one would expect from a people who had only recently left Egypt.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A pitch-sealed basket in the reeds, a princess bathing, and a sister watching from the bank.
items.reveal: According to Exodus, when the pharaoh of Egypt ordered that newborn Israelite baby boys be killed, one Israelite mother instead set her infant son adrift on the Nile in a waterproofed basket, hidden among the reeds at the riverbank, while his older sister watched nearby to see what would happen. An Egyptian princess found the basket while bathing and adopted the baby, naming him Moses; his sister then arranged, without revealing the truth, for their own mother to be hired as his nurse. A very similar story, of a baby set adrift on a river and later rising to greatness, is also told about the Mesopotamian king Sargon of Akkad, in a text written down long before Exodus was compiled, though this is generally understood as a shared story pattern found across the ancient Near East rather than proof of direct borrowing in either direction.

items.subtitle: A night of unleavened bread and blood on the doorposts, then a whole people walking east.

place.label: From Pi-Ramesse in the delta toward the Sinai

time.label: Kitchen: early in the reign of Ramesses II

items.reveal: The Exodus is the biblical account of the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt, beginning on a single night when the Israelites, marked by lamb's blood on their doorposts, ate a hurried meal of unleavened bread before a plague struck Egypt's firstborn and the pharaoh finally let them leave. From there, the text describes the entire people setting out on foot, traveling east from the delta city of Pi-Ramesse toward the Sinai peninsula. Scholars who argue for a later date, in the reign of Ramesses II, point to a mention of Israelites building the store-city "Raamses" in Exodus, a place known to have been founded in the thirteenth century BC, along with an Egyptian inscription from around 1208 BC that already mentions a people called Israel living in Canaan; scholars who argue for an earlier date instead rely on a biblical time reference in 1 Kings that would place the Exodus around 1446 BC, and the biblical text itself never actually states a specific calendar date for the event at all.

items.subtitle: Seven days of marching, seven priests with rams' horns, and a shout.

time.label: Kitchen scheme, a generation after the Exodus

items.reveal: According to the Book of Joshua, the Israelites captured the Canaanite city of Jericho by marching around its walls once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day, blowing ram's-horn trumpets, until the walls collapsed and the city fell. This story is one of the sharpest, most direct collisions in the whole corpus between the biblical text and physical archaeology: the archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon, excavating the site in the 1950s, found that Jericho's great fortification walls had actually been destroyed around 1550 BC, and that no walled city stood at Jericho at all during the thirteenth century BC, when this conquest is traditionally dated. A later archaeologist, Bryant Wood, has argued that Kenyon's dating of the pottery she found was mistaken, and this dispute remains unresolved.

items.subtitle: A pharaoh's victory boast that includes one line about a people, not a place, called Israel.
items.reveal: The Merneptah Stele is a large stone monument set up by the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah to boast about his military victories, and it includes one brief line claiming to have defeated a group called Israel, describing it as a people rather than as an established kingdom or city. It is the oldest known mention of Israel found anywhere outside the Bible. Because this inscription can be dated fairly precisely to around 1208 BC, it plays a crucial role in arguments over the date of the Exodus: if a people called Israel already existed in Canaan by that year, most scholars who accept a historical Exodus argue it must have happened somewhat earlier than that.

items.subtitle: Drawn out of the river, raised in a palace, and sent back to the palace with a demand.

place.label: The eastern delta, Midian, and Sinai

items.reveal: Moses is the central figure of the Exodus story: rescued as a baby from the Nile by an Egyptian princess, raised within the Egyptian royal household, but later forced to flee Egypt after killing an Egyptian overseer he saw beating a Hebrew slave. After years in exile in the region of Midian, he returned to confront the pharaoh with God's demand to free the Israelite slaves, eventually leading them out of Egypt and to Mount Sinai. According to the biblical account he lived to be 120 years old, and was said to be eighty at the time he confronted the pharaoh, figures drawn directly from the biblical text itself rather than from any outside historical record, and his entire traditional timeline shifts by roughly two centuries depending on which method is used to date the Exodus.

items.subtitle: Eaten standing, with sandals on and staff in hand, because you are leaving before morning.
items.reveal: Passover is the Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt, traditionally marked by a special meal that, according to the biblical instructions, was originally eaten standing up, fully dressed and ready to travel, with sandals already on and a walking staff in hand, because the Israelites were meant to leave Egypt at a moment's notice. The name comes from the story of a plague that "passed over" the houses of Israelites marked with lamb's blood, sparing their firstborn children while striking those of the Egyptians. Whatever the exact historical date of the underlying events, Passover is considered the oldest continuously observed religious festival in the world, celebrated every spring without interruption since ancient times.

items.subtitle: Thunder on a mountain, a people told to keep back, and two tablets of stone.

time.label: Kitchen scheme, shortly after the Exodus

items.reveal: According to the Book of Exodus, after leaving Egypt, Moses led the Israelites to a mountain in the wilderness, traditionally called Mount Sinai, where amid thunder, lightning, and smoke, God gave Moses the Ten Commandments carved onto two stone tablets, while the rest of the people were commanded to keep their distance from the mountain itself. This became the foundational law code for the nation of Israel. The specific mountain traditionally identified as Sinai today, known as Jebel Musa, was only given that identification by Christian monks in the fourth century AD, many centuries after the events described, and several other locations in northwest Arabia and the northern Sinai peninsula have also been seriously proposed by scholars as the real site.

items.subtitle: Manna, quail, complaining, and a generation that had to die before the next one could cross.

place.label: The Sinai peninsula and the Negev

items.reveal: After leaving Egypt, the Israelites are described in the Bible as wandering for forty years in the desert regions of the Sinai peninsula and the Negev before finally entering the land of Canaan, surviving on food the text describes as manna and flocks of quail, while frequently complaining to Moses about their hardships. According to the account, this long delay was itself a punishment: the generation of adults who had left Egypt was required to die out in the wilderness before their children would be allowed to cross into the promised land. Kadesh Barnea, the oasis where the Israelites are said to have camped for much of these forty years, is a real, identifiable site that has been excavated by archaeologists, though no remains from this particular time period, the Late Bronze Age, have been found there.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Greek-speakers from the north who moved into the ruins, and whose descendants founded Sparta.
items.reveal: The Dorians were a Greek-speaking people who, according to later Greek legend and the pattern of Greek dialects, moved into the Peloponnese region of southern Greece from the northwest sometime after the collapse of Mycenaean civilization, eventually founding, among other city-states, Sparta. Unlike many ancient migrations, no clear layer of destruction in the archaeological record can be directly tied to a "Dorian invasion," and the case for it rests mainly on how Greek dialects are distributed across different regions and on stories told by much later Greek writers. Because of this, some modern scholars doubt that an organized Dorian invasion happened at all, and think the spread of Dorian-speaking peoples may have been a slower, less dramatic process.

items.subtitle: Four centuries with no palaces, no trade goods, and no writing — Greeks forgot how to read.
items.reveal: The Greek Dark Ages refer to roughly four centuries following the collapse of Mycenaean civilization, during which archaeological evidence for trade, monumental building, and writing in Greece almost completely disappears. Most strikingly, the Greeks seem to have entirely forgotten how to write during this period, since their earlier script, Linear B, vanished along with the palace administrations that had used it, and no replacement appeared for centuries. When writing finally returned to Greece, it came in the form of a new alphabet borrowed and adapted from the Phoenicians, making this one of the few clearly documented cases in history of an entire society losing a technology it had once possessed.

items.subtitle: Palace inventories in an early form of Greek, baked hard by the fires that destroyed the palaces.
items.reveal: Linear B was a writing system used by Mycenaean Greek palace administrations to keep detailed records, mostly simple lists and inventories: counts of sheep, chariot wheels, jars of oil, and enslaved workers. It survives today mainly because clay tablets bearing it were accidentally baked hard and preserved by the very fires that destroyed the palaces where they were kept. It was deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect working on the puzzle as an amateur outside his own profession, whose breakthrough proved that the language recorded was an early form of Greek, pushing back the known history of written Greek by roughly five hundred years earlier than historians had previously believed possible.

items.subtitle: Two headless lionesses flanking a column above a doorway, over a lintel weighing twenty tons.
items.reveal: The Lion Gate was the grand main entrance to the fortified citadel of Mycenae, named for the relief carving above its massive stone lintel showing two lionesses (now headless) standing on either side of a central column. That lintel alone is estimated to weigh around twenty tons, an impressive feat of engineering for the Bronze Age builders who set it in place. Remarkably, the gate has never been buried or lost to history: it has stood visible above ground continuously for more than three thousand years, and was already considered a mysterious relic of the deep past by classical-era Greeks visiting the site.

items.subtitle: Rich in gold, according to Homer — a citadel on a ridge between two mountains.
items.reveal: Mycenae was a powerful fortified citadel in mainland Greece, built on a defensible ridge between two mountains, and was famous enough in later Greek legend that Homer described it as "rich in gold." In 1876, the archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann excavated royal shaft graves at the site and uncovered a beaten-gold funeral mask, which he dramatically announced was the face of the legendary King Agamemnon, leader of the Greeks in the Trojan War. In fact, the mask dates from roughly three centuries before any plausible date for a Trojan War, making Schliemann's famous claim almost certainly wrong.

items.subtitle: Greek-speaking warlords in hilltop fortresses, buried with gold masks and bronze swords.
items.reveal: The Mycenaeans were a Greek-speaking Bronze Age civilization based in fortified hilltop citadels across mainland Greece, ruled by warrior kings who were buried with elaborate gold funeral masks, bronze weapons, and other rich grave goods. Unlike the earlier Minoans of Crete, who built largely unwalled towns decorated with peaceful images of sea life, the Mycenaeans surrounded their major settlements with massive defensive walls, some over twenty feet thick, reflecting a far more warlike and militarized society. This sharp contrast between the two Bronze Age Aegean civilizations, one seemingly peaceful and the other clearly fortified for war, is part of why historians usually study them side by side.

items.subtitle: The palace at Knossos keeps running, but the clerks start writing in Greek.
items.reveal: After the collapse of independent Minoan civilization, Mycenaean Greeks took control of Crete, including its great palace at Knossos, which continued operating as an administrative center much as before. What changed was the language of its official records: the palace scribes switched from the undeciphered Minoan script, Linear A, to Linear B, used to write an early form of Greek. This event is essentially the same moment described from the opposite side in the story of the Minoan collapse, marking the point when Greek-speakers replaced Minoans as the rulers of Crete.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A defensible hill, a market below it, and farmland around — repeated a thousand times and never unified.
items.reveal: Beginning in this period, communities across Greece and the Aegean coast began organizing themselves into independent city-states, or poleis, each typically built around a defensible hill topped by a fortress, with a marketplace below it and farmland spreading out around the settlement. This same basic pattern repeated itself hundreds of times across the Greek world, but the individual city-states were never united into a single Greek nation. Greece's rugged geography, cut up by mountain ranges and surrounding sea, did much of the work here: it divided the land into pockets small enough for a single community to govern on its own, but difficult enough to cross that no one city-state ever managed to conquer and hold all the others permanently.

items.prompt: The Sea Peoples and the Bronze Age collapse
items.subtitle: Within fifty years every great palace from Greece to Syria burns, and nobody agrees who did it.
items.reveal: Within roughly fifty years, at the very end of the Bronze Age, nearly every major palace and city across the eastern Mediterranean collapsed or burned, including the Hittite Empire in Anatolia, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece, and the trading city of Ugarit in Syria. Egyptian records blame much of the destruction on a mysterious coalition of raiders and migrants the Egyptians called the "Sea Peoples," though who exactly they were and where they came from is still debated. Historians today generally think several problems struck at once — invasion, drought, earthquake, and a breakdown of the trade networks that had connected all these societies — rather than any single cause bringing the whole system down.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Twenty-two signs instead of six hundred — writing a merchant could learn in a week rather than a scribe in a decade.
items.reveal: The Phoenician alphabet reduced writing down to just twenty-two simple signs, each standing for a single consonant sound, in sharp contrast to earlier writing systems like Egyptian hieroglyphs or Mesopotamian cuneiform, which used hundreds of different signs and could take a professional scribe a decade to fully master. Because it was so much simpler, an ordinary merchant could realistically learn to read and write it in about a week. This alphabet descended from an even earlier Semitic script first used around 1800 BC by workers at turquoise mines in the Sinai, and it is itself the direct ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew, and Arabic alphabets, arguably making it one of the single most consequential inventions in all of human history.

items.subtitle: The papyrus port — which is why a Greek word for its trade goods became the word for book, and then for the Book.
items.reveal: Byblos was a Phoenician port city on the coast of what is now Lebanon, one of the longest continuously inhabited settlements anywhere on Earth. It became famous across the ancient Mediterranean as a major exporter of Egyptian papyrus, the plant-based writing material used before paper was invented. Because so many scrolls were shipped through this port, the Greek word for a papyrus scroll, "biblion," came to also mean "book," and it is this same word that eventually gave us the English word "Bible," meaning simply "the book."
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Settlers from Tyre on a North African headland, and a queen who bargained for as much land as an oxhide would cover.
items.reveal: According to tradition, Carthage was founded on a headland on the North African coast, near modern-day Tunis, by settlers who had sailed from the Phoenician city of Tyre, led by a queen remembered as Dido. Legend says that local rulers agreed to sell her only as much land as a single oxhide could cover, so Dido cleverly cut the hide into one extremely thin, long strip and used it to encircle an entire hill instead. This oxhide story is the kind of founding legend colonies often told about themselves; the traditional founding date of 814 BC actually comes from later Greek and Roman writers, while the earliest archaeological remains actually found at the site date to a few decades after that.

items.subtitle: A gland from a sea snail, rotted in vats until the smell drove the dyeworks outside the city, and worth its weight in silver.
items.reveal: Tyrian purple was a rare and extremely expensive dye made by Phoenician workers from a gland found in a particular species of sea snail called the murex. Producing it required crushing and rotting huge numbers of these snails in open vats, a process so foul-smelling that the dye-making workshops had to be located outside city walls. It took roughly 12,000 snails to produce just a gram and a half of dye, which is the real, practical reason the color purple became so strongly associated with royalty and wealth throughout history, not because people simply preferred the color, but because almost nobody besides royalty could afford it.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Trading posts a day's sail apart, strung west past Sicily and out through the Pillars of Hercules.

place.label: Carthage, Motya, Cadiz, and the western Mediterranean

items.reveal: Beginning around 900 BC, Phoenician traders established a chain of colonies and trading posts stretching west across the Mediterranean, each typically about a day's sail from the next, reaching past Sicily and eventually out through the Strait of Gibraltar, known to the ancients as the Pillars of Hercules. The most famous of these colonies was Carthage, on the coast of North Africa, but there were many others, including Motya off Sicily and Cadiz in Spain. Cadiz is especially notable because it was founded entirely outside the Mediterranean Sea, on the Atlantic coast, meaning Phoenician sailors were confidently navigating past Gibraltar centuries before any Greek ship attempted the same voyage.

items.subtitle: Canaanite traders on a strip of coast too narrow to farm, who therefore took to the sea.
items.reveal: The Phoenicians were a seafaring, trading civilization based along a narrow strip of the Levantine coast, in what is now Lebanon, where the land was too limited and mountainous for large-scale farming, pushing its people toward the sea for their livelihood instead. They actually called themselves Canaanites; the name "Phoenician" is a Greek word, thought to come from a term for the purple dye they were famous for producing and trading. Their rise to prominence largely filled the power vacuum left across the eastern Mediterranean after the Bronze Age collapse destroyed so many of the region's earlier great powers.

items.subtitle: Tyre's older rival up the coast, famous for glass.
items.reveal: Sidon was one of the oldest and most important Phoenician cities, an older rival to nearby Tyre along the same stretch of Lebanese coast, and it was especially famous throughout the ancient world for the quality of its glassware. Some historians believe the technique of glassblowing, which allowed craftsmen to shape glass by blowing air through a tube into molten glass rather than laboriously carving or molding it, may have actually been invented at Sidon around the first century BC. This innovation was significant because it made glass objects, once luxury items only the wealthy could afford, cheap enough to become common household items even for ordinary Roman families.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A city on an island half a mile offshore, which is why it held out against Assyria, Babylon, and everyone else until Alexander built a causeway.

time.label: From the Phoenician height to Alexander's siege

items.reveal: Tyre was a major Phoenician city built partly on an island roughly half a mile off the coast of what is now Lebanon, a location that let it withstand siege after siege by powerful empires, including Assyria and Babylon, since attacking a walled island was extremely difficult without a strong navy. It finally fell in 332 BC to Alexander the Great, who solved the problem by having his army build an entire artificial causeway of rubble out to the island so his forces could reach its walls directly. That causeway silted up over the following centuries and never washed away; as a result, the island of Tyre is today permanently joined to the mainland as a peninsula, meaning the very geography that made the city famous no longer exists.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A king who boasted of reading the writing of the age before the flood, and of flaying his enemies, in the same inscriptions.
items.reveal: Ashurbanipal was a king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire who took unusual pride in his own literacy, boasting in his inscriptions that he could read ancient writings said to predate the great flood, a genuinely rare skill among Mesopotamian kings, most of whom relied entirely on professional scribes. In those same inscriptions, he also boasted, in graphic detail, about brutally torturing and executing his defeated enemies. He is remembered today mainly for assembling a vast library of clay tablets at his capital, Nineveh, though his once-mighty empire collapsed entirely within about twenty years of his death.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.prompt: The spread of the Assyrian Empire
items.subtitle: Assyria's second act, taking advantage of everyone else's bad century.
items.reveal: Several centuries before Assyria's later, far larger empire, an earlier Assyrian kingdom known to historians as the Middle Assyrian period expanded its territory and influence across northern Mesopotamia, particularly under the king Tukulti-Ninurta I and his successors. This expansion took advantage of a period when many of the region's other major powers, including Egypt, the Hittites, and Babylon, were all weakened or in decline. This earlier phase of Assyrian power should not be confused with the much larger and more famous Neo-Assyrian Empire that would rise roughly three centuries later.

items.subtitle: Medes and Babylonians together, and the greatest empire in the world is gone inside three months.
items.reveal: In 612 BC, a combined army of Medes and Babylonians attacked and destroyed Nineveh, the capital of the once-mighty Assyrian Empire, ending Assyrian power within only about three months. The destruction of the city was so thorough and complete that, roughly two centuries later, the Greek soldier and historian Xenophon marched an army of Greek mercenaries directly past the ruins without being able to find out from anyone what city they had once belonged to. Nineveh's fall marked the sudden, total collapse of what had, until then, been the largest empire the world had yet seen.

items.subtitle: The northern kingdom ends after a three-year siege, and its people are marched away and do not come back.
items.reveal: Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and after a siege lasting roughly three years, it was finally captured by the Assyrian Empire, bringing an end to the kingdom of Israel as an independent state. As part of standard Assyrian policy, large numbers of the kingdom's inhabitants, remembered afterward as the ten "lost" northern tribes, were deported far from their homeland and never returned, effectively disappearing from later history. The southern kingdom of Judah survived on as an independent state for another 136 years after this, which is why the religious and cultural tradition that survived into later history was specifically the Judahite one, and why the word "Jew" itself ultimately comes from the name Judah.

items.subtitle: Thirty thousand clay tablets collected on royal orders — and preserved because the building burned.
items.reveal: The library of Ashurbanipal was a vast royal collection of roughly thirty thousand clay tablets, gathered at the Assyrian king's own order from across his empire, covering subjects ranging from literature and myth to medicine, law, and government records. It is the single richest surviving source of Mesopotamian literature known to historians, and it was here, in 1853, that archaeologists recovered the tablets containing the Epic of Gilgamesh. The collection survives today largely by accident: when the palace at Nineveh was burned during the city's destruction in 612 BC, the fire baked the clay tablets hard, preserving them for thousands of years rather than destroying them.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The first empire to rule from the Nile to the Persian Gulf, and the first to deport whole nations as policy.
items.reveal: The Neo-Assyrian Empire was the first empire in world history to rule a continuous stretch of territory from Egypt, in the west, all the way to the Zagros Mountains, in the east, near the Persian Gulf. It was also the first empire known to have used the mass deportation of entire conquered populations as a deliberate, routine tool of government policy, rather than as an occasional punishment. This forced relocation was a practical administrative technique: moving a conquered people far from their homeland made it much harder for them to organize a successful rebellion, since they no longer lived in the territory they might otherwise have fought to reclaim.

items.subtitle: Seven miles of wall on the Tigris, gardens watered by an aqueduct, and reliefs of a lion hunt.
items.reveal: Nineveh was the last and grandest capital of the Assyrian Empire, protected by roughly seven miles of massive city walls along the Tigris River, and famous for its lush palace gardens, kept watered by an impressive system of aqueducts, as well as for detailed stone relief carvings, including scenes of a royal lion hunt. In the Bible, Nineveh is the city the prophet Jonah is sent to warn, and it is also the target of the prophet Nahum's prophecy foretelling the city's total destruction. That prophecy was fulfilled with unusual thoroughness in 612 BC, when the city was destroyed so completely that its very location was eventually forgotten.

items.subtitle: Judah's king strips the temple gold to pay tribute, the Assyrians come anyway, and then abruptly go home.
items.reveal: In 701 BC, facing an invading Assyrian army under King Sennacherib, King Hezekiah of Judah stripped the gold from his own temple in Jerusalem in a desperate attempt to pay enough tribute to make the Assyrians go away. The Assyrians came anyway and laid siege to Jerusalem, but then unexpectedly withdrew without actually capturing the city. This is one of very few ancient events for which detailed accounts survive from both sides: the biblical Book of 2 Kings says an angel struck down the Assyrian camp, while Sennacherib's own inscription instead boasts of having shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage," notably, without ever claiming to have actually taken the city.

items.subtitle: Rebuilt the army into a standing professional force and turned raiding into administration.
items.reveal: Tiglath-Pileser III was an Assyrian king who transformed his kingdom's military from a seasonal force of conscripted farmers into a permanent, professional standing army, and reorganized conquered territories into administered provinces rather than simply raiding them for loot and moving on. This shift from raiding to genuine administration is considered the start of Assyria's transformation into a true, lasting empire. From his reign onward, Assyrian scribes kept detailed year-by-year records known as eponym lists, meaning historians can date events from this point forward with unusual precision, accurate to the exact year.

items.subtitle: One apple, three goddesses, the words 'for the fairest', and a shepherd asked to judge.
items.reveal: According to Greek myth, the goddess of discord, Eris, was deliberately left off the guest list for a wedding attended by the other gods, and in retaliation she tossed a golden apple into the celebration inscribed simply "for the fairest." Three goddesses, Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, each claimed the apple for herself, and a Trojan shepherd prince named Paris was chosen to judge which of them truly deserved it. Paris's judgment, and the reward Aphrodite offered him for choosing her, set off the chain of events that Greek legend says eventually led to the ten-year Trojan War, a story meant to illustrate how a small, seemingly petty slight can spiral into enormous consequences.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Blind, according to tradition, and claimed by seven cities — if he existed at all.
items.reveal: Homer is the name traditionally given to the poet credited with composing the Iliad and the Odyssey, two of the foundational works of Greek literature, though ancient tradition disagreed even about basic facts of his life: he was said to have been blind, and at least seven different Greek cities claimed to be his birthplace. Many modern scholars doubt that a single historical poet named Homer, as usually imagined, ever existed at all. Fieldwork done in the 1930s by the scholar Milman Parry, who studied illiterate oral poets still performing long epic poems from memory in the Balkans, made a strong case that poems like the Iliad and Odyssey were most likely shaped gradually over centuries of oral performance, only being written down in something like their final form much later.

items.subtitle: Fifty-one days in the tenth year of a war, beginning with the word for rage.

place.label: Composed in Ionia; set at Troy

items.reveal: The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem describing just fifty-one days, near the very end of a ten-year war between Greeks and Trojans, opening with a single word in the original Greek meaning "rage," referring to the anger of the Greek hero Achilles. Rather than covering the whole ten-year war, it focuses tightly on this brief period and the consequences of Achilles's fury after a quarrel with his own commander. The poem was likely composed roughly four hundred years after the war it describes is supposed to have taken place, a gap of time roughly comparable to the distance between the present day and the age of Shakespeare.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The king of Sparta, and the wife whose departure every other Greek king had sworn an oath to avenge.
items.reveal: Menelaus was the legendary king of Sparta, and his wife, Helen, was said to be the most beautiful woman in the world; when she left Sparta for Troy with the Trojan prince Paris, it set off the Trojan War. Before marrying Helen, all of her many royal suitors had been bound by a solemn oath to defend her marriage and come to her husband's aid if anyone ever tried to take her away. It was this earlier oath, sworn purely to settle a marriage dispute peacefully among rival Greek kings, that Greek legend says was the actual mechanism drawing every major Greek kingdom into the war once Helen left with Paris.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The man of many turns — who thought of the horse, and who told the Cyclops his name was Nobody.
items.reveal: Odysseus, known by his Latin name Ulysses, was a Greek king from the island of Ithaca famous in legend for his cunning intelligence rather than simply his strength, remembered in Homer's epithet as "the man of many turns." He is credited with devising the trick of the Trojan Horse that finally ended the Trojan War, and later, on his long journey home, he outwitted a man-eating one-eyed giant called the Cyclops by cleverly telling it his name was "Nobody." Whether the modern Greek island still called Ithaca today is really the same island described in Homer's poem has been argued by scholars for two centuries, since the geographical details given in the Odyssey don't quite match the real island's layout.

items.subtitle: Ten more years spent trying to get home, with monsters, and a wife unpicking her weaving every night.

time.label: Composition, probably a generation after the Iliad

items.reveal: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic poem describing the ten additional years the hero Odysseus spent struggling to sail home after the Trojan War ended, facing monsters, angry gods, and constant delays, while back home his wife, Penelope, held off a houseful of unwanted suitors by secretly unraveling each night the weaving she claimed she had to finish before remarrying. It is a very different kind of poem from the Iliad: more domestic in scale, more interested in clever trickery than battlefield glory, and focused on the goal of getting home safely rather than winning honor in war. It was probably composed roughly a generation after the Iliad, and the sharp difference in tone and focus between the two poems has led some scholars to argue they cannot have been written by the very same author.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The Greeks sail away, leaving behind an enormous wooden offering and one man to explain it.
items.reveal: According to Greek legend, after ten years of failing to take the city of Troy by force, the Greeks pretended to sail away for good, leaving behind on the beach an enormous hollow wooden horse as an apparent offering to the gods, along with a single Greek soldier to convince the Trojans it was safe to bring inside their walls. The Trojans hauled the horse into their city to celebrate what they believed was their victory, not realizing that a group of armed Greek soldiers was hidden inside it, waiting to open the gates for the returning Greek army that night. Interestingly, the story of the Trojan Horse never actually appears in the Iliad itself, which ends before Troy falls; it comes instead from later sources, including the Odyssey and the Roman poet Virgil's Aeneid, and the modern idea that it was really some kind of siege engine rather than a literal wooden horse is a purely modern guess with no ancient evidence behind it.

items.subtitle: A thousand ships, ten years of siege, and a quarrel between two kings that takes up most of the poem.

time.label: Traditional: Eratosthenes dated the fall to 1184

items.reveal: The Trojan War is the legendary ten-year conflict between a coalition of Greek kingdoms and the city of Troy, said to have been fought over the abduction of Helen of Sparta by the Trojan prince Paris, and involving a fleet said to number a thousand ships. Much of the Iliad, the great poem describing part of the war, actually focuses less on the fighting itself than on a bitter quarrel between two Greek leaders, Agamemnon and Achilles. Ancient Greeks themselves calculated the traditional date for the fall of Troy, 1184 BC, simply by counting back through generations of legendary genealogy, much the same method later used, thousands of years afterward, by scholars trying to date events in Genesis; a real layer of destruction by fire has indeed been found at Troy from around 1180 BC, suggestively close to the traditional date but proving nothing about whether the legendary war actually happened as described.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A fortified mound commanding the straits between two seas, rebuilt nine times on its own rubble.
items.reveal: Troy was a fortified city built on a mound commanding the narrow straits connecting the Aegean Sea to the Black Sea, a strategically valuable position that brought it wealth from ships that had to wait nearby for favorable winds before attempting the passage. Archaeologists have found that the site was rebuilt at least nine separate times, one city built directly on the rubble of the last, over thousands of years of occupation. When the archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann excavated the site in the 1870s, eager to find the Troy of legend, he dug so aggressively straight down through the mound that he tore through and destroyed much of the very layer that later archaeologists believe actually corresponds to the Troy of the Trojan War stories.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Taken from home at seven, underfed on purpose so as to learn stealing, and beaten for being caught rather than for stealing.

time.label: The Lycurgan system, to the defeat at Leuctra

items.reveal: The agoge was the harsh, state-run upbringing given to boys in ancient Sparta, who were taken from their families at around age seven to live and train together under military discipline. They were deliberately kept underfed, not out of cruelty alone but as part of their training, since going hungry pushed them to steal food, and boys were punished not for stealing itself, but only for being clumsy enough to get caught. Most of what is known about this system actually comes from the Greek writer Plutarch, writing roughly six hundred years later and clearly admiring what he described, and modern historians point out that Spartan discipline was at least partly a way of controlling a much larger population of enslaved workers, called helots, who likely outnumbered Spartan citizens by as much as seven to one.

items.subtitle: Officials chosen by lot rather than election, on the reasoning that voting favours the well-known and the rich.

place.label: Athens: the Pnyx and the Agora

time.label: From Cleisthenes to the Macedonian suppression

items.reveal: Athenian democracy was a system of government in which many public officials were chosen not by election but by random lot, on the reasoning that ordinary voting tends to favor candidates who are already wealthy or well known, rather than necessarily the most capable. It flourished from the reforms of the statesman Cleisthenes until Athens eventually lost its independence to Macedonian control. It's worth being clear-eyed about how limited this democracy actually was by modern standards: the right to participate belonged only to adult male citizens, probably no more than about a sixth of the total population, since it excluded all women, enslaved people, and foreign residents living in the city.

items.subtitle: Named for the goddess who offered an olive tree when her rival offered salt water.

time.label: From Mycenaean settlement to the Roman sack

items.reveal: Athens, the leading city of the region of Attica in Greece, took its name from a legendary contest between the gods Athena and Poseidon over who would become the city's patron: Poseidon offered a spring of salt water, while Athena offered an olive tree, and the city chose Athena's gift instead. The city has been continuously inhabited for well over three thousand years, from its earliest Mycenaean settlement all the way to the present day. Its famous "golden age," the roughly fifty-year period of its greatest wealth, democracy, and cultural achievement that most people think of when they picture ancient Athens, was actually just a brief slice of that far longer history.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: One race the length of the stadium, won by a cook, and a truce so that everyone could travel there safely.
items.reveal: The first Olympic Games, held at the sanctuary of Olympia in the western Peloponnese in 776 BC, consisted of essentially one event: a single footrace the length of the stadium, won, according to tradition, by a cook. A special truce was declared beforehand so that athletes and spectators from rival Greek city-states could travel to and from the games safely without fear of attack. Because later Greeks used this year as a fixed reference point, counting subsequent Olympic Games, held every four years, to number and date other events, 776 BC is remembered with unusual precision; it's worth noting the games were held at Olympia in the Peloponnese, a religious sanctuary, not at the separate, much more famous Mount Olympus roughly 300 km to the north.

items.subtitle: Borrowed consonants from traders, with the leftover signs repurposed for something no one had written before: vowels.
items.reveal: The Greek alphabet was adapted from the Phoenician alphabet, which Greek traders encountered through contact with Phoenician merchants; the Phoenician script, however, only had letters for consonant sounds. Greek speakers cleverly repurposed several Phoenician letters representing consonant sounds that didn't exist in Greek to instead represent vowel sounds, something no earlier writing system in the world had done, making Greek the first fully alphabetic script to represent both consonants and vowels. Even today, the names of Greek letters like alpha and beta are barely changed from their original Phoenician names, aleph and bet, which literally meant "ox" and "house" in that Semitic language, four hundred years and an entire sea away from wherever those original meanings still made sense.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Too many sons and not enough farmland, so cities sent out shiploads of settlers — like frogs around a pond, said Plato.
items.reveal: Facing growing populations and limited farmland at home, many Greek city-states responded by sending out organized groups of settlers to found entirely new, independent Greek cities all around the coasts of the Mediterranean and Black Seas; the philosopher Plato later compared the pattern to frogs settling all around the edge of a pond. Cities founded this way included Syracuse in Sicily, Massalia (modern Marseille) in France, Byzantion (later Constantinople, and today Istanbul) on the Bosphorus, and Cyrene in North Africa. Southern Italy in particular became so densely settled with Greek colonies that the Romans later nicknamed the whole region Magna Graecia, meaning "Greater Greece."

items.subtitle: Built with no straight lines — every column leans inward and swells at the middle so that it will look straight.
items.reveal: The Parthenon, a great marble temple built atop the Acropolis of Athens in honor of the goddess Athena, was constructed with remarkable architectural sophistication: despite looking perfectly straight to the eye, it actually contains almost no truly straight lines at all, since its columns lean subtly inward and bulge slightly outward at the middle, subtle corrections designed to counteract natural optical illusions that would otherwise make a perfectly straight building look warped from a distance. The building survived remarkably intact for over two thousand years, serving at different times as a pagan temple, a Christian church, and finally an Ottoman mosque. It was seriously damaged only in 1687, when attacking Venetian forces fired a mortar shell that struck a store of gunpowder the Ottomans had been keeping inside the building, causing a massive explosion.

items.subtitle: Re-elected general year after year, he spent the allies' defence fund on marble for his own city.
items.reveal: Pericles was the leading statesman of Athens during its golden age, re-elected repeatedly to the office of general year after year, giving him enormous practical influence over Athenian policy even though Athens was technically a democracy without any single formal ruler. He controversially used funds originally collected from Athens's allies for their mutual defense to instead pay for grand new building projects in Athens itself, including the Parthenon. He died of a plague that struck Athens early in the Peloponnesian War, a war he himself had strongly advocated for; the historian Thucydides later wrote him an especially famous funeral speech honoring Athenian democracy, a speech which, since no exact transcript existed, Thucydides largely composed himself in Pericles's name.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Given absolute power to write laws, he cancelled debts, freed those enslaved for them, and then left the country for ten years so nobody could ask him to amend anything.
items.reveal: Solon was an Athenian statesman given nearly absolute temporary power specifically to rewrite the city's laws and resolve a severe crisis caused by widespread personal debt. He canceled outstanding debts across the city and freed citizens who had been enslaved as punishment for failing to repay what they owed, a reform remembered by the Greek name seisachtheia, meaning "the shaking-off of burdens." Once his reforms were in place, Solon deliberately left Athens for ten years, reportedly so that no one could pressure him into changing the laws he had just written.

items.subtitle: A city with no walls, on the theory that its men were the walls.

time.label: From the Dorian settlement to the end of Spartan independence

items.reveal: Sparta was a powerful Greek city-state that, unlike most other Greek cities, built no defensive walls around itself, on the theory that its own well-trained soldiers were a stronger defense than any wall could be. The historian Thucydides, writing while Sparta was still at the height of its power, predicted that if the city were ever abandoned, its ruins alone would give future visitors no real sense of how powerful it had actually been. He turned out to be exactly right: unlike Athens, with its dramatic ruins still standing today, almost nothing remains to be seen at the site of ancient Sparta.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Born from sea foam and stepping ashore on an island — which is why her oldest sanctuary is not in Greece at all.
items.reveal: Aphrodite was the Greek goddess of love and beauty, said in myth to have been born from sea foam and to have stepped ashore for the first time on the island of Cyprus. Her oldest and most important sanctuary was accordingly located not on the Greek mainland at all, but at Paphos, on Cyprus. This Cypriot cult sits directly on top of an even older Near Eastern religious tradition, and Aphrodite shares a great deal in common with earlier Near Eastern goddesses like Ishtar and Astarte, suggesting she originally arrived in Greek religion from the east rather than being a purely Greek invention.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Born fully armed from her father's head, and better at war than the god of war because she thought about it first.
items.reveal: Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, said to have been born fully grown and fully armed directly from the head of her father, Zeus. Greek myth considered her a more effective war goddess than Ares, the actual god of war, precisely because she approached conflict through careful strategy and thought rather than raw aggression and bloodlust. She was the patron goddess of Athens, having won that role in a legendary contest against the sea god Poseidon by offering the city an olive tree instead of his gift of a salt spring, a contest the Athenians themselves are shown judging, choosing the useful gift, on the west pediment of the Parthenon.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A priestess on a tripod over a cleft in the rock, answering questions in verses that could be read two ways.

place.label: Delphi, on the slopes of Parnassus

items.reveal: The oracle at Delphi was ancient Greece's most respected site for consulting the gods about the future, where a priestess called the Pythia sat on a tripod stool positioned over a cleft in the rock and delivered answers to visitors' questions in the form of verses that were often deliberately ambiguous, open to more than one interpretation. In one famous story, the wealthy king Croesus was told that if he attacked the Persian Empire he would destroy a great empire; he did attack, and the great empire destroyed turned out to be his own. Modern geologists have actually found fault lines directly beneath the ancient temple capable of releasing gases such as ethylene, which may help explain the ancient reports of intoxicating vapors the priestess was said to have breathed in before delivering her prophecies.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A daughter carried underground, a mother who lets nothing grow until she is returned, and six pomegranate seeds that spoil the bargain.
items.reveal: According to Greek myth, Persephone, daughter of the harvest goddess Demeter, was seized and carried down to the underworld by its ruler, Hades, and while she was missing, her grieving mother refused to let anything grow on Earth at all. Persephone was eventually allowed to return, but because she had eaten six pomegranate seeds while in the underworld, she was bound to spend part of each year back below the earth, an arrangement the Greeks used to explain the changing seasons. This myth was also the basis of a secret religious rite called the Eleusinian Mysteries, practiced for roughly a thousand years near Athens; the details were so well protected by initiates sworn to silence that, to this day, historians still don't actually know exactly what happened during the secret ceremony itself.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Queen of the gods, patron of marriage, and permanently occupied with her husband's affairs.
items.reveal: Hera was queen of the Greek gods, wife of Zeus, and the goddess most closely associated with marriage, though Greek myths about her focus constantly on her jealous reactions to her husband's numerous affairs with other women. Some of her most important sanctuaries, particularly at Argos and on the island of Samos, are actually older than most temples built for Zeus himself. This suggests to historians that Hera may originally have been an especially important, independent goddess in her own right, well before the later Greek pantheon settled into its familiar family structure organized around Zeus.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The highest thing in Greece, usually in cloud, and therefore where the gods were said to live.

time.label: As the home of the gods in Greek belief

items.reveal: Mount Olympus, the tallest mountain in Greece and usually shrouded in cloud near its peak, was believed by the ancient Greeks to be the home of their principal gods, the Olympians. No ancient source records anyone ever actually climbing to its summit in antiquity, likely because doing so was both physically difficult and would have seemed like trespassing on the gods' own territory. The mountain's actual summit was not successfully reached by climbers until 1913, in the modern era, long after ancient Greek religion had faded away.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Earth-shaker and horse-tamer, worshipped hardest by people about to get into a boat.
items.reveal: Poseidon was the Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, worshipped with particular devotion by people about to set out on a sea voyage, given how dangerous ancient sailing could be. His temple at Cape Sounion was deliberately built on a dramatic cliff overlooking the sea, positioned so it would be the very last landmark sailors leaving Athens would see, and the very first one they'd spot on their way back home. In Homer's Odyssey, it is Poseidon's anger, provoked when the hero Odysseus blinds the god's monstrous son, the Cyclops, that causes most of the delays and disasters keeping Odysseus from getting home for ten long years.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Sky-father and thrower of lightning, whose forty-foot ivory statue at his sanctuary was counted a wonder of the world.

time.label: To the closing of the sanctuary

items.reveal: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods, ruler of the sky and famously depicted hurling thunderbolts, whose main sanctuary at Olympia housed a colossal ivory-and-gold statue of him roughly forty feet tall, considered one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. His name is actually the very same word, traced back through a shared ancestral language, as the Latin "Jupiter" (from Ju-piter, "sky-father") and the Sanskrit "Dyaus Pita," used in ancient India. This linguistic connection is some of the strongest evidence historians have that Greek, Roman, and Indian civilizations all ultimately descend from a shared, much older Indo-European-speaking ancestor culture.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Rome's northern neighbours and early masters — engineers, tomb-painters, and readers of livers.

place.label: Etruria, between the Arno and the Tiber

time.label: From the Villanovan period to absorption into Rome

items.reveal: The Etruscans were a sophisticated civilization based in the region of Etruria, north of Rome between the Arno and Tiber rivers, known for skilled engineering, elaborately painted tombs, and a religious practice of predicting the future by examining the livers of sacrificed animals. Their written language survives in an alphabet borrowed from the Greeks, which modern scholars can sound out and pronounce, but still cannot fully translate or understand, leaving Etruscan in almost exactly the same frustrating position as the undeciphered Minoan script, Linear A. Rome's last three legendary kings were actually Etruscan, and early Rome borrowed a great deal directly from Etruscan civilization, including its distinctive rounded arches, its advanced drainage engineering, and its religious practice of predicting omens.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A furrow ploughed around a hill, and a brother who jumped over it.
items.reveal: According to Roman tradition, the city of Rome was founded on a specific date, 21 April 753 BC, when its legendary founder Romulus marked out the city's sacred boundary by plowing a furrow around the hill he had chosen. This precise date was actually calculated centuries later, in the first century BC, by the Roman scholar Varro, and Romans afterward used it as a fixed starting point for numbering years, counting "since the founding of the city." Real archaeology tells a messier story: it shows scattered villages already existing on Rome's hills from around 1000 BC, gradually growing into a genuine town by around the seventh century BC, meaning the famous founding date is best understood as a convenient later convention rather than an actual historical event.

items.subtitle: Twins set adrift, suckled by a wolf, and reunited only long enough for one to kill the other over a wall.
items.reveal: According to Roman legend, the twin brothers Romulus and Remus were abandoned as infants and set adrift, but survived after being discovered and nursed by a she-wolf, eventually growing up to found a new city together. The partnership ended violently when Remus mockingly leapt over a low wall Romulus had built around his new settlement, and Romulus killed his own brother for the insult, going on to rule the city alone and give it his name. This story of an infant set adrift and later achieving greatness closely echoes similar legends told about other ancient figures, including Sargon of Akkad and Moses; even the Roman historian Livy, writing about seven hundred years after these events supposedly happened, reported the story honestly while declining to personally vouch for whether any of it was actually true.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.prompt: The seizure of the Sabine women
items.subtitle: A new city of men without wives invites the neighbours to a festival, and the festival has a signal.
items.reveal: According to Roman legend, the newly founded city of Rome had far more men than women, so Romulus invited a neighboring people, the Sabines, to attend a religious festival, and at a prearranged signal during the celebration, Roman men seized and carried off the unmarried Sabine women to become their wives. This led to war between Rome and the furious Sabines, but according to the Roman historian Livy, the conflict was finally stopped by the Sabine women themselves, who by then were mothers of Roman children and walked out between the two opposing armies to beg both sides for peace. It's a founding story that is unusually honest about the fact that Rome's founding involved a genuine crime, rather than presenting the city's origins as purely noble.

items.subtitle: Defensible high ground above a marsh, at the first place upstream where the river could be forded.

time.label: From the first hill villages to the Republic

items.reveal: Rome grew up on a cluster of seven low hills rising above a marshy river valley, chosen originally because the hills offered defensible high ground and because the site sat at the first point upstream on the Tiber River where travelers and traders could easily cross on foot. This combination, a natural river crossing along a trade route, plus hills that were easy to defend, is much of the reason a city grew here at all rather than somewhere else nearby. The marshy valley between the hills was eventually drained, a project historians credit to the Etruscans, and it later became the site of the Roman Forum, the political and social center of the city.

items.prompt: The expulsion of the last king
items.subtitle: Tarquin the Proud is driven out, and Rome decides never to have a king again — a resolution it keeps for 460 years and then evades by inventing a new word.

time.label: Traditional date for the founding of the Republic

items.reveal: According to Roman tradition, Rome's seventh and final king, Tarquin the Proud, was driven out of the city after a member of his own family committed a terrible crime against a Roman noblewoman, and the outraged Romans afterward swore never to be ruled by a king again. This resolution launched the Roman Republic, a system in which power was shared among elected officials rather than concentrated in a single monarch, and Rome kept faith with it for the next 460 years. The Roman horror of kingship shaped politics for centuries afterward: it is part of why Julius Caesar publicly refused a crown offered to him, and why his successor Augustus, though he ruled with something close to total power, carefully called himself princeps, meaning "first citizen," rather than "king."

items.subtitle: Rome's law written down and posted in the forum, because law kept secret by the patricians was law that could be invented as needed.
items.reveal: The Twelve Tables were ancient Rome's first written law code, drawn up and publicly displayed in the Roman Forum so that every citizen could see exactly what the laws actually said. Before this, Rome's laws had existed only as unwritten tradition controlled by patrician officials, the wealthy noble class, which meant ordinary citizens had to simply trust powerful men not to invent or twist the rules to suit themselves. The original bronze tablets were destroyed when Gaulish invaders sacked Rome in 390 BC, so their exact text survives today only through later quotations by Roman writers; the statesman Cicero, writing centuries later, claimed that schoolboys of his own era still memorized the Twelve Tables by heart.

items.subtitle: The city made new again, with high walls and a gate of blue glazed brick.

time.label: From the rise of the Neo-Babylonian dynasty to the city's eclipse by Seleucia

items.reveal: A thousand years after Hammurabi's empire had faded, Babylon rose again under the Neo-Babylonian dynasty, above all under King Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th century BC, who rebuilt the city on a spectacular scale, with towering walls, the glazed-brick Ishtar Gate, and, by tradition, the Hanging Gardens. It briefly became the largest and richest city in the world for a second time, and it was here that the Persian king Cyrus the Great arrived in 539 BC, ending Neo-Babylonian rule with barely a fight. The rebuilt city remained important even under Persian and later Greek rule — Alexander the Great died there in 323 BC, reportedly planning to make it his own capital — before gradually being eclipsed once a new nearby city, Seleucia, drew away its population.

items.subtitle: A feast using the temple vessels as cups, a hand that appears and writes four words, and a kingdom weighed and found wanting.
items.reveal: According to the Book of Daniel, King Belshazzar of Babylon held a great feast on the very night the city fell, drinking from sacred cups looted from the Jewish temple in Jerusalem, when a mysterious hand suddenly appeared and wrote four strange words on the wall. Daniel was called in to interpret the writing, and explained that it meant Belshazzar's kingdom had been weighed by God and found wanting, and would soon be given to others. Belshazzar was long assumed by skeptics to be a purely fictional character invented for the story, until cuneiform tablets were discovered naming him as the son and co-ruler of the actual Babylonian king Nabonidus, which also neatly explains why the biblical story has Belshazzar offering Daniel only the third-highest position in the kingdom rather than the second, since Belshazzar himself was not the top ruler.

items.subtitle: Seven stages of mud brick called the foundation of heaven and earth — and very probably the tower of the Genesis story.

time.label: Nebuchadnezzar's rebuilding of a much older structure

items.reveal: Etemenanki was a massive stepped temple tower, or ziggurat, in the city of Babylon, built up in seven levels of mud brick and known by a name meaning something like "the foundation of heaven and earth." Many historians think this specific structure, or one very like it, likely inspired the Genesis story of the Tower of Babel. Only its foundation survives today; centuries later, Alexander the Great had the ruined tower cleared away, intending to rebuild it grander than before, but he died before construction could even begin, and by that point ziggurats had already been built in Mesopotamia for some 1,500 years.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The greatest city in the world changes hands with almost no fighting, and the priests seem glad of it.
items.reveal: In 539 BC, the Persian king Cyrus the Great captured Babylon, at the time the greatest and richest city in the world, with remarkably little actual fighting. The Greek historian Herodotus later claimed the Persians achieved this by diverting the Euphrates River and marching their soldiers into the city along the newly dry riverbed. Babylonian sources instead suggest the city's own priests may have simply opened the gates for Cyrus, since the previous Babylonian king, Nabonidus, had neglected the traditional festival of the chief god Marduk for years, leaving the priesthood frustrated and unwilling to defend him.

items.prompt: The destruction of Jerusalem and the Exile
items.subtitle: Eighteen months of siege, the temple burned, and the population marched to Babylon.
items.reveal: After an eighteen-month siege, Babylonian forces under Nebuchadnezzar II captured Jerusalem, burned the city's temple to the ground, and marched much of its surviving population off into exile in Babylon. Both the Babylonian Chronicle, an official Babylonian record, and the biblical Book of 2 Kings independently confirm the same year for this event, 586 BC. It stands as one of the most consequential events in the whole span of ancient history covered here, since it forced a religion that had until then been centered entirely on one temple in one city to figure out how to survive in exile, without either.

items.subtitle: Terraces of trees watered by machinery, built — the story goes — to console a queen who missed her mountains.
items.reveal: The Hanging Gardens were said to be a spectacular series of terraces planted with trees and greenery, kept watered by an ingenious system of machinery, supposedly built by King Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon to comfort a homesick queen who missed the green mountains of her own country. It is the one Wonder of the Ancient World that archaeologists have never been able to locate or confirm actually existed. No surviving Babylonian text mentions such gardens at all, and one modern historian, Stephanie Dalley, has argued convincingly that the real gardens described by ancient sources were actually built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib at Nineveh, roughly 500 km to the north, and were only later mistakenly credited to the far more famous city of Babylon.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A processional entrance in deep blue glaze, covered in bulls and dragons in yellow relief.
items.reveal: The Ishtar Gate was a grand ceremonial entrance to the city of Babylon, covered in glossy deep-blue glazed bricks and decorated with rows of bulls and dragons molded in yellow relief. It was built under King Nebuchadnezzar II as part of his larger rebuilding of the city. German archaeologists excavated the gate before the First World War and shipped its remains back to Germany, where it was later reconstructed inside a museum in Berlin; it remains there today, making it one of the more contested objects in modern debates over whether ancient artifacts should be returned to their countries of origin.

items.subtitle: Rebuilt Babylon in glazed blue brick, and destroyed Jerusalem when it rebelled a second time.
items.reveal: Nebuchadnezzar II was the most powerful king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, famous for rebuilding Babylon into a spectacular city decorated with glazed blue brick, including the famous Ishtar Gate. He is also remembered for destroying Jerusalem and its temple after the kingdom of Judah rebelled against Babylonian rule for a second time, sending much of its population into exile. The biblical Book of Daniel describes a period when Nebuchadnezzar was struck with madness and lived like a wild animal for a time; no surviving Babylonian record mentions any such episode, though this silence doesn't necessarily prove it didn't happen.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Babylon's second age of greatness, won by helping to destroy Assyria and lost in a single night.
items.reveal: The Neo-Babylonian Empire was Babylon's second great age of power, won partly by helping a coalition destroy the previously dominant Assyrian Empire. It reached its height under Nebuchadnezzar II, who alone ruled for roughly half of this empire's entire 87-year existence. Almost everything the Bible and modern tourist guides describe as characteristically "Babylonian," including its grandest architecture and its role in the biblical exile, actually belongs to this relatively brief later period rather than to the much earlier, more ancient Babylon of Hammurabi.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The largest empire the world had yet seen, run by satraps, couriers, and a policy of leaving local customs alone.

place.label: From the Aegean to the Indus

items.reveal: The Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great and formally known as the Achaemenid Empire, was the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching all the way from the Aegean Sea in the west to the Indus River in the east. It was governed through a network of regional governors called satraps, connected by an efficient system of royal couriers, and it followed a deliberate policy of leaving conquered peoples' local customs, religions, and laws largely intact rather than forcing them to adopt Persian ways. At its height it may have ruled as much as 44 percent of the entire world's population, a larger share than any empire before or since; this tolerance was a practical strategy rather than simple kindness, since a conquered people allowed to keep their own gods and customs was less likely to rebel.

items.subtitle: Conquered from the Aegean to the Indus and made a policy of sending captive peoples home with their gods.
items.reveal: Cyrus the Great was the founder of the Persian Empire, conquering territory that stretched from the Aegean Sea all the way to the Indus River. Unlike many conquerors of his time, he followed a deliberate policy of allowing peoples his empire had conquered, and their gods, to return home rather than remaining displaced, including allowing the exiled Jewish community to return from Babylon to Jerusalem. Because of this act, the biblical Book of Isaiah calls Cyrus God's "anointed," the only non-Jewish figure in the entire Hebrew Bible ever given that title.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: A clay barrel buried in a foundation, announcing that the new king has restored the gods to their proper homes.
items.reveal: The Cyrus Cylinder is a small clay barrel-shaped object, inscribed in cuneiform and buried in the foundation of a building in Babylon, on which the Persian king Cyrus the Great announced, in the traditional style of Mesopotamian royal propaganda, that he had restored various gods and peoples to their rightful homes after conquering the city. It is sometimes described in popular accounts as the first charter of human rights in history, though most historians consider this a considerable overstatement, since it closely follows a standard, familiar genre of Mesopotamian royal inscription rather than being a genuinely revolutionary legal document.
