Even so, its content closely matches the policy the biblical Book of Ezra describes Cyrus carrying out, allowing the exiled Jewish community to return home and rebuild their temple.

items.subtitle: Seized the throne in a coup, reorganised the empire into twenty provinces, and carved his account of it 100 metres up a cliff.
items.reveal: Darius I became king of the Persian Empire after seizing power in a palace coup, and once in control he reorganized the vast empire into twenty administrative provinces, each governed by an official called a satrap. He also had a lengthy account of his rise to power carved in three different languages high up on a cliff face at Behistun, roughly 100 meters above the ground, where it would be difficult to alter or destroy. That trilingual Behistun inscription later played the same crucial role for cuneiform writing that the Rosetta Stone played for Egyptian hieroglyphs, giving scholars the key they needed to finally decipher Old Persian and, from there, the more widely used Akkadian language.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Horsemen of the Zagros who broke Assyria, and were then absorbed by their own southern cousins.
items.reveal: The Medes were a people from the Zagros Mountains, related to the Persians, who built a powerful kingdom that helped bring down the Assyrian Empire. Not long afterward, the Medes were themselves absorbed into the growing Persian Empire by their close relatives to the south, under Cyrus the Great. Almost everything historians know about the Medes comes from the Greek historian Herodotus and from records left by their various enemies, since no Median archive of their own has ever been discovered; the well-known phrase "the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not" actually comes from the biblical Book of Daniel.

items.subtitle: A plain gabled stone chamber on six steps, standing alone in a plain.
items.reveal: The tomb of Cyrus the Great stands at Pasargadae, in southern Iran: a simple gabled stone chamber raised on a stepped platform of six stone tiers, standing alone in an open plain with none of the elaborate decoration usually associated with the burial of a world-conquering king. When Alexander the Great later conquered the Persian Empire and visited the tomb, he reportedly found it had already been looted by robbers, and ordered it restored out of respect — a striking case of one great conqueror honoring the memory of the conqueror whose empire he had just taken for himself.

items.subtitle: A ceremonial capital with a staircase carved to show every subject nation bringing its tribute.

time.label: From Darius's foundation to Alexander's burning

items.reveal: Persepolis was a grand ceremonial capital built by the Persian kings, used mainly for royal celebrations and receiving official visitors rather than as an everyday seat of government. Its most famous feature is a monumental stone staircase carved with detailed relief images showing representatives from every nation under Persian rule, each shown in their own distinctive clothing, bringing tribute gifts specific to their own culture. These reliefs depict twenty-three separate delegations in total, and together they form perhaps the best surviving picture of how an ancient empire wanted to present itself to the world.

items.subtitle: Fifty years after the temple burned, a Persian decree sends the exiles home to rebuild it.

time.label: From the decree to the second temple's completion

items.reveal: Roughly fifty years after Babylonian forces had destroyed Jerusalem's temple and exiled much of the Jewish population, the Persian king Cyrus the Great issued a decree allowing the exiles to return home and rebuild their temple, following his empire's general policy of restoring displaced peoples to their homelands. Reconstruction of the temple took years and was completed only gradually. Notably, many exiled Jews actually chose not to return at all, and the Jewish community that remained in Babylonia continued on afterward as one of the largest Jewish communities anywhere in the world for the next 1,500 years.

items.subtitle: 1,600 miles of maintained highway with posting stations a day's ride apart, and riders who did not stop for weather.
items.reveal: The Royal Road was a major highway built and maintained by the Persian Empire, stretching some 1,600 miles from the city of Susa to Sardis, with regularly spaced posting stations along the route roughly a day's ride apart, where royal messengers could quickly exchange tired horses for fresh ones. This system let official messages travel across the vast empire far faster than an ordinary traveler ever could. The Greek historian Herodotus's admiring description of the Persian couriers, who he said were stopped by neither snow, rain, heat, nor darkness, is actually the direct source of the famous unofficial motto later inscribed on the main post office building in New York City.

items.subtitle: Cattle-herding, chariot-driving, Sanskrit-speaking newcomers moving down into the Punjab.

place.label: The Punjab and the upper Indus

items.reveal: Beginning sometime in the second millennium BC, cattle-herding, chariot-driving peoples who spoke an early form of Sanskrit began moving into the Punjab region of northwest India, eventually spreading their language and culture across much of northern India. The older idea that these newcomers, often called Aryans, arrived as invaders who violently destroyed the Indus Valley cities has been abandoned by historians, since archaeology shows those cities were already abandoned well before this migration took place. Whether this movement of peoples happened through large-scale migration, gradual small-scale infiltration, or mainly through the spread of language and culture without huge numbers of people actually moving, remains genuinely debated among scholars, and the question remains politically sensitive in India today; the word "Aryan" itself simply means "noble" in Sanskrit and has no real connection to its later, entirely unrelated misuse by twentieth-century European racist ideology.

items.prompt: The enlightenment under the bodhi tree
items.subtitle: Six years of starving himself having failed, he eats a bowl of rice, sits down under a fig tree, and refuses to get up.
items.reveal: According to Buddhist tradition, after six years of extreme fasting and self-denial failed to bring him spiritual insight, the spiritual seeker who would become known as the Buddha finally accepted a bowl of rice from a village girl, sat down beneath a large fig tree, and resolved not to get up again until he achieved enlightenment. He remained there until he did, achieving the spiritual awakening that became the foundation of Buddhism. A descendant of the very same tree is reportedly still growing at the site today, since a cutting from the original tree was carried to Sri Lanka in the third century BC, and a cutting from that Sri Lankan tree was later brought back to replace the original tree in India after it died.

items.subtitle: Priests from the mouth, warriors from the arms, merchants from the thighs, labourers from the feet of a primeval man.
items.reveal: According to an ancient Indian religious hymn, the four traditional social classes of Hindu society, called varnas, are said to have been created from different parts of the body of a cosmic primeval man: priests from his mouth, warriors from his arms, merchants and farmers from his thighs, and laborers from his feet. This idea comes from the Purusha Sukta, a hymn found in the Rigveda, one of Hinduism's oldest sacred texts. It's worth being clear that these four broad varnas are not the same thing as the many thousands of much more specific hereditary birth-groups, called jati, that have actually structured Indian society in practice, a distinction that many simplified accounts blur together.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: In a deer park, to five men who had walked out on him, he sets out four truths and a middle way.
items.reveal: According to Buddhist tradition, shortly after achieving enlightenment, the Buddha traveled to a deer park at Sarnath, near the city of Varanasi, to deliver his first teaching to five former companions who had earlier abandoned him when he gave up extreme fasting. In this sermon, he laid out what became known as the Four Noble Truths and recommended a "middle way" of moderate living, between extreme self-denial and excessive indulgence. About 250 years later, the Indian emperor Ashoka had a stone pillar erected at this same site; its carved lion capital is now the official emblem of the Republic of India, and the wheel design from its base appears on the modern Indian national flag.

items.subtitle: A king's penance brings a river down from heaven, and a god stands under it to break the fall.

time.label: Attested in the epics and Puranas

items.reveal: According to Hindu mythology, an ancient king performed intense religious penance to bring the sacred Ganges River down from heaven to Earth, but the river's fall was so powerful it would have shattered the world, so the god Shiva stood beneath it and caught it in his hair, breaking its fall and letting it flow gently down to the earth from there instead. This myth reflects a real historical shift: over the course of India's Vedic period, the center of Indian civilization gradually moved eastward, away from the Indus River valley and toward the Ganges River valley, and Hindu mythology shifted its focus to follow the population. Varanasi, on the banks of the Ganges, remains one of the holiest cities in Hinduism today, closely tied to this myth of the river's descent from heaven.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Ascetic on a mountain and lord of the dance, who caught the falling river in his hair so it would not shatter the earth.

time.label: From Vedic Rudra to the classical deity

items.reveal: Shiva is one of the most important gods in Hinduism, worshipped both as an ascetic who sits in meditation on a remote mountain and, in a very different aspect, as Lord of the Dance, whose cosmic dance is said to both create and destroy the universe. In the myth of the Ganges' descent from heaven, it is Shiva who catches the falling river in his own hair, breaking its fall so it doesn't shatter the earth below. Shiva developed gradually out of an earlier Vedic storm god named Rudra; a much older carved seal found at Mohenjo-daro, showing a horned figure seated in a meditative pose, has been claimed by some as an early proto-Shiva figure, which, if true, would push his origins back an entire additional millennium, though the claim is disputed and unprovable as long as the Indus script itself remains unread.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A prince kept from seeing anything unpleasant, who saw four things and left the palace that night.

time.label: Union of the long and short chronologies

items.reveal: Siddhartha Gautama, who would later become known as the Buddha, was born a prince and was deliberately kept inside the palace by his father, sheltered from ever witnessing suffering, old age, sickness, or death. According to tradition, he eventually saw all four of these things anyway during trips outside the palace walls, and was so shaken by what he saw that he left his royal life behind that same night to search for a way to end human suffering. His exact dates remain uncertain: calculating backward from the more securely dated reign of the later emperor Ashoka produces different results depending on whether Sri Lankan or Indian historical traditions are used, so even the century of his birth isn't fully settled among scholars.
items.flag: 163-year window — the widest in this batch. The book uses the traditional long chronology (563-483); most specialists since Bechert have moved to a death date near 400. If you would rather ask a real question than avoid a wrong answer, score the book's 563-483 and put the dispute in the reveal.

items.subtitle: Forest dialogues asking what is behind the ritual — and answering that the self and the ultimate are the same thing.

place.label: The Ganges plain, east of Delhi

items.reveal: The Upanishads are a collection of Hindu philosophical texts, often written as dialogues that take place in forest settings, exploring what deeper meaning or truth lies behind traditional religious rituals. Their central teaching is that a person's innermost self, called atman, and the ultimate reality underlying the entire universe, called Brahman, are actually one and the same thing. They were composed at roughly the same time as the Hebrew prophets, the earliest Greek philosophers, and Confucius in China, a strikingly similar cluster of new religious and philosophical thinking across separate civilizations that some historians call the "Axial Age," though whether this timing is meaningful or simply a coincidence is a genuinely open question.

items.subtitle: Hymns memorised syllable by syllable and passed down by voice for a thousand years before anyone wrote them.
items.reveal: The Vedas are Hinduism's oldest sacred texts, a large collection of hymns, chants, and ritual instructions that were composed, memorized, and passed down entirely by spoken word for many centuries before anyone wrote them down. To keep the memorized text from drifting or changing over such a long period, reciters used specific, deliberately redundant patterns of repeating and rearranging the words, a system designed specifically to catch and correct any mistakes, and it worked: scholars believe the text has come down through the centuries with extraordinary accuracy. The Vedas are considered among the oldest surviving literature in any Indo-European language, the large language family that also includes English, Greek, and Persian.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Fragments of conversation collected by students — the Master said, and then a sentence.
items.reveal: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and brief conversations involving the Chinese philosopher Confucius, mostly following a simple pattern: "the Master said," followed by a single line of teaching. Confucius himself never wrote any of it down; the text was instead assembled after his death by his students, and in some cases by the students of his students. This same pattern, a teacher's original words surviving only through later disciples writing them down generations afterward, also describes how the Christian Gospels and many Buddhist scriptures came into being, all within roughly the same few centuries across very different parts of the world.

items.subtitle: A minor official who could not get a ruler to employ him, and spent his life teaching instead.

place.label: Qufu, in the state of Lu

items.reveal: Confucius was a Chinese philosopher and minor government official who spent much of his career trying, unsuccessfully, to convince a ruler to actually employ him and put his political ideas into practice. Unable to find such a position, he spent much of his life teaching students instead, emphasizing respect for tradition, proper conduct, and moral character in both rulers and ordinary people. He considered himself something of a failure during his own lifetime, seeing himself as a transmitter of older wisdom rather than an original innovator, and he lived at roughly the same time as the Buddha in India and the birth of democracy in Athens, on the other side of the ancient world.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Said to have left China westward on an ox, stopping at the pass only because a guard asked him to write something down first.

time.label: Traditional 6th century; the text is 4th-3rd century

items.reveal: Laozi, whose name simply means "Old Master," is the legendary founder of Taoism, traditionally said to have grown so disillusioned with the corruption of Chinese court life that he decided to leave China entirely, riding west out of the country on an ox. According to legend, he only agreed to write down his teachings after a border guard stopped him and asked him to record his wisdom before he disappeared, and the resulting short book became known as the Daodejing. Most modern scholars doubt that Laozi was actually a single historical person at all, and think the Daodejing was more likely composed gradually by multiple authors, with "Old Master" functioning more as a title or literary device than as the name of one real individual.

items.subtitle: Heaven appoints the ruler and can withdraw the appointment — so a successful rebellion proves it already has.

time.label: From the Zhou conquest onward; scored to the end of the ancient period (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: The Mandate of Heaven is a Chinese political idea holding that a ruler's right to govern comes from the approval of Heaven itself, but that Heaven can withdraw that approval from a ruler who becomes unjust or incompetent. In a clever piece of political logic, the theory also holds that a successful rebellion against a ruler is itself proof that Heaven had already withdrawn its support, meaning the very act of successfully overthrowing a government justifies having done so. The idea was originally invented by the Zhou dynasty to justify its own violent overthrow of the earlier Shang dynasty, and Chinese rulers and rebels alike continued invoking the same doctrine to justify both holding power and seizing it for roughly the next three thousand years.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The Zhou kings still on the throne, and nobody paying attention to them.
items.reveal: The Spring and Autumn period gets its name from a chronicle recording events in the Chinese state of Lu, a chronicle traditionally credited to Confucius himself. During this period, kings of the Zhou dynasty technically still sat on China's throne, but real political and military power had shifted almost entirely to the rulers of individual regional states, who increasingly ignored the Zhou kings altogether. Warfare between these rival states during this era was still conducted according to shared aristocratic codes of conduct and honor, a restraint that would break down completely in the far more brutal Warring States period that followed.

items.subtitle: Thirteen chapters arguing that the best battle is the one you never have to fight.

place.label: The state of Wu, lower Yangtze

items.reveal: The Art of War is a short but highly influential Chinese military treatise, spread across thirteen brief chapters, whose central argument is that the very best kind of victory is one achieved through clever strategy and positioning rather than through actual fighting at all. It is traditionally credited to a strategist named Sun Tzu, said to have lived in the state of Wu along the lower Yangtze River. Whether Sun Tzu was really a single historical individual, similarly to the debate over Laozi, remains genuinely disputed among scholars, and some think the text may instead be a compiled work by multiple later authors writing under his name.

items.prompt: The Period of the Warring States
items.subtitle: Seven kingdoms, mass conscript armies with crossbows, and no rules left.
items.reveal: The Warring States period was an era of near-constant warfare among seven major rival kingdoms competing for control of China, marked by huge conscripted armies equipped with powerful crossbows and by the near-total breakdown of the more restrained rules of warfare that had governed the earlier Spring and Autumn period. Paradoxically, this brutal, unstable era was also one of the most creative and productive periods in the entire history of Chinese philosophy, since rival thinkers from many different schools of thought competed intensely to offer struggling rulers the best advice on how to survive and govern effectively. The period finally ended when one of the seven warring kingdoms, Qin, succeeded in conquering all the others and unifying China under a single rule.

items.subtitle: China's longest dynasty, which spent its last five centuries unable to control anyone.

place.label: The Yellow River valley, ruled from Luoyang

items.reveal: The Zhou dynasty was China's longest-ruling royal dynasty, governing, at least in name, from its capital at Luoyang in the Yellow River valley for nearly eight centuries. For roughly the last five hundred of those years, however, the Zhou kings held only symbolic authority and had essentially no real ability to control the increasingly independent regional states that were nominally still under their rule. Historians generally think the Zhou kings genuinely governed with real power for perhaps only the first 250 years or so of this very long dynasty, with the rest consisting of gradual, then total, decline.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Argued for the Sicilian expedition, was recalled to stand trial, defected to Sparta, then to Persia, then came home to a hero's welcome.
items.reveal: Alcibiades was a brilliant but famously unreliable Athenian politician and general, a student of the philosopher Socrates, who convinced Athens to launch its disastrous military expedition against Sicily during the Peloponnesian War. Shortly after the campaign began, he was recalled to Athens to stand trial on serious charges, but instead of returning to face them, he defected first to Athens's enemy Sparta, and later to Persia, before eventually returning to Athens once again to a hero's welcome. His remarkable, repeatedly self-serving career is often cited as one of the strongest contemporary arguments that Athenian democracy, for all its achievements, struggled to control the very talented, ambitious individuals it sometimes produced.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: An alliance against Persia whose treasury Athens moved to Athens, and whose members discovered they could not leave.
items.reveal: The Delian League was a military alliance of Greek city-states formed to continue defending against the threat of Persian invasion, originally headquartered on the sacred island of Delos, with each member state contributing ships or money to a shared treasury. Athens, as the alliance's leading member, eventually moved that shared treasury from Delos to Athens itself, and it was money from this fund that helped pay for the construction of the Parthenon. Over time, member states discovered they were no longer free to simply leave the alliance whenever they wished; the historian Thucydides bluntly describes the Delian League as having become, in practice, an Athenian empire in all but name, and has Athenian speakers in his history openly admit as much themselves.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Greek cities under Persian rule rebel, Athens sends twenty ships, and the Great King asks who these Athenians are.
items.reveal: The Ionian Revolt began when Greek cities along the coast of Asia Minor, then under Persian control, rose up in rebellion against Persian rule. Athens sent a modest force of twenty ships to help the rebels, a contribution that ultimately did little to change the revolt's outcome, which was defeated by Persia. According to the historian Herodotus, this minor Athenian involvement angered the Persian king Darius so much that he ordered a servant to repeat the phrase "master, remember the Athenians" to him at every single meal, ensuring the insult was never forgotten, and it was this grudge that set in motion the much larger Persian invasions of Greece that followed.

items.subtitle: Outnumbered hoplites charge at a run across the last stretch of open ground, and the Persian line does not hold.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Marathon, a heavily outnumbered force of Athenian soldiers, called hoplites, famously charged at a run across the last open stretch of ground toward the invading Persian army, catching the Persians off guard and breaking their battle line. The Greek historian Herodotus records roughly 192 Athenian dead against some 6,400 Persian casualties, a striking imbalance that modern historians generally treat with considerable caution, since ancient battle casualty figures were often exaggerated for effect. Notably, Sparta's own soldiers, considered the finest in Greece, arrived only the day after the battle was already won, having been delayed by a religious festival they were unwilling to interrupt.

items.subtitle: Twenty-seven years of Athens at sea against Sparta on land, and neither able to reach the other.
items.reveal: The Peloponnesian War was a long, exhausting conflict between Athens and Sparta and their respective allies, lasting twenty-seven years, in which Athens's strength lay mainly at sea while Sparta's strength lay on land, meaning neither side could easily strike a decisive blow directly against the other for a very long time. The war was eventually recorded in unusually rich detail by the historian Thucydides, who had actually fought in it himself and was later exiled from Athens after failing to prevent the loss of a city under his command. His resulting history is considered the first major work to explain human events through careful, rational analysis of politics and human motivation, rather than by attributing them to the will of the gods.

items.subtitle: A messenger runs the twenty-five miles back to the city, delivers one word, and dies.
items.reveal: According to a famous legend, after the Battle of Marathon, a messenger ran roughly twenty-five miles from the battlefield back to Athens, delivered a single word, "Nike," meaning "victory," and then immediately collapsed and died from the exertion. This particular version of the story does not actually appear anywhere in Herodotus, our earliest and most reliable source for the battle, whose own account instead describes a runner named Pheidippides who ran about 150 miles to Sparta to request military help before the battle even began, and who survives the ordeal. The famous dying-messenger version of the story doesn't appear in surviving sources until roughly 600 years later, in the writings of Plutarch and Lucian, and the modern marathon race's specific distance of 26.2 miles was only fixed as recently as 1908, chosen simply to match the layout of the London Olympic course that year.

items.subtitle: Wrote his teacher into every book, and founded a school in an olive grove that ran for 900 years.
items.reveal: Plato was an Athenian philosopher and devoted student of Socrates, who wrote nearly all of his surviving philosophical works in the form of dialogues in which his teacher Socrates is the central speaker. He founded a school of philosophy called the Academy, located in an olive grove outside Athens, which continued operating for roughly 900 years after his death. Witnessing Athens's democratic government vote to execute his beloved teacher Socrates left Plato permanently distrustful of democracy as a system of government, a deep skepticism that runs through much of his most famous work, the Republic.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The Greeks let themselves be trapped in a narrow strait, where a bigger fleet was a worse fleet.

place.label: The straits of Salamis, off Athens

items.reveal: At the Battle of Salamis, the outnumbered Greek fleet deliberately allowed itself to be drawn into a narrow sea strait, a location where the much larger Persian fleet's numerical advantage actually became a serious disadvantage, since its ships had too little room to maneuver freely against the more agile Greek vessels. The Persian king Xerxes reportedly watched the entire battle unfold from a specially placed throne set up on the shore overlooking the strait. According to tradition, the Athenian commander Themistocles had deliberately sent Xerxes a false message claiming the Greeks were about to retreat, luring the overconfident Persian fleet into the narrow waters where it could be decisively defeated.

items.subtitle: Athens sends its fleet 800 miles west in the middle of a war it has not won, and gets none of it back.
items.reveal: During the middle of an already difficult and unresolved war against Sparta, Athens made the risky decision to send its main fleet nearly 800 miles west to attack the powerful city of Syracuse, on the island of Sicily. The campaign ended in complete catastrophe: the entire expedition, roughly two hundred ships and forty thousand men, was destroyed or captured, with almost none of it ever returning home to Athens. The historian Thucydides closes his account of the disaster by simply noting that of the many who went, few returned home, a line that has since become one of the most frequently quoted warnings in history about the dangers of military overreach.

items.subtitle: Convicted of corrupting the young and not believing in the city's gods, he declines to escape and drinks the hemlock.
items.reveal: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher put on trial and convicted by an Athenian jury on charges of corrupting the city's young people and failing to believe in Athens's official gods. Rather than accepting an offer to escape into exile before his sentence could be carried out, he chose to remain in Athens and accept the court's verdict, drinking a cup of poisonous hemlock as his prescribed execution. His trial took place only five years after Athens had lost the long and exhausting Peloponnesian War, and his own close personal association with Alcibiades and other prominent Athenians who had betrayed the city during the war forms an unspoken political backdrop to the formal charges brought against him, one the official accusations themselves never directly mention.

items.subtitle: A pass wide enough for one cart, held for three days, until somebody showed the Persians a path over the mountain.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Thermopylae, a small Greek force held a narrow mountain pass, wide enough for only a single cart to pass through at a time, against a massively larger invading Persian army for three full days. The defenders were finally overcome only after a local resident showed Persian forces a hidden mountain path that let them outflank the Greek position from behind. The defense is popularly remembered today as "the 300 Spartans," but in reality several thousand allied soldiers from other Greek city-states fought alongside them, a detail usually left out of the more dramatic version of the story; the coastline near the battle site has also since silted up so extensively that the actual battlefield now lies roughly a mile inland from the modern shore.

items.subtitle: Never lost a battle, and had run out of world he was interested in by the age of thirty-two.
items.reveal: Alexander the Great was a king of Macedonia who conquered a vast empire stretching from his home in Macedonia all the way to the Punjab region of northwest India, and remarkably, he never lost a single battle throughout his entire military career. By the time he was thirty-two years old, he had run out of any territory he was still genuinely interested in conquering. What actually stopped his conquests wasn't military defeat at all, but his own exhausted army, which finally refused to march any farther east once it reached the Beas River in India, forcing Alexander to turn back.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: He marked out the street plan with barley meal, and the birds ate it — which the seers decided was a good omen.
items.reveal: When Alexander the Great founded the Egyptian city that would bear his name, Alexandria, he reportedly marked out its planned street layout using barley meal scattered on the ground, since no other suitable marking material was available; birds then swooped in and ate the barley, which local religious advisers interpreted as a favorable omen for the new city's future. Alexander went on to found perhaps twenty different cities across his empire that he also named Alexandria after himself. This particular Egyptian Alexandria was by far the most successful of them all, growing into the largest and most important city in the entire Mediterranean world for the next three centuries.

items.subtitle: Plato's best student, Alexander's tutor, and the man who tried to classify everything there is.
items.reveal: Aristotle was one of ancient Greece's greatest philosophers, considered the most brilliant student of Plato's philosophical school, the Academy, and he later went on to personally tutor the young Alexander the Great before Alexander began his famous conquests. Aristotle's own scholarly interests were extraordinarily broad, and he attempted to observe, describe, and classify an enormous range of subjects, from biology and physics to ethics, politics, and logic. His original Greek writings were largely lost to Western Europe for centuries during the medieval period, and were reintroduced mainly through Arabic translations and commentary, which is part of why the medieval philosopher Thomas Aquinas, writing centuries later, simply refers to Aristotle as "the Philosopher," as though no other needed naming.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The Greek city-states lose their independence in an afternoon, to a kingdom they had thought half-barbarian.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Chaeronea, the combined forces of the Greek city-states, led by Athens and Thebes, were decisively defeated in a single afternoon by the army of Macedonia, a kingdom many Greeks had previously dismissed as barely civilized. The battle ended Greek city-states' independence for good, bringing them permanently under Macedonian control. Thebes's elite fighting unit, the Sacred Band, died fighting where it stood rather than retreat, and a stone lion monument still marks their mass grave today; excavation there found 254 skeletons buried beneath it, and the eighteen-year-old prince Alexander, the future Alexander the Great, personally commanded the Macedonian cavalry unit that broke through and defeated them.

items.subtitle: A fever at thirty-two, and no heir — asked who should have the empire, he is said to have answered: the strongest.
items.reveal: Alexander the Great died suddenly of a fever in Babylon at only thirty-two years old, having conquered one of the largest empires the world had ever seen but leaving behind no clear adult heir to inherit it. According to legend, when his generals asked him on his deathbed who should receive his empire, he answered simply: "the strongest," an answer that virtually guaranteed decades of war among his former commanders. Historians have long debated what actually killed him, with theories ranging from malaria and typhoid fever to deliberate poisoning; his embalmed body was later hijacked en route back to Macedonia by one of his generals, Ptolemy, who took it to Egypt instead, where it remained on public display even during Roman times before being lost entirely at some point afterward.

items.subtitle: Forty years of Alexander's generals fighting over the pieces, until three of them are left.
items.reveal: After Alexander the Great's sudden death left no clear heir, his former generals, known to historians as the Diadochi, or "successors," fought each other for control of pieces of his enormous empire for roughly forty years. This brutal power struggle eventually claimed the lives of nearly all of Alexander's own family, including his mother, his wife, and his young son, all murdered in the course of the fighting. By the time the dust settled, Alexander's once-unified empire had been permanently carved up into several separate successor kingdoms, having actually held together as one unified state for less than two years after his death.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Darius picks flat ground and levels it further for his chariots; Alexander rides at a gap in the line and the Great King runs.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Gaugamela, the Persian king Darius III chose flat, open ground and had it further leveled to give his war chariots room to maneuver, but Alexander the Great instead drove his cavalry directly at a gap that opened in the Persian line, causing Darius to flee the battlefield. This decisive Macedonian victory effectively brought about the end of the Persian Empire as an independent power. Remarkably, the exact date of the battle, 1 October 331 BC, can be confirmed precisely thanks to a surviving Babylonian astronomical record that also happens to note a lunar eclipse occurring eleven days beforehand.

items.subtitle: Whoever unties it will rule Asia, said the oracle, and he found a way that was not untying.
items.reveal: According to legend, an oracle had prophesied that whoever managed to untie an extremely elaborate knot tying an old wagon to a post in the city of Gordium would go on to rule all of Asia. When Alexander the Great arrived and was unable to find either end of the knot to untie it normally, he is famously said to have simply drawn his sword and sliced straight through it instead. One ancient version of the story instead has him quietly pull out a hidden pole-pin to release the yoke without cutting anything at all, a cleverer solution, though far less dramatic and memorable than the sword version that became the popular legend.

items.subtitle: Every ship entering the harbour had its books seized and copied — the library kept the originals and returned the copies.

time.label: From its founding under Ptolemy II to its decline

items.reveal: The Library of Alexandria was an enormous ancient collection of books and scrolls established in the Egyptian city of Alexandria, said to have operated in part through a policy of seizing and copying books found aboard every ship that entered the city's harbor, keeping the original copy for the library's own collection and returning only a duplicate to the ship's owner. It aimed to gather a copy of essentially every significant text in the ancient world. Contrary to the popular image of the library being destroyed in one single dramatic fire, historians now think it actually declined gradually over several centuries, through a combination of reduced funding, wartime damage, and simple long-term neglect, a considerably less dramatic but more historically accurate story than the one usually told.

items.subtitle: Built the army his son would use, took Greece with it, and was murdered at his daughter's wedding.
items.reveal: Philip II of Macedon transformed his kingdom's military into a formidable, highly disciplined professional fighting force, which his son Alexander the Great would later use to conquer a vast empire. Using this reformed army, Philip successfully brought the independent Greek city-states under Macedonian control. He was assassinated at his own daughter's wedding celebration, and Alexander inherited not just his father's throne, but also this already-powerful military instrument, including the sarissa, an eighteen-foot-long pike that Philip's army had pioneered using.

items.subtitle: A Macedonian family ruling Egypt as pharaohs for three centuries, in Greek, from a Greek city.
items.reveal: Ptolemaic Egypt was the kingdom ruled for nearly three centuries by the Ptolemies, a Macedonian Greek family descended from one of Alexander the Great's own generals, who took the traditional Egyptian title of pharaoh while governing the country largely in Greek, from their capital at the Greek-founded city of Alexandria. Remarkably, not a single ruler in this long dynasty bothered to actually learn the Egyptian language until its very last ruler, the famous Cleopatra VII. The dynasty came to an end with Cleopatra's death, after which Egypt was absorbed as a province of the Roman Empire.

items.subtitle: The largest and most unmanageable of Alexander's fragments, stretching from Anatolia toward India and shrinking every generation.
items.reveal: The Seleucid Empire was the largest, but also the least stable and hardest to govern, of the several kingdoms that emerged from the breakup of Alexander the Great's empire, stretching at its peak from Anatolia in the west toward India in the east, though it steadily lost territory to rivals and rebellions with each passing generation. Its rulers eventually attempted to force Greek religious practices onto the Jewish population of Judea, a policy that provoked the Maccabean revolt in 167 BC. That successful Jewish rebellion against Seleucid rule is the historical origin of the holiday of Hanukkah, which is part of why this otherwise sprawling and often chaotic empire still matters to the story this corpus is telling.

items.subtitle: Conquered one more kingdom, was appalled at what he had done, and spent the rest of his reign apologising in stone.

place.label: The Mauryan Empire, ruled from Pataliputra

items.reveal: Ashoka was a Mauryan emperor of India who, after winning a brutally violent war of conquest, was reportedly so horrified by the massive suffering it had caused that he spent the rest of his reign publicly renouncing further military conquest and promoting nonviolence and moral rule instead, carving his new principles into rock inscriptions across his empire. The writer H. G. Wells later called him possibly the only military monarch on historical record to have genuinely renounced war after winning a decisive victory. Ashoka was largely forgotten within India itself for roughly two thousand years, and his historical importance was only rediscovered once his scattered inscriptions were finally deciphered by scholars in 1837.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Instructions on mercy, vegetarianism, and shade trees, cut into rocks and polished pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka.

place.label: Across the empire: Sarnath, Sanchi, Dhauli, Kandahar

items.reveal: The edicts of Ashoka are a large collection of moral and administrative instructions the Mauryan emperor had carved onto rock faces and tall polished stone pillars set up across his enormous empire, covering subjects from mercy toward prisoners and animals to planting shade trees along roads for travelers. These inscriptions have been found scattered from as far away as Afghanistan to as far south as Karnataka in southern India. One edict found at Kandahar, in modern Afghanistan, is written in Greek and Aramaic rather than an Indian language, specifically addressed to the Greek-speaking populations Alexander the Great's conquests had left behind in the region; the carved lion capital found atop a similar pillar at Sarnath has since become the official emblem of the modern Republic of India.

items.subtitle: Took northern India while Alexander's generals were still quarrelling, and traded five hundred war elephants for the Indus provinces.
items.reveal: Chandragupta Maurya seized control of much of northern India while Alexander the Great's former generals were still busy fighting each other over the pieces of his empire, and went on to found the Mauryan Empire. He later negotiated a treaty with one of those generals, Seleucus, trading five hundred war elephants in exchange for gaining control of territory near the Indus River. According to Jain religious tradition, Chandragupta eventually abdicated his throne voluntarily and died by deliberate fasting as a religious ascetic, and his elephant-for-territory deal with Seleucus stands as the earliest documented diplomatic exchange between India and the Mediterranean world.

items.subtitle: Five hundred and forty-seven stories of the Buddha's previous lives, most of them as an animal.
items.reveal: The Jataka tales are a large collection of 547 traditional stories describing the Buddha's many previous lives before his final human birth, in most of which he actually appears in the form of an animal rather than as a person. These stories were used to teach moral lessons about virtues like generosity, patience, and wisdom. Remarkably, some of these tales appear to have traveled all the way west along trade routes and turn up, in altered form, in the Greek fables attributed to Aesop and in later medieval European story collections, making them one of the few clearly demonstrable examples of a story genuinely spreading across the entire span of ancient Eurasia.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A hundred thousand dead and a hundred and fifty thousand deported — and the victor says so himself, in an inscription, with regret.

place.label: Kalinga, on the Bay of Bengal

items.reveal: The Kalinga war was a brutal military campaign fought by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka to conquer the independent kingdom of Kalinga, on India's Bay of Bengal coast, resulting in roughly a hundred thousand deaths and the forced deportation of another hundred fifty thousand people. Unusually, the victorious emperor himself later wrote candidly about the war's horrific human cost in one of his own rock inscriptions, expressing genuine remorse rather than simply boasting of victory as most ancient rulers did. That inscription, known as the thirteenth Rock Edict, stands as the only known ancient royal inscription anywhere in the world that describes its author's own military victory as a source of regret rather than pride.

items.subtitle: The great vehicle — an argument that the goal is not to escape alone but to stay and bring everyone else along.
items.reveal: Mahayana Buddhism, whose name means "the great vehicle," is a major branch of Buddhism built around the idea that the highest spiritual goal isn't simply to escape suffering for oneself alone, but to remain engaged with the world and help guide every other being toward enlightenment as well. This particular branch of Buddhism was the version that eventually spread eastward along the Silk Road into China, Korea, and Japan, becoming the dominant form of Buddhism practiced across East Asia. Sculptors working in the region of Gandhara, in an artistic style directly inherited from the Greek kingdoms Alexander the Great's successors had left behind in the area, are credited with creating the very first images ever made showing the Buddha in human form, rather than only through earlier symbolic representations.

items.subtitle: The first state to rule nearly all of India, run by a bureaucracy and a great many spies.
items.reveal: The Mauryan Empire was the first state in history to bring nearly the entire Indian subcontinent under one unified government, administered through an extensive bureaucracy and famously supported by a large network of official spies and informants. It reached its greatest extent and influence under the emperor Ashoka. The empire actually continued limping along in a weakened state for roughly another fifty years after Ashoka's death before finally collapsing entirely; a surviving manual of practical statecraft from this period, the Arthashastra, offers startlingly cold, calculating political advice, considered by many historians even more ruthlessly pragmatic than anything the later Italian writer Machiavelli ever put in writing.

items.subtitle: A capital nine miles long behind a timber palisade with 570 towers, described by a Greek ambassador who lived there.

time.label: As an imperial capital (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: Pataliputra was the grand imperial capital of the Mauryan Empire, a city stretching roughly nine miles along the Ganges River, protected by a massive timber wall studded with 570 defensive towers. A Greek ambassador named Megasthenes, sent to the Mauryan court by the Seleucid ruler Seleucus, lived in the city for a time and wrote the earliest surviving detailed foreign description of India to reach the Mediterranean world. Most of the ancient city now lies directly beneath the modern Indian city of Patna, making large-scale archaeological excavation of the ancient site essentially impossible today.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The three baskets — discipline, discourses, and analysis — memorised for four centuries and then finally written on palm leaves.
items.reveal: The Tripitaka, meaning "three baskets," is the core collection of early Buddhist scripture, traditionally divided into three sections covering monastic discipline, the Buddha's own recorded teachings, and detailed philosophical analysis. For roughly four centuries after the Buddha's death, this entire body of teaching was preserved purely through memorization and oral recitation by generations of monks, rather than being written down. It was finally committed to writing on palm leaves in Sri Lanka during a severe famine, when the monks who had until then carried the entire text in memory were dying faster than new monks could be trained to memorize and replace them.

items.subtitle: A temple in a high Andean valley honeycombed with dark passages, at the centre of a cult that spread across Peru.
items.reveal: Chavín de Huántar was a major religious center built high in a valley of the Peruvian Andes, its temple complex honeycombed with a maze of dark interior passages and galleries. It became the focal point of a widely shared religious and artistic culture that spread across much of ancient Peru, making it something of an Andean counterpart to the roughly contemporary Olmec civilization of Mexico. It is generally considered the earliest widely shared culture to emerge in South America, influencing art and religious practice across a wide surrounding region.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Seventeen basalt portraits up to eleven feet high, each in a helmet, hauled fifty miles from the nearest source of that stone.

time.label: Carved during the San Lorenzo phase

items.reveal: The Olmec colossal heads are seventeen enormous stone sculptures, carved from solid basalt and standing as tall as eleven feet, each showing a distinct human portrait wearing what looks like a fitted helmet. The basalt stone used to carve them had to be hauled roughly fifty miles from the nearest quarry that had it, an extraordinary feat of labor and organization given that Olmec civilization had no wheeled vehicles or large draft animals to help move such enormous weights, likely relying instead on rafts and log rollers. Because each head has distinctly individual facial features rather than a single generic face repeated, archaeologists generally believe they were meant to depict specific, real Olmec rulers.

items.subtitle: An Olmec centre on an island in a swamp, with the earliest pyramid in Mesoamerica — made of clay.
items.reveal: La Venta was a major Olmec religious and political center, built on what was effectively an island rising out of a surrounding swamp, and it contains the earliest known pyramid anywhere in Mesoamerica, though this early pyramid was built simply from mounded clay rather than from cut stone. Archaeologists excavating the site have found elaborate buried offerings, including detailed mosaic pavements made from carefully arranged blocks of serpentine stone, laid out to form the image of a jaguar's face. Strikingly, these elaborate mosaic offerings were deliberately covered over and buried again almost immediately after being completed, meaning they were created specifically to be hidden from view rather than to be seen and admired.

items.subtitle: A calendar counting days continuously from a starting point in 3114 BC, which is how Maya dates can be converted exactly to ours.

place.label: The Maya area and the Isthmus

time.label: Earliest to latest known Long Count dates (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: The Maya Long Count was a calendar system used by ancient Mesoamerican civilizations that counted days continuously forward from a single fixed starting point corresponding to 3114 BC on the modern calendar, rather than resetting on a repeating cycle the way many other ancient calendars did. Because this starting point can be precisely calculated, Long Count dates carved on ancient Maya monuments can be converted exactly into corresponding modern calendar dates. Mesoamerican astronomers using this calendar system tracked the movement of the planet Venus accurately enough that their calculations were off from the true value by only about two hours per century, and the widely publicized "end of the world in 2012" scare some years back was simply based on one long calendar cycle completing and rolling over to begin again, exactly the kind of thing calendars are designed to do.

items.subtitle: Dozens of rival kingdoms in the rainforest, with stone cities, a written history, and mathematics including zero.

time.label: Preclassic through Classic Maya (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: The Maya were a civilization made up of dozens of separate, often rival kingdoms spread across the rainforests of the Yucatán peninsula, Guatemala, and Belize, who built elaborate stone cities, kept detailed written historical records, and developed a sophisticated mathematical system that included the concept of zero. Contrary to a common misconception, the Maya never actually disappeared as a people. While the great Classic-period cities of the rainforest lowlands were largely abandoned by around AD 900, several million people across the region still speak Mayan languages and maintain Maya cultural traditions today.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: The only fully worked-out writing system invented in the Americas — and it records kings, wars, and dates.

time.label: Period of use (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: Maya writing is the only fully developed writing system known to have been independently invented anywhere in the Americas, capable of recording detailed information about specific kings, wars, and exact calendar dates. Modern scholars only really succeeded in deciphering most of the script starting in the 1970s, largely by finally accepting an insight that had been resisted for decades: that many of the symbols represented actual spoken sounds, not just abstract ideas or whole words. Spanish colonial friars later burned nearly all of the original Maya books they found, believing them to be pagan and dangerous; only four of these original books are known to have survived to the present day.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Farmers of a coastal desert who dug underground aqueducts still in use today, and buried trophy heads.

time.label: Nazca culture (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: The Nazca were a civilization of farmers living in an extremely dry coastal desert region of southern Peru, who engineered impressive underground aqueduct systems, called puquios, to bring water to their fields, systems still in active use by local farmers today. They are also well known for burying so-called "trophy heads," severed human heads prepared and kept as part of their religious or ceremonial practices. Their region remains one of the driest inhabited places on Earth, receiving only a few millimeters of rainfall per year, and it is precisely this extreme dryness that has allowed the Nazca's famous large-scale ground drawings, or geoglyphs, to survive largely undisturbed for many centuries.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A hummingbird 300 feet long, a monkey with a spiral tail, and straight lines running for miles — made by moving stones aside.
items.reveal: The Nazca lines are enormous ground drawings scratched into the desert surface of the Nazca plain in Peru, created simply by moving aside the dark surface stones to reveal the lighter-colored ground underneath, forming huge images such as a hummingbird some 300 feet long and a monkey with a distinctive spiral tail, along with perfectly straight lines running for miles across the landscape. Researchers have demonstrated that designs this large and precise could realistically have been laid out using nothing more than wooden stakes and lengths of cord, without needing any advanced technology. The leading explanation among archaeologists is that the lines and figures served as ritual pathways connected to sources of water, important in such an extremely dry environment; the popular idea that they were created for or by visitors from space has no serious archaeological support at all.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Mesoamerica's first civilization, in swampy lowlands, with a taste for jade, rubber, and jaguars.
items.reveal: The Olmecs were the first major civilization to develop in Mesoamerica, based in the swampy lowlands along the Gulf coast of Mexico, known for their skilled work in carved jade, their early use of natural rubber, and their artistic fascination with jaguar imagery. They are often called the "mother culture" of later Mesoamerican civilizations, since features like the Mesoamerican ballgame, calendar systems, and the layout of pyramids around open plazas all appear to trace back to Olmec origins. Remarkably, the Olmecs developed methods of processing natural rubber roughly a thousand years before any other civilization in the world is known to have done so.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A grid-planned city of 125,000 with two enormous pyramids, abandoned so long before the Aztecs that they assumed the gods had built it.

time.label: Occupation (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: Teotihuacan was a massive, carefully grid-planned city in the Valley of Mexico, home to as many as 125,000 people at its height and dominated by two enormous pyramids. By the time the much later Aztec civilization encountered its ruins, the city had already been abandoned for so long that the Aztecs assumed it must have been built by gods rather than by ordinary human beings, and gave it its current name, which means roughly "the place where the gods were created." Remarkably little is actually known about the people who built and ruled it: no royal portraits, king lists, or fully readable writing have ever been found there, so historians don't even know what its own inhabitants called the city, what language they spoke, or exactly who governed it.

items.subtitle: The queen of roads — polygonal basalt blocks fitted so closely that stretches are still drivable.

place.label: Rome to Capua, later extended to Brundisium

time.label: From Appius Claudius's censorship to the Brundisium extension

items.reveal: The Appian Way was one of ancient Rome's most important roads, originally built to connect Rome to the city of Capua and later extended much further to the port of Brundisium, earning it the nickname "the queen of roads." It was paved with tightly fitted polygonal blocks of hard volcanic basalt stone, engineered so precisely that some stretches of the original road surface remain drivable even today, over two thousand years later. The road was originally built to move Roman armies quickly to the front lines during the Samnite wars, and in 71 BC, following the defeat of a massive slave rebellion led by Spartacus, some six thousand of his surviving followers were crucified at intervals along its entire length, from Capua all the way to Rome.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Water brought fifty miles on a gradient of a few inches per mile, mostly underground, arcaded only where the ground fell away.

time.label: From the Aqua Appia to the Aqua Alexandrina

items.reveal: The Roman aqueducts were an extensive system of channels engineered to bring fresh water into the city of Rome from sources up to fifty miles away, using an extraordinarily gentle downward slope of only a few inches per mile to keep water flowing steadily by gravity alone. Most of each aqueduct ran underground for practical and defensive reasons, only rising onto the tall stone arches most people picture today where the natural terrain dropped away and needed to be bridged. At the system's peak, eleven separate aqueducts supplied the city with roughly a million cubic meters of water a day, providing a per-person water supply that most of Europe would not match again until the nineteenth century.

items.subtitle: Goddess of grain and the harvest, whose temple doubled as the headquarters of the common people.

time.label: From the dedication of the Aventine temple

items.reveal: Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain and the harvest, and her temple on Rome's Aventine Hill served a double purpose, functioning at the same time as an important political headquarters for Rome's common citizens, known as plebeians. Her name survives today in the everyday word "cereal." The location of her temple on the Aventine, deliberately positioned as a plebeian counterweight to the patrician nobility's stronghold on the Capitoline Hill, reflects Roman political rivalry between social classes at least as much as it reflects religious devotion.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Found at his plough, made dictator, won the war in sixteen days, and went back to the plough.
items.reveal: Cincinnatus was a Roman farmer, according to legend found working his own plow, who was urgently called upon by the Roman Senate to accept absolute emergency power as dictator during a serious military crisis. He led Rome's army to victory in only sixteen days, and then, rather than clinging to the immense power he had been given, promptly resigned his position and returned quietly to farming his land. The Roman historian Livy, writing about four centuries after these events supposedly took place, clearly knew exactly what moral lesson he wanted the story to teach; the legend mattered enormously to America's own founders, who nicknamed George Washington "the American Cincinnatus" for similarly giving up power voluntarily, and the city of Cincinnati is named after a society of American Revolutionary War officers who took Cincinnatus's name as their own model of civic virtue.

items.subtitle: Matched by type rather than at random — a man with a big shield and short sword against a man with a net and trident.

time.label: From the first recorded munus to the last games at Rome

items.reveal: Roman gladiators were professional fighters who battled in carefully matched pairs, typically pitting different fighting styles against each other rather than simply matching combatants at random, such as a heavily armored fighter carrying a large shield and short sword against a more lightly equipped opponent fighting with a net and trident. The practice began as a solemn funeral ritual meant to honor important dead Romans, and only gradually developed into large-scale public entertainment. Because trained gladiators represented a considerable financial investment, most contests were not actually intended to end in death; historians estimate that perhaps only around one bout in ten during the early Roman Empire ended with a fighter being killed.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Two faces, one looking forward and one back — god of doorways, beginnings, and the gate that stood open whenever Rome was at war.

place.label: The Janus Geminus in the Forum, Rome

items.reveal: Janus was a uniquely Roman god, shown with two faces looking in opposite directions at once, one toward the future and one toward the past, and was associated with doorways, beginnings, and transitions of all kinds. His temple, the Janus Geminus in the Roman Forum, had a special pair of doors that Roman custom required to be left standing open during any time Rome was actively at war, and closed only during times of genuine peace. Unlike most Roman gods, Janus has no equivalent at all in Greek mythology, making him a genuinely original Roman religious invention; the later emperor Augustus proudly boasted of having closed the temple's doors three separate times during his reign, a rare achievement, since in the seven centuries before him the doors had reportedly only been closed twice, and the month of January still carries his name today.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Best and greatest — sky-father, thrower of lightning, and the god a victorious general dressed as during his triumph.

time.label: From the dedication of the Capitoline temple to the ban on public sacrifice

items.reveal: Jove, more commonly known as Jupiter, was the king of the Roman gods, ruler of the sky and famously associated with thunder and lightning; a Roman general celebrating a formal military triumph would dress up specifically to resemble Jupiter for the occasion. His name is directly related, through a shared ancient linguistic ancestor, to both the Greek "Zeus" and the Sanskrit "Dyaus Pita," since "Jupiter" literally breaks down to mean "sky-father" in Latin. His grand temple on Rome's Capitoline Hill was formally dedicated in the very first year of the Roman Republic, right after Rome expelled its last king.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Queen of the gods and guardian of Rome, whose sacred geese are said to have woken the garrison when the Gauls came up the cliff.

place.label: The temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx, Rome

time.label: From the dedication of Juno Moneta

items.reveal: Juno was queen of the Roman gods, wife of Jupiter, and served as a special protective guardian of the city of Rome itself. According to legend, when Gallic invaders once attempted to sneak up a steep cliff to attack Rome's citadel by surprise at night, the honking of sacred geese kept in Juno's temple woke the sleeping garrison in time to repel the attack. Rome's official mint for producing coins was actually housed inside her temple, and her particular title there, Moneta, meaning roughly "the warner," is the direct linguistic ancestor of the modern English words "money" and "mint."
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: God of war and father of the twins — and taken far more seriously in Rome than his Greek counterpart ever was in Greece.

time.label: From the dedication of his temple outside the walls

items.reveal: Mars was the Roman god of war, and according to Roman mythology, the father of the legendary twins Romulus and Remus who founded Rome. Unlike the Greek war god Ares, who was generally viewed by the Greeks with suspicion and even contempt, the Romans took Mars extremely seriously, ranking him second in importance only to Jupiter himself and naming an entire month, March, directly after him. This sharp contrast in how each culture treated its own war god reveals a great deal about the differing values and self-image of Greek versus Roman civilization.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Carried off to the underworld and allowed back for part of each year — the Roman name for a Greek story.

time.label: From the establishment of her state cult

items.reveal: Proserpine was the Roman name for the same goddess the Greeks called Persephone, carried off by the god of the underworld to become his wife, but permitted to return to the surface world for part of each year, an arrangement Romans, like the Greeks, used to explain the changing seasons. Her worship was formally imported into Rome from the Greek cities of southern Italy during the First Punic War. Roman religious officials consulted a set of prophetic texts called the Sibylline Books before deciding to bring her cult officially into the city, a common Roman practice of adopting useful foreign gods rather than inventing entirely new ones.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Hot room, warm room, cold plunge, and a floor raised on brick pillars with a furnace underneath.
items.reveal: Roman public baths typically included a sequence of rooms at different temperatures, moving from a hot steam room through a warm room and finally to a cold plunge pool, with floors raised on rows of small brick pillars so hot air from a furnace underneath could circulate and heat the rooms from below. The largest of these complexes, such as the Baths of Caracalla, could accommodate as many as 1,600 bathers at once, and included additional amenities like libraries and formal gardens. Entry typically cost only about a quarter of a day's price of bread, meaning Roman baths functioned as genuine mass public infrastructure available to ordinary citizens, not as an exclusive luxury reserved only for the wealthy.

items.subtitle: A household including slaves and freedmen, headed by a father with legal power of life and death over all of it.
items.reveal: The Roman familia was a legal household unit that included not just blood relatives but also enslaved people and formerly enslaved freedmen living under one roof, all placed under the absolute legal authority of the household's oldest living male head, called the paterfamilias. Under Roman law, this authority, known as patria potestas, technically gave a father legal power of life and death over every member of his household. This power was extraordinary even by ancient standards, and technically applied to adult sons regardless of their own age or status, meaning even a powerful forty-year-old Roman senator remained, in strict legal theory, still under his own father's absolute authority; in actual practice, though, this extreme power was almost never exercised to its full legal extent.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A drained marsh between the hills where Romans went to shop, sue, vote, gossip, and hear the news.

time.label: In use as the civic centre

items.reveal: The Roman Forum was the civic and social heart of ancient Rome, built in what had originally been a marshy valley drained and leveled between several of the city's famous seven hills, and it served as the place where Romans went to shop, bring lawsuits, vote on public matters, socialize, and hear the latest public news. The valley had originally been drained by the Etruscans, using a large sewer called the Cloaca Maxima, built as early as the sixth century BC. Remarkably, that same ancient sewer system is still, in part, connected to Rome's modern drainage infrastructure today.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Five thousand men in small manoeuvrable units, who dug a fortified camp every single night whether or not an enemy was near.

time.label: From the manipular reform to the high empire

items.reveal: The Roman legion was Rome's standard military unit, typically made up of around five thousand soldiers organized into smaller, flexible, independently maneuverable groups, and legionaries were expected to dig and fortify a defensible camp every single night while on campaign, whether or not any enemy force was known to be nearby. Rome's real military advantage over its rivals came less from any single superior weapon than from this kind of relentless engineering discipline, combined with a seemingly limitless willingness to recruit fresh soldiers to replace battlefield losses again and again. Rome actually lost more individual battles over its history than most of its major enemies did, but it nonetheless managed to win essentially every war that ultimately mattered.

items.subtitle: Goddess of love, and — through Aeneas — the claimed ancestress of the Julian family.

place.label: Rome; her temple in Caesar's forum

time.label: From the temple of Venus Erycina

items.reveal: Venus was the Roman goddess of love and beauty, equivalent to the Greek Aphrodite, and according to Roman legend, she was also the divine ancestor of the powerful Julian family, through her mortal son, the Trojan hero Aeneas. Julius Caesar, a member of that same Julian family, built Venus a grand temple within his own new forum in Rome and openly emphasized his claimed descent from her. This connection conveniently gave Caesar's own family a claim to literal divine ancestry, which proved useful for a politician who was already facing accusations of secretly wanting to make himself king.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: Six priestesses who kept a fire alight for a thousand years, sworn to chastity for thirty — and buried alive if they broke it.
items.reveal: The Vestal Virgins were an order of six Roman priestesses whose central religious duty was keeping a sacred fire continuously burning in the temple of the goddess Vesta for well over a thousand years, and who were bound by a strict vow of chastity for a thirty-year term of service; a Vestal who broke that vow faced the extraordinarily harsh punishment of being buried alive. Uniquely among Roman women, Vestal Virgins were legally permitted to own property in their own name, write a will, and give testimony in court without needing a male guardian to represent them. Romans genuinely believed the safety and good fortune of the entire Roman state depended on that sacred fire never being allowed to go out.
items.precisionLabel: known only as a long era

items.subtitle: A deliberately weak centre gives way, the wings hold, the cavalry closes the back — and the largest army Rome ever fielded is surrounded and killed.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Cannae, the Carthaginian general Hannibal deliberately let his weaker center give ground under Roman attack while his stronger flanks held firm, then closed his cavalry in around the back of the advancing Roman army, completely surrounding and destroying the largest single army Rome had ever put into the field. Roman casualties that single afternoon are estimated at around fifty thousand dead, a rate of killing by hand-to-hand combat not matched again in warfare until the twentieth century. Despite this catastrophic defeat, Rome refused to negotiate for peace, instead raising entirely new legions and continuing the war.

items.subtitle: A trading power ruling the western sea from Spain to Sicily, fighting its wars with hired soldiers.

place.label: North Africa, western Sicily, Sardinia, and southern Spain

items.reveal: The Carthaginian empire was a powerful trading state based in North Africa that came to dominate much of the western Mediterranean Sea, controlling territory stretching from Spain to Sicily, largely through naval power and by hiring foreign mercenary soldiers to fight its wars rather than relying mainly on its own citizens. Almost everything modern historians know about Carthage comes from the writings of its eventual enemies and conquerors, particularly the Romans, since virtually no Carthaginian written accounts of their own history survive today. This means the historical picture of Carthage that has come down to us is inevitably shaped by the perspective of the people who ultimately destroyed it.

items.prompt: Claudius Pulcher and the sacred chickens
items.subtitle: Told the chickens would not eat and the omens were bad, he threw them overboard so they could drink instead — and then lost the fleet.
items.reveal: Before a naval battle, Roman commanders traditionally consulted sacred chickens, and the omens were considered favorable only if the chickens ate eagerly when offered food. When the Roman commander Claudius Pulcher was told his sacred chickens refused to eat, meaning the omens for battle were bad, he reportedly threw the chickens overboard instead, joking that if they wouldn't eat, they could at least drink, and then went on to lose the naval battle disastrously anyway. Upon his return to Rome, he was formally tried and fined, not specifically for losing ninety-three ships in the defeat itself, but for the religious offense of impiety, since Roman religion placed enormous importance on performing traditional rituals correctly and respectfully, which Claudius had openly mocked.

items.subtitle: Thirty-seven elephants, snow in October, a landslide blocking the path, and about half the army left by the bottom.
items.reveal: During the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led his invading army, including thirty-seven war elephants, across the western Alps into Italy, battling early snowfall in October and a landslide that blocked the mountain path partway through the crossing. By the time his forces reached the bottom on the Italian side, roughly half of the army that had started the crossing had been lost to the harsh conditions along the way. Exactly which mountain pass Hannibal actually used has been debated by historians for two centuries, though a 2016 scientific study found a layer of churned-up soil and horse manure dating to the right period at the Col de la Traversette, a strong candidate for the actual route; only a single one of the original thirty-seven elephants is known to have survived through the following winter.

items.subtitle: A city that had not threatened Rome for fifty years is besieged for three, taken street by street, and erased.
items.reveal: Even though the city of Carthage had posed no real military threat to Rome for roughly fifty years, Roman forces besieged it for three years before finally capturing and utterly destroying it street by street, effectively erasing the city from existence. The Roman senator Cato the Elder had famously ended every single speech he gave in the Senate, no matter the topic under discussion, by declaring his opinion that Carthage must be destroyed. The popular modern story that Roman soldiers deliberately sowed the ruined city's fields with salt to prevent anything from ever growing there again is actually a nineteenth-century invention with no support in any ancient source.

items.subtitle: A land power decides to build a navy, copies a wrecked enemy ship, and adds a boarding bridge so its soldiers can fight on deck.
items.reveal: The First Punic War began when Rome, traditionally a land-based military power with little experience at sea, decided it needed to build its own war fleet in order to compete with Carthage, reportedly by copying the design of a wrecked Carthaginian ship that had washed ashore, and adding a hinged boarding bridge, called a corvus, that let Roman soldiers fight their preferred style of close combat directly on an enemy ship's deck. Over the course of the war, Rome lost several entire fleets, perhaps around a hundred thousand men altogether, to violent storms at sea, yet simply built replacement fleets each time rather than giving up. The corvus boarding bridge, while tactically useful, also made Roman ships dangerously top-heavy and unstable, which was part of why so many of them were lost to bad weather in the first place.

items.subtitle: Made to swear at nine years old that he would never be a friend to Rome, and kept it for the next fifty.
items.reveal: Hannibal was a Carthaginian general who, according to legend, was made by his father at age nine to swear a solemn oath that he would remain an enemy of Rome for his entire life, an oath he kept for the following fifty years. He led Carthaginian forces against Rome in a long and devastating war, invading Italy directly and famously bringing war elephants across the Alps to do so. After his final defeat, Hannibal spent years in exile from Carthage and eventually took poison rather than allow himself to be captured and handed over to the Romans; Roman military commanders studied his tactics for centuries afterward, and his famous double-envelopment maneuver at the Battle of Cannae is still taught in military academies today.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime
