items.subtitle: Three wars over 118 years between the two powers of the western Mediterranean, ending when there is only one.

place.label: Italy, Sicily, Spain, and North Africa

items.reveal: The Punic Wars were three separate major wars fought over a span of 118 years between Rome and Carthage, the two dominant powers of the western Mediterranean, ending only once one of the two powers, Carthage, had been completely destroyed. The word "Punic" comes from the Latin word for "Phoenician," since Carthage had originally been founded centuries earlier as a colony of Phoenician settlers from Tyre. By naming their long rivalry after the enemy's distant ethnic origin, the Romans were, in effect, still identifying Carthage by where its founders had come from seven hundred years before.

items.subtitle: Survived Cannae as a young officer, learned from the man who inflicted it, and beat him with his own tactics.
items.reveal: Scipio Africanus survived the catastrophic Roman defeat at Cannae as a young military officer, and rather than being discouraged, he studied and learned from the very tactics Hannibal had used to inflict that devastating loss. He eventually applied lessons learned from his old enemy to defeat Hannibal decisively himself at the Battle of Zama, effectively winning the Second Punic War for Rome. Remarkably, Scipio and Hannibal both died in the very same year, each having fallen out of favor with his own home city by that point; Scipio, bitter about how Rome had treated him despite his service, specifically asked not to be buried in the very city he had saved.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: Sixteen years with an undefeated enemy army camped inside Italy, and Rome refusing to negotiate for any of them.
items.reveal: The Second Punic War saw the Carthaginian general Hannibal maintain an undefeated army camped inside Italy itself for sixteen consecutive years, inflicting repeated defeats on Roman forces, yet Rome consistently refused to negotiate any kind of peace settlement with him throughout the entire ordeal. Hannibal's entire strategy for the war depended on convincing Rome's Italian allies to abandon Rome and join his cause instead. Rome's crucial advantage, and the reason it ultimately won the war despite Hannibal's battlefield successes, was that the vast majority of those Italian allies chose to remain loyal to Rome rather than defect, denying Hannibal the additional troops and resources he desperately needed.

items.subtitle: Scipio leaves lanes open in his line so the charging elephants run harmlessly through, and Hannibal loses his only battle.
items.reveal: At the decisive Battle of Zama, the Roman general Scipio Africanus deliberately left open lanes running through his battle line, so that Hannibal's charging war elephants would simply run harmlessly through the gaps rather than trampling Roman soldiers, neutralizing what had once been one of Hannibal's most feared weapons. Scipio went on to win the battle decisively, handing Hannibal the only defeat of his entire military career. While the exact date of the battle is well established, its precise location in inland Tunisia has never been confirmed archaeologically, with several candidate sites proposed but none conclusively identified; as a direct result of this defeat, Carthage lost its war fleet, most of its overseas territory, and was forbidden from ever waging war again without first getting Rome's explicit permission.

items.subtitle: Histories of the conquered states, and the Confucian classics, ordered destroyed — so that the past could not be used to criticise the present.
items.reveal: Under the first emperor of China's Qin dynasty, an official decree ordered the destruction of historical records from the states China's Qin rulers had recently conquered, along with copies of the Confucian classics, specifically so that references to the past could not be used to criticize or undermine the emperor's present policies. Practical technical works on subjects like medicine, farming, and fortune-telling were specifically excluded from the order and allowed to survive. The later Han dynasty historians who recorded this event held a strong dislike for the Qin dynasty they had replaced, so the true scale of the book-burning may be somewhat exaggerated in their accounts, though the resulting loss of pre-Qin Chinese historical records is nonetheless considered genuine and significant.

items.subtitle: A work gang delayed by rain, facing execution for lateness either way, decides it may as well rebel.

time.label: From the first rising to the dynasty's end

items.reveal: According to tradition, the collapse of China's Qin dynasty began when a group of conscripted laborers, delayed on their way to a work assignment by heavy rain, realized that Qin law required execution for arriving late regardless of the reason, and concluded they had nothing left to lose by rebelling instead of continuing on to face certain punishment. This uprising is considered the first recorded peasant rebellion in Chinese history, and it demonstrated in practice that the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that Heaven grants and can withdraw a ruler's legitimacy, could be invoked by ordinary rebels just as easily as by a new dynasty's founders. The Qin dynasty collapsed entirely only about four years after its founding emperor's death.

items.subtitle: Existing frontier walls joined into one line by conscripts and convicts, rammed earth rather than the stone tourists photograph.
items.reveal: The Great Wall of China, in its earliest form, was created when China's first unifying emperor ordered several separate pre-existing regional frontier walls joined together into one continuous defensive line along the northern border, built largely using forced labor from conscripted workers and convicted criminals. This original Qin-era wall was constructed mainly from rammed earth, not the impressive cut stone that modern tourists typically photograph and associate with the wall today. The famous brick-faced sections most visitors see near Beijing were actually built roughly seventeen centuries later, during the Ming dynasty, and stand hundreds of miles from where the original Qin wall ran, most of which has since disappeared entirely; despite a popular myth, the wall has never actually been visible to the naked eye from space.

items.subtitle: Kept the Qin machinery and dropped the cruelty — four centuries so successful that Chinese people still call themselves by its name.
items.reveal: The Han dynasty inherited much of the centralized government structure the earlier Qin dynasty had built, but abandoned the Qin's notoriously harsh, punishing style of rule, going on to govern China successfully for roughly four centuries. Its rule was considered such a golden age that Chinese people still commonly refer to themselves today as "the Han people," using the dynasty's own name as an ethnic and cultural identity. The Han Empire existed at roughly the same time as the Roman Empire, and was comparable to it in both size and population, with valuable goods like silk traveling back and forth between the two great empires along early trade routes, even though neither civilization actually knew very much about the other.

items.subtitle: Fifteen years of the harshest government China had seen, and the template every later dynasty used.
items.reveal: The Qin dynasty governed China for only fifteen years, but imposed what was, by contemporary standards, the harshest and most rigidly controlling government China had yet experienced, built around a governing philosophy called Legalism. Legalism held that people are fundamentally selfish by nature, that laws must therefore be strict, uniform, and harshly enforced without exception, and that Confucian talk of ruling through virtue and moral example was, in practice, a dangerous distraction from effective government. This harsh system worked well enough to unify China's previously separate warring states into a single empire, but it collapsed only a few years later, and every Chinese dynasty that followed borrowed heavily from the centralized administrative structure the Qin had first put in place.

items.subtitle: Six rival kingdoms swallowed one at a time in nine years, and for the first time one ruler from the steppe to the southern rivers.

place.label: The Qin conquests across north and central China

items.reveal: The unification of China took place over just nine years, as the state of Qin conquered six separate rival Chinese kingdoms one after another, bringing them all for the first time under the rule of a single ruler, from the northern steppe frontier all the way to the rivers of southern China. China has fractured apart and been reassembled into separate warring states many times again since this original unification, but it has always eventually come back together into something recognizably similar in shape and extent to this first unified state. The very name "China" itself, used in English and many other languages, is thought to derive directly from the name of the Qin dynasty that first achieved this unification.

items.subtitle: King of one state at thirteen, master of all of them at thirty-eight, and thereafter First Emperor — a title he invented.

place.label: Xianyang, the Qin capital, near modern Xi'an

items.reveal: Qin Zheng became king of his home state of Qin at only thirteen years old, and by the time he was thirty-eight, he had conquered every rival Chinese kingdom and unified the country for the first time, taking for himself an entirely new title of his own invention: Shi Huangdi, meaning "First Emperor." He ruled his new empire from the capital city of Xianyang, near modern Xi'an. He spent his later years obsessively searching for a way to achieve physical immortality, and likely died from mercury poisoning caused by pills he had been taking in that very pursuit; his empire itself outlived him by only about four more years before collapsing entirely.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: One script, one currency, one set of weights — and a fixed axle width, so that carts would fit the same ruts everywhere.
items.reveal: Under the Qin dynasty, China's first emperor ordered sweeping standardization reforms across his newly unified empire, establishing a single official writing script, one standard currency, one uniform system of weights and measures, and even a fixed standard width for cart axles, so that wheeled vehicles would fit consistently into the same wheel-ruts on roads everywhere in the empire. Of all these reforms, the standardization of the Chinese writing script proved by far the most historically durable and consequential. Because written Chinese characters represent meaning directly rather than recording specific pronunciation, speakers of otherwise mutually unintelligible regional Chinese dialects could still read and understand exactly the same written documents, arguably making this single reform the strongest unifying force holding Chinese civilization together as one culture ever since.

items.subtitle: Eight thousand life-size soldiers in battle order, each with a different face, buried in pits facing east.
items.reveal: The Terracotta Army is a vast collection of roughly eight thousand life-size clay soldier statues, arranged in realistic battle formation and each sculpted with distinctly individual facial features, buried in underground pits facing east near the tomb of China's first emperor. It was discovered entirely by accident in 1974, when local farmers digging a well happened to strike buried fragments of the ancient statues. The emperor's own actual burial mound nearby has never been opened by archaeologists; ancient written accounts claim it contains rivers of flowing liquid mercury inside, and modern soil surveys around the mound have indeed detected unusually high concentrations of mercury in the surrounding ground, lending some credibility to the old descriptions.
items.precisionLabel: dated to a reign or lifetime

items.subtitle: The Qin capital, where the emperor had replicas of each conquered kingdom's palace built as trophies.
items.reveal: Xianyang served as the capital of the Qin dynasty, where China's first emperor reportedly had exact replica palaces built for each of the rival kingdoms he had conquered, displaying them as trophies of his conquest. The city was burned to the ground, reportedly over a period of as long as three months, when the short-lived Qin dynasty finally collapsed. The nearby city of Xi'an, just a few miles away, went on to serve as China's capital for most of the following thousand years.

items.subtitle: Caesar builds one wall facing in and a second facing out, and fights a relief army and a besieged army at the same time.
items.reveal: At the siege of Alesia, the Roman general Julius Caesar had his forces build two massive parallel walls of fortification around the besieged Gaulish stronghold: one facing inward to keep the trapped defenders from escaping, and a second facing outward to hold off a large relief army arriving from outside, letting his troops fight both enemy forces simultaneously. His soldiers dug roughly twenty-five miles of fortifications in only a few weeks. The Gaulish leader Vercingetorix eventually surrendered to Caesar, was held prisoner for six years afterward, and was finally executed by strangulation as part of the public celebration marking Caesar's official triumph back in Rome.

items.subtitle: Two crossings to an island most Romans doubted existed, both of them achieving very little except the crossing.
items.reveal: Julius Caesar led two separate military expeditions across the English Channel to Britain, an island many Romans at the time doubted even genuinely existed, though both expeditions achieved relatively little beyond simply managing to make the crossing at all. Caesar's forces took no lasting territory in Britain and left no permanent garrison behind after either expedition. Even so, the political and propaganda value back home in Rome, of having a Roman general reach such a distant, half-mythical island, was considered enormous; actual Roman conquest and occupation of Britain would not happen for nearly another century, under the emperor Claudius.

items.subtitle: Chasing Pompey, he is handed a head he did not want and finds a queen in a civil war with her brother.
items.reveal: Chasing his defeated rival Pompey to Egypt, Julius Caesar arrived expecting to find him there, but was instead handed Pompey's severed head by Egyptian officials hoping to please him, a gift Caesar reportedly did not want and was horrified to receive. He found Egypt itself in the middle of a civil war between the young queen Cleopatra and her own brother, and Caesar ultimately intervened on Cleopatra's side. The famous story of Cleopatra having herself smuggled into Caesar's presence rolled up inside a carpet actually comes from the later writer Plutarch, who specifically describes it as a bed-sack rather than a carpet; part of Alexandria's famous library district was accidentally burned during the fighting that broke out while Caesar was there.

items.subtitle: A general, a financier, and an ambitious politician agree privately to run the Republic between them.

time.label: From the compact to Crassus's death

items.reveal: The First Triumvirate was an informal private political arrangement among three of Rome's most powerful men, a successful general, a wealthy financier, and an ambitious rising politician, who agreed privately among themselves to jointly dominate Roman politics and share power between them. It was never an official government office and had no legal standing whatsoever; it functioned purely as a private understanding between Julius Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus. The arrangement collapsed after Crassus was killed leading a disastrous military invasion of Parthia, leaving only two powerful rivals, Caesar and Pompey, with no third partner left to help mediate between them.

items.subtitle: Eight years of campaigning that gave Rome a new province, and Caesar an army loyal to him rather than to the Senate.
items.reveal: The Gallic Wars were an eight-year military campaign led by Julius Caesar to conquer the region of Gaul, roughly modern-day France, which both expanded Roman territory with a valuable new province and gave Caesar personal command of a large, battle-hardened army whose loyalty belonged to him personally rather than to the Roman Senate. Caesar wrote his own detailed account of the campaign himself, written in the third person as though narrated by someone else, and published it back in Rome in serialized installments as the fighting progressed, functioning simultaneously as a military dispatch and a piece of political self-promotion. The Greek writer Plutarch later estimated that roughly a million Gauls were killed during the campaign and another million enslaved, though such ancient casualty figures are difficult to verify precisely.

items.subtitle: Captured by pirates as a young man, he complained their ransom demand was too low, and crucified them after they let him go.
items.reveal: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and politician who, according to a famous anecdote, was once captured by pirates as a young man and reportedly complained that the ransom they demanded for his release was insultingly too low, jokingly suggesting they ask for more; once freed after the ransom was paid, he raised a fleet, hunted the very same pirates down, and had them crucified. He went on to conquer Gaul, win a civil war against his political rivals, and effectively end the Roman Republic by concentrating power in his own hands. His family name, Caesar, later became the direct source of the word for "emperor" in German (Kaiser), Russian (Tsar), and Turkish, among other languages.

items.subtitle: Outnumbered two to one, Caesar hides a fourth line behind his cavalry and tells them to strike at the faces of Pompey's young noblemen.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Pharsalus, though heavily outnumbered roughly two to one, Julius Caesar hid an additional, unexpected fourth line of veteran soldiers behind his own cavalry, with specific orders to aim their weapons directly at the faces of Pompey's inexperienced young noble cavalrymen, correctly gambling that vanity and fear of disfigurement would break their nerve faster than ordinary combat would. The tactic worked, and Caesar won a decisive victory that effectively settled the outcome of Rome's civil war in his favor. After the battle, Caesar showed considerable mercy, pardoning most of the defeated survivors who had fought against him, including Brutus, who would later become one of Caesar's own assassins.

items.subtitle: Cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in three months, conquered the east, and was then outmanoeuvred by his own father-in-law.
items.reveal: Pompey the Great was a celebrated Roman general who cleared the entire Mediterranean Sea of pirate fleets in only about three months and went on to conquer large territories in the eastern Mediterranean, expanding Roman power significantly. Despite his military successes, he was later politically outmaneuvered by his own former ally and son-in-law, Julius Caesar, in the civil war that eventually broke out between them. After being decisively defeated, Pompey fled to Egypt seeking refuge, but was murdered by Egyptian officials the moment he stepped ashore, hoping to win favor with the victorious Caesar; Caesar himself is said to have wept with genuine grief when he was later presented with Pompey's severed head.

items.subtitle: A stream a general may not cross with an army, and a decision that cannot be taken back.
items.reveal: The Rubicon was a small stream in northern Italy that, under Roman law, no general was permitted to cross while leading an army into Italy proper, since doing so was considered an open declaration of civil war against the Roman state itself. When Julius Caesar deliberately led his own legion across the Rubicon anyway, it marked a decisive, irreversible political choice, launching him directly into civil war against the Roman Senate. Caesar is said to have remarked "the die is cast," a gambler's expression about a decision that cannot be undone, likely spoken in Greek rather than Latin; exactly which small modern stream corresponds to the ancient Rubicon was actually disputed by historians until as recently as 1933, since the original stream had been so minor that nobody had bothered recording its exact location precisely at the time.

items.subtitle: A campaign concluded in five days, and reported to the Senate in three words.
items.reveal: "Veni, vidi, vici," Latin for "I came, I saw, I conquered," is the famously brief message Julius Caesar reportedly sent back to the Roman Senate after concluding an entire military campaign in only five days. He wrote it following his swift, decisive defeat of King Pharnaces of Pontus at the Battle of Zela, in northern Anatolia. The three Latin words are notable for rhyming and having matching rhythmic structure in the original Latin, which is likely exactly why the phrase was carefully composed and preserved for posterity — it was a deliberately crafted piece of writing meant to be memorable, not simply an offhand spoken remark.

items.subtitle: A naval battle in which one fleet breaks out and runs, and the war is over anyway.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Actium, a major naval engagement fought off the western coast of Greece, the combined fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra suffered such a serious setback partway through the fighting that a large portion of it, including Cleopatra's own ships, broke away and fled the battle entirely. Their army, left without naval support, largely surrendered afterward without any further major fighting, effectively deciding the entire war. This battle is generally considered the conventional end point of both the Roman Republic and the wider Hellenistic world founded by Alexander the Great's successors; Egypt, the very last of those Hellenistic successor kingdoms to survive independently, became a Roman province the following year.

items.subtitle: A Roman general and the last pharaoh of Egypt, whose alliance was also a marriage and also a bid for the whole east.
items.reveal: Mark Antony was a powerful Roman general and political leader, and Cleopatra VII was the last independent pharaoh of Egypt; their political alliance, which was also a genuine romantic partnership and marriage, represented a serious joint attempt to control the entire eastern Mediterranean world together. Cleopatra herself was ethnically Macedonian Greek rather than Egyptian, descended from one of Alexander the Great's own generals, and she was actually the very first ruler in her three-hundred-year dynasty to bother learning to speak the Egyptian language. After their defeat, Antony's rival Octavian's own political propaganda deliberately portrayed Cleopatra as a scheming foreign seductress who had corrupted a good Roman general, since attacking Antony directly as a fellow Roman would have looked uncomfortably like starting another Roman civil war.

items.subtitle: Kept every republican form and all the actual power, and called himself merely first citizen.
items.reveal: Caesar Augustus, originally named Octavian, became Rome's first emperor while carefully preserving the outward appearance of every traditional Republican political office and institution, even while actually holding all real political and military power personally; he modestly referred to himself as princeps, meaning simply "first citizen," rather than claiming any grander royal title. He famously boasted that he had found Rome a city built of brick and left it a city built of marble, reflecting his extensive building program. He ruled for forty-one years following his victory at Actium, long enough that, by the time he died, almost nobody left alive could actually remember a time when the Roman Republic had genuinely functioned.

items.subtitle: The last men to kill for the Republic, and the men who ended it — the tyrannicide produced a civil war and then an emperor.
items.reveal: Brutus and Cassius were Roman senators who led the conspiracy to assassinate Julius Caesar, believing they were saving the Roman Republic from being turned into a monarchy. Ironically, their act of tyrannicide instead triggered a new round of civil war, which ultimately ended not with the Republic restored, but with an even more powerful single emperor, Augustus, in control. Both men eventually died by their own hand after being decisively defeated in battle at Philippi; Brutus, notably, claimed descent from the legendary Roman who had originally expelled Rome's last king back in 509 BC, meaning his family had, by his own account, been fighting against monarchy in Rome for some 460 years.

items.subtitle: He asked whether he had played his part well in the comedy of life, and told his friends to applaud as he went out.
items.reveal: As he lay dying, the Roman emperor Augustus reportedly asked those gathered around him whether he had played his part well in what he compared to a stage comedy representing his own life, and asked his friends to applaud as he made his exit. His death marked the end of a reign that had lasted over four decades. The true test of whether Augustus had actually built something lasting came immediately afterward: power passed to his successor without triggering renewed civil war, something that had seemed almost unthinkable a few decades earlier; the modern month of August is named directly in his honor.

items.subtitle: Twenty-three wounds at the foot of a statue of the man he had beaten, delivered by senators he had pardoned.
items.reveal: Julius Caesar was assassinated by a group of Roman senators, receiving twenty-three stab wounds, at the base of a statue of his former rival Pompey, a man Caesar had already decisively defeated in war. Many of the men who killed him were senators Caesar had personally pardoned after that same civil war, sparing their lives. The assassination actually took place not in the Senate's usual meeting hall, but in an assembly room attached to Pompey's theater, since the Senate's own building was being rebuilt at the time; the Roman historian Suetonius records that Caesar's last words were spoken in Greek and addressed directly to Brutus, one of the men stabbing him.

items.subtitle: Nineteen years old, holding an office with a minimum age of forty-two, having marched on Rome to ask for it.
items.reveal: Octavian, Julius Caesar's adopted heir and the future emperor Augustus, became consul, one of Rome's two highest annually elected offices, at only nineteen years old, despite Roman law setting the minimum legal age for the position at forty-two. He achieved this remarkable feat by marching an army on Rome himself and essentially demanding the Senate grant him the position. The statesman Cicero had initially supported the young Octavian, believing he would be an easily manageable political ally, but Cicero was proscribed, meaning declared an enemy of the state, and killed within months of Octavian gaining real power.

items.subtitle: Two centuries in which a traveller could go from Britain to the Euphrates on Roman roads, in one currency, without crossing a frontier.

time.label: From Augustus to the death of Marcus Aurelius

items.reveal: The Pax Romana, Latin for "Roman peace," refers to roughly two centuries during which a traveler could journey all the way from Britain to the Euphrates River using Roman-built roads, spending a single common currency, without ever having to cross a heavily defended international border. This long era of relative internal peace and stability across the Roman world came at the cost of near-continuous warfare being fought along the empire's external frontiers to maintain it. The Roman historian Tacitus, notably, records a British chieftain accusing the Romans of making a desert and then calling it peace, a striking case of a Roman historian himself putting this exact criticism directly into the mouth of one of Rome's own conquered enemies.

items.subtitle: Two engagements three weeks apart, and both assassins dead by their own hands rather than captured.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Philippi, forces loyal to the assassinated Julius Caesar decisively defeated the army of his killers, Brutus and Cassius, in two separate engagements fought roughly three weeks apart. Rather than allow themselves to be captured, both Brutus and Cassius chose to take their own lives following their respective defeats. Centuries later, the early Christian missionary Paul founded a church in this very same town, and his letter addressed to that church, known as the Epistle to the Philippians, is preserved today as a book of the New Testament.

items.subtitle: An imperial secretary with access to the archives, who wrote twelve biographies full of omens, rumours, and other people's bedrooms.
items.reveal: Suetonius was a Roman writer who served as an imperial secretary with direct personal access to official government archives, and used that access to write a collection of twelve detailed biographies of Rome's earliest emperors, filled with vivid anecdotes about omens, palace rumors, and the private lives of powerful Romans. Many of the most memorable and colorful stories people know today about Rome's early emperors come directly from his writing. Suetonius was not especially careful about verifying his sources before including a juicy story, so historians generally recommend reading him alongside the more careful, if considerably gloomier, Roman historian Tacitus for a more balanced picture.

items.subtitle: A census, no room at the inn, and a manger in a town of a few hundred people.

time.label: Union of the book's date and the common scholarly range

items.reveal: According to the Gospel of Luke, Jesus was born in the small town of Bethlehem in Judea while his parents were there to be counted in a Roman census, and because no room was available at the local inn, he was laid in a manger, a feeding trough for animals, shortly after his birth. Bethlehem itself was a genuinely tiny settlement at the time, home to only a few hundred people. Working out the actual calendar year of Jesus's birth is famously tricky: the Gospel of Matthew places it before the death of King Herod the Great, usually dated to 4 BC, meaning Jesus was likely born a few years "before Christ" by later reckoning; this odd discrepancy traces back to a mathematical miscalculation made by the monk Dionysius Exiguus, who invented the modern AD dating system itself back in AD 525.

items.subtitle: A Roman execution reserved for slaves and rebels, carried out under a prefect who did not want the case.
items.reveal: The crucifixion of Jesus was a Roman method of execution normally reserved for enslaved people and those the Romans considered dangerous rebels, and it was carried out under Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect governing Judea at the time, who according to the Gospels was personally reluctant to condemn Jesus. Historians generally place the exact year of the crucifixion as either AD 30 or AD 33, since both years are calendrically consistent with Gospel details about the timing of Passover falling on the correct day of the week that year. Notably, the event is also independently mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus, entirely separate from any Christian religious source, providing outside historical confirmation that the execution took place.

items.subtitle: A client king who built magnificently and killed three of his own sons — better to be his pig than his son, Augustus is supposed to have said.
items.reveal: Herod the Great ruled Judea as a client king under Roman authority, known both for his enormously ambitious building projects, including a dramatic expansion of the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, and for his ruthless paranoia toward anyone he suspected of threatening his throne, including three of his own adult sons, whom he had executed. The Roman emperor Augustus is supposed to have joked, in a pun that only works in Greek, that it was safer to be Herod's pig than his son, since as an observant Jew, Herod would never have one of his pigs slaughtered. A minority of modern scholars argue Herod actually died in 1 BC rather than the more commonly cited 4 BC, a distinction that matters directly for dating the traditional nativity story of Jesus's birth.

items.subtitle: The second temple rebuilt on a platform of stones weighing hundreds of tons, on a scale nothing in Judea had approached.

time.label: From the start of works to their completion

items.reveal: Herod's Temple was King Herod the Great's massive reconstruction and expansion of Jerusalem's Second Temple, built on an artificially enlarged platform supported by retaining walls made of individual stone blocks weighing hundreds of tons each, on a scale nothing previously built in Judea had ever approached. Construction took decades to fully complete. Remarkably, the temple complex was only finished in its final form about six years before Roman forces destroyed it entirely during the Jewish Revolt; part of the massive supporting retaining wall from Herod's platform survives today as Jerusalem's Western Wall, one of Judaism's holiest sites.

items.subtitle: A small, difficult province governed by prefects who did not understand it and garrisoned by troops recruited from neighbours who disliked it.

time.label: From Pompey to the Bar Kokhba revolt

items.reveal: Roman Judea was a relatively small but persistently difficult Roman province to govern, administered by Roman officials called prefects who frequently failed to understand local Jewish religious sensitivities, and it was garrisoned by Roman auxiliary troops often recruited from neighboring peoples who had their own historical grievances against the local Jewish population. Rome's usual approach to governing conquered peoples was to let them keep worshipping their own traditional gods, simply adding those gods alongside Rome's existing collection of deities without much difficulty. Judaism's firm, uncompromising insistence on worshipping only one god, and refusing that usual Roman religious arrangement, created an ongoing governing problem that Rome ultimately never fully managed to resolve in this particular province.

items.subtitle: A Seleucid king puts a pagan altar in the temple, and a village priest's family fights back and wins.
items.reveal: The Maccabean revolt began after the Seleucid king ruling Judea installed a pagan altar inside the sacred Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, provoking a rebellion led by a village priest's family, known afterward as the Maccabees. Against significant odds, this relatively small Jewish rebel force succeeded in defeating Seleucid forces and winning genuine independence. The rededication of the cleansed and restored temple in 164 BC is the direct historical origin of the modern Jewish holiday of Hanukkah, and the independent Jewish kingdom the Maccabees established afterward, known as the Hasmonean kingdom, remained the last fully independent Jewish state in the ancient world until the modern nation of Israel was founded in 1948.

items.subtitle: A village in the Galilean hills so obscure that no earlier writer mentions it at all.
items.reveal: Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hills of Galilee, so minor and unremarkable during ancient times that no surviving writer before the Christian era ever mentions it at all in any other context. Archaeological excavation of the site suggests it was home to perhaps only two to four hundred people at most during this period. Notably, the substantial and actively growing Roman-era city of Sepphoris sat only about four miles away from this tiny village, meaning Nazareth's inhabitants would have had regular, close contact with a genuinely significant regional city nearby.

items.subtitle: Invited in to settle a quarrel between two brothers, he besieges the temple mount and then walks into the Holy of Holies to look.
items.reveal: The Roman general Pompey was originally invited into Jerusalem to help settle a political dispute between two rival Jewish brothers competing for power. Instead, he ended up laying siege to the Temple Mount itself, and after capturing it, he personally walked into the Holy of Holies, the temple's innermost and most sacred chamber, which only the Jewish high priest was normally permitted to enter, simply to see what was inside. He reportedly found the chamber completely empty, which reportedly puzzled him considerably; from this point onward, Judea effectively became a client state under Roman authority and was never again fully independent for the remainder of ancient history.

items.subtitle: Jars in cliff caves above the salt sea, found by a shepherd throwing stones after a lost goat.

time.label: When the scrolls were written and hidden

items.reveal: The Dead Sea Scrolls are a large collection of ancient Jewish religious texts, discovered stored inside sealed clay jars hidden in caves along cliffs overlooking the Dead Sea. According to the traditional discovery story, they were first found in 1947 by a young shepherd who was throwing stones into a cave opening while searching for a lost goat. The scrolls turned out to push back the oldest known surviving Hebrew biblical manuscripts by roughly a thousand years compared to what had previously been available, and remarkably, when compared closely, the ancient text turned out to be startlingly similar to the far later medieval versions of the same biblical books that scholars already had.

items.subtitle: A capable general and reluctant emperor who withdrew to an island and governed by letter for eleven years.
items.reveal: Tiberius was a capable and experienced Roman military general who became emperor somewhat reluctantly after Augustus, and who eventually withdrew from Rome entirely to rule the empire remotely from the island of Capri for the last eleven years of his reign, governing largely through written correspondence rather than in person. His retreat from public life was widely seen at the time as unusual and troubling for an emperor. The Gospel of Luke specifically dates the beginning of John the Baptist's public preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius's reign, making this one of the very few historically fixed reference points available for dating the broader narrative of the Christian Gospels.

items.subtitle: A widowed queen, flogged and her daughters assaulted by the officials seizing her husband's estate, who raised the tribes and burned three cities.
items.reveal: Boudica was a British queen whose husband's kingdom was seized by Roman officials after his death; when she protested, Roman officials had her publicly flogged and her daughters assaulted, prompting her to raise a large coalition of British tribes in violent revolt against Roman rule. Her forces successfully burned three major Roman settlements in Britain to the ground before eventually being defeated. The Roman historian Tacitus records some 70,000 people killed across the three destroyed cities during her uprising; she was ultimately defeated in a single decisive battle at a location that has never been definitively identified, and her name is actually a centuries-old scribal error, since the original Latin spelling was Boudica, meaning "victory."

items.subtitle: Four legions, elephants for the triumphal entry, and an emperor who needed a military reputation in a hurry.
items.reveal: The Roman emperor Claudius ordered a full-scale invasion of Britain using four legions, and reportedly brought war elephants along specifically for a dramatic ceremonial entrance into the British town of Camulodunum, since he badly needed a genuine military achievement to strengthen his still-shaky political reputation as emperor. This invasion succeeded where Julius Caesar's earlier limited raids into Britain, nearly a century before, had not, establishing lasting Roman control over the island. Britain would then remain part of the Roman world for almost the next four centuries.

items.subtitle: Fifty thousand seats emptied in minutes through eighty numbered entrances, built on the drained lake of Nero's private palace.
items.reveal: The Colosseum was a massive Roman amphitheater seating roughly fifty thousand spectators, engineered with eighty separate numbered entrances so the entire venue could be emptied of its crowd within just a few minutes. It was built directly on top of an artificial lake the notoriously extravagant emperor Nero had created as part of his own private palace grounds. Its construction was funded using treasure looted from the destruction of Jerusalem's temple, and partly built using forced labor from Jewish prisoners taken during that same conflict; the emperor Vespasian deliberately chose this location, land Nero had previously seized purely for his own private enjoyment, specifically to symbolically give the site back to the Roman public instead.

items.subtitle: Six days of burning in a city of timber tenements, and ten of the fourteen districts damaged or destroyed.

place.label: Rome, the Circus Maximus and the valleys below the hills

items.reveal: The Great Fire of Rome burned for six days through a city built largely of closely packed, flammable timber apartment buildings, ultimately damaging or completely destroying ten of Rome's fourteen administrative districts. The fire broke out and spread while the emperor Nero, contrary to a persistent popular legend, was not even in the city at the time it started, and in any case, the fiddle, the instrument he is famously supposed to have played while Rome burned, had not even been invented yet in ancient Rome. The Roman historian Tacitus does record a rumor that Nero sang about the ancient fall of Troy while watching the fire from a safe distance, but Tacitus himself is careful to explicitly describe this story as an unconfirmed rumor rather than a verified fact.

items.subtitle: Four years of revolt end with a five-month siege, and a building finished six years earlier is pulled down to the foundations.

time.label: The First Jewish Revolt, ending AD 70

items.reveal: The First Jewish Revolt against Roman rule lasted four years before finally ending with a brutal five-month Roman siege of Jerusalem, during which Roman forces completely tore down the city's grand Second Temple to its very foundations, a building that had only been finished in its final form some six years earlier. The Jewish historian Josephus, who had originally served as a rebel military commander before surrendering to Roman forces, went on to write the most detailed surviving historical account of the war, doing so essentially from within the Roman camp. Following the temple's destruction, Judaism reorganized itself permanently around synagogue worship and the study of sacred text rather than around temple sacrifice, and it has remained fundamentally that kind of religion ever since.

items.subtitle: A trading settlement founded at the first point upriver where the Thames could be bridged.
items.reveal: Londinium was a Roman trading settlement founded at the first point along the Thames River where the river could realistically be bridged, making it a natural crossing point for trade and travel. Within about fifteen years of its founding, it was burned to the ground during the British queen Boudica's revolt against Roman rule, leaving a distinct layer of burnt debris that archaeologists can still find in excavations across the modern City of London today. The settlement was rebuilt afterward and eventually grew to become the provincial capital of Roman Britain.

items.subtitle: A rock fortress above the desert, taken by building a ramp up the cliff — and the defenders were dead before the Romans got in.
items.reveal: Masada was a fortified rock plateau rising dramatically above the desert near the Dead Sea, held by Jewish rebels during the First Jewish Revolt against Rome, which Roman forces finally captured only after constructing an enormous siege ramp up the side of the cliff. According to the traditional account, when Roman soldiers finally broke through, they found that the defenders had already chosen to take their own lives rather than be captured or enslaved. This dramatic account comes entirely from the historian Josephus, who was not himself present at the siege; while the massive Roman siege ramp and surrounding army camps remain clearly visible at the site today, archaeological excavation has only actually recovered the remains of roughly 28 people, considerably fewer than the traditional figure of 960 defenders.

items.subtitle: Had his mother killed, competed in the Greek games and won everything he entered, and was declared a public enemy by his own Senate.
items.reveal: Nero was a Roman emperor notorious for having his own mother murdered, and he took a strange personal pride in competing in Greek athletic and artistic competitions, always somehow managing to "win" every single event he entered. His rule eventually grew so unpopular among Rome's political elite that the Roman Senate itself formally declared him a public enemy shortly before his death. Nearly every surviving ancient account of Nero was written by members of the senatorial class he had spent years terrorizing, meaning his overwhelmingly negative historical reputation is, by its very nature, a hostile one; he actually remained genuinely popular among ordinary people in Rome's eastern provinces even after his death.

items.subtitle: Needing someone to blame for the fire, he chose a sect that was already unpopular and small enough to be safe to attack.

place.label: Nero's circus on the Vatican hill, Rome

time.label: From the fire to Nero's death

items.reveal: After the Great Fire of Rome, the emperor Nero, needing someone else to publicly blame for the disaster, deliberately targeted Christians, then a small, already unpopular religious minority that made a politically safe scapegoat. Roman authorities under Nero subjected Christians in Rome to brutal, theatrical executions as public entertainment. The Roman historian Tacitus, who had no particular sympathy for Christians himself, nonetheless records that the cruelty of these punishments was severe enough that ordinary Romans actually began to feel pity for the victims; Christian tradition holds that the apostles Peter and Paul were both killed during this same wave of persecution.

items.subtitle: A column of ash eighteen miles high, then a surge of hot gas that killed everyone still there in moments.

place.label: Pompeii, Herculaneum, and the Bay of Naples

items.reveal: The eruption of Mount Vesuvius sent a towering column of volcanic ash roughly eighteen miles into the sky above the Bay of Naples, before eventually collapsing into a fast-moving surge of superheated gas and ash that killed anyone still remaining in nearby towns like Pompeii and Herculaneum within moments. The Roman writer Pliny the Younger watched the eruption unfold from across the bay and described it in two detailed surviving letters, the only genuine eyewitness account of a major volcanic eruption to survive from the ancient world; volcanologists today still use the term "Plinian eruption" in his honor to describe this same type of violent, ash-column volcanic event. The traditional date of 24 August for the eruption is now doubted by many researchers, since preserved food remains and warm-weather clothing found at the sites seem to better match an eruption occurring later in the autumn instead.

items.subtitle: Made Christianity legal, called the first general council of the church, and was baptised on his deathbed.
items.reveal: Constantine was a Roman emperor who made Christianity a legal religion within the empire, convened the first major worldwide council of Christian bishops, and was formally baptized as a Christian only on his deathbed, at the very end of his life. His troops had actually first proclaimed him emperor at York, in Britain, roughly six years before the more famous battle usually used to mark the true start of his reign. Whether Constantine's embrace of Christianity reflected genuine personal religious conviction or a calculated political strategy has been debated by historians for seventeen centuries, and the question remains genuinely unresolved today.

items.subtitle: A new Rome on a peninsula with water on three sides, at the point where Europe and Asia are half a mile apart.

time.label: From the decision to the dedication

items.reveal: Constantinople was founded by the emperor Constantine as a new imperial capital, deliberately built on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, at the precise geographic point where Europe and Asia are separated by barely half a mile of water. It was built directly on the site of an older Greek colony called Byzantion. The city went on to survive for 1,123 years after its founding, ultimately outlasting the original city of Rome, which it had been named to rival, by nearly a thousand additional years.

items.subtitle: Around three hundred bishops, many of them scarred from the persecutions, summoned by an emperor to settle what Christians believe.
items.reveal: The Council of Nicaea brought together roughly three hundred Christian bishops from across the empire, many of whom bore physical scars from earlier periods of persecution, summoned by the emperor Constantine specifically to settle a serious theological dispute over core Christian beliefs. The central disagreement was whether Jesus, the Son, was made of exactly the same divine substance as God the Father, or merely something similar to it, a distinction that in the original Greek came down to the difference of a single letter. The council also settled how the date of Easter should be calculated each year, and the formal statement of belief it produced, known as the Nicene Creed, is still recited weekly in church services across most of Christendom today.

items.subtitle: The son of freed slaves who reorganised the empire from top to bottom, and then did the one thing no emperor did: retired.
items.reveal: Diocletian was a Roman emperor born to formerly enslaved parents, who thoroughly reorganized the entire structure of Roman government from top to bottom, dividing administrative and military power in new ways to make the sprawling empire easier to govern. Remarkably, he then did something almost no Roman emperor before him had ever chosen to do: he voluntarily retired from power rather than dying in office or being violently overthrown. He spent his retirement growing cabbages at a fortified palace he had built on the Dalmatian coast; the modern city of Split eventually grew up inside the walls of that same palace and still stands there today, and it's worth noting he actually governed the empire from his eastern capital at Nicomedia, never from Rome itself.

items.subtitle: Too much frontier for one man on one horse, so the world is cut in half and each half gets an emperor.

place.label: The line between east and west, through the Balkans

items.reveal: Recognizing that the Roman Empire's borders had simply become too vast and threatened for one single ruler on one horse to defend effectively, the emperor Diocletian divided administrative responsibility for the empire roughly in half, assigning a separate emperor to govern each half along a rough line running through the Balkans. This was originally intended purely as a practical administrative convenience rather than a permanent political division. The division nonetheless became effectively permanent over time, and the rough dividing line Diocletian originally drew still roughly corresponds today to the historical boundary between Europe's Latin-influenced western half and its Greek-influenced eastern half.

items.subtitle: Christians may worship freely, and the property taken from them must be given back.
items.reveal: The Edict of Milan was an agreement issued in the names of the emperors Constantine and Licinius, granting full freedom of religious worship to Christians throughout the Roman Empire and ordering that property previously confiscated from Christian communities during earlier persecutions be formally returned to them. Importantly, the edict granted genuine religious toleration to everyone in the empire generally, not special privileged status specifically to Christianity, which would only come somewhat later. Strictly speaking, it functioned more as a formal political agreement between the two co-emperors than a single legal edict in the usual sense, and it was issued while Constantine happened to be in Milan rather than being specifically enacted as Milan's own local law.

items.subtitle: Churches pulled down, scriptures burned, and clergy required to sacrifice — the last and most systematic attempt to end Christianity by law.

place.label: The empire, enforced hardest in the east

time.label: From the first edict to the edict of toleration

items.reveal: The Great Persecution was the last, and by far the most systematic and thorough, official Roman government attempt to eliminate Christianity entirely through law, involving the demolition of churches, the burning of Christian scriptures, and a legal requirement that Christian clergy publicly perform pagan sacrifices or face punishment. It was enforced with particular severity in the eastern half of the Roman Empire. The persecution finally ended when the dying emperor Galerius, suffering from a painful illness, unexpectedly issued an edict of toleration and specifically asked Christians to pray for his recovery; remarkably, within only nine years afterward, Christianity had become fully legal throughout the empire, and within roughly eighty years, it had become the empire's compulsory official religion.

items.subtitle: An innkeeper's daughter who became an emperor's mother, and went to Jerusalem in her seventies to look for the cross.
items.reveal: Helena was originally the daughter of an innkeeper who rose dramatically in status to become the mother of the Roman emperor Constantine. In her seventies, she traveled to Jerusalem on a religious pilgrimage specifically searching for physical relics connected to the crucifixion of Jesus, including the True Cross itself. The famous Church of the Holy Sepulchre was later built on the exact site she identified as the location of Jesus's crucifixion and burial, a site archaeological excavation has confirmed was indeed a quarry and burial ground located just outside Jerusalem's first-century city walls, though the specific story of her discovering the actual cross itself first appears only in written accounts composed decades after her lifetime.

items.subtitle: A soldier promoted to rule the west while his colleague ruled the east — and much less willing to retire when told to.
items.reveal: Maximian was a Roman military officer promoted by Diocletian to co-rule the western half of the Roman Empire, while Diocletian himself governed the eastern half. Unlike Diocletian, who genuinely retired from power willingly, Maximian proved considerably more reluctant to give up his own authority when the time eventually came. He came out of retirement to seize power twice more, eventually rebelled against his own son-in-law Constantine, and was ultimately forced to take his own life in AD 310.

items.prompt: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
items.subtitle: A vision in the sky, a sign painted on the shields, and a rival emperor drowned in the Tiber behind a collapsing pontoon.

place.label: The Milvian Bridge, north of Rome

items.reveal: At the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, the emperor Constantine reportedly experienced a vision in the sky before the fighting began, and had his soldiers paint a Christian symbol onto their shields in response. His rival, Maxentius, drowned in the Tiber River when a temporary pontoon bridge his retreating forces were using collapsed beneath them during the battle. Two separate surviving accounts, both written by men who personally knew Constantine, actually disagree on the exact details of his vision: one writer describes a dream Constantine had the night before the battle, while another describes a vision supposedly seen by Constantine's entire army at once; the original stone bridge itself still stands today and still carries road traffic across the river.

items.subtitle: Two senior emperors, two juniors ready to succeed them, and a plan for orderly succession that worked exactly once.
items.reveal: The Tetrarchy, meaning "rule of four," was a Roman system of government devised by Diocletian, dividing supreme power between two senior emperors, each paired with a designated junior emperor intended to smoothly succeed him later, an attempt to guarantee stable, orderly transitions of imperial power. None of the system's four capital cities, Nicomedia, Milan, Trier, and Sirmium, was actually the city of Rome itself. The arrangement worked exactly once, during Diocletian's own lifetime while he personally enforced it, but collapsed almost immediately after his retirement, with as many as six separate rival claimants to imperial power emerging within just two years.

items.prompt: The crisis of the third century
items.subtitle: Fifty years, more than twenty emperors, plague, invasion on two frontiers, and a currency debased until nobody would take it.

time.label: From the murder of Severus Alexander to Diocletian

items.reveal: The crisis of the third century was a roughly fifty-year period of severe instability for the Roman Empire, during which more than twenty different emperors held power, often for only brief periods before being violently overthrown, while the empire simultaneously struggled with widespread plague, invasions along two separate frontiers at once, and a currency so debased through repeated devaluation that people increasingly refused to accept it as payment. At one particularly chaotic point, the empire briefly split into three separate, rival states before eventually being forcibly reunified. Nearly every major administrative and military reform that the later emperors Diocletian and Constantine introduced afterward was, in one way or another, a direct response to the instability of this earlier crisis period.

items.subtitle: A North African bishop who wrote the first real autobiography, and then wrote a defence of Christianity against the charge that it had lost Rome.

place.label: Hippo Regius, in Roman North Africa

items.reveal: Augustine of Hippo was a Christian bishop in Roman North Africa, widely credited with writing the first true personal autobiography in Western literature, a work called the Confessions, describing his own spiritual and moral development. He later wrote a major work called The City of God specifically to answer pagan critics who blamed Rome's decline on its abandonment of the old Roman gods in favor of Christianity. He died while Vandal invaders were actively besieging his own city; The City of God went on to profoundly shape how medieval European thinkers understood and interpreted the whole sweep of human history for centuries afterward.

items.subtitle: Miles of tunnels cut into soft rock outside the city walls, with the dead in shelves stacked to the ceiling.

place.label: Outside the walls of Rome, along the Appian Way

items.reveal: The catacombs were extensive networks of tunnels dug into soft volcanic rock outside the walls of ancient Rome, lined with narrow burial shelves stacked from floor to ceiling to hold the bodies of the dead. Contrary to popular legend, these tunnels functioned primarily as ordinary burial grounds rather than as secret hiding places for persecuted Christians, since Roman law already forbade burial within the city walls and separately protected the legal sanctity of tombs, which actually made cemeteries relatively safe, legally protected locations. The popular romantic image of early Christians secretly living down in the catacombs is largely a later invention, mostly added by nineteenth-century writers rather than reflecting how the catacombs were actually used in antiquity.

items.subtitle: The first great argument: must a gentile become a Jew before he can become a Christian? The answer decided what the religion would be.
items.reveal: The Council of Jerusalem was an early meeting of Christian leaders convened to settle Christianity's very first major internal dispute: whether non-Jewish converts to the new faith needed to first formally convert to Judaism, including undergoing circumcision, before they could become genuine Christians. The council ultimately decided that gentile converts did not need to become Jews first in order to become Christians. Had this decision gone the other way, Christianity would likely have remained a relatively small internal sect within Judaism rather than developing into an entirely separate world religion; nearly everything about how Christianity subsequently spread and developed depends directly on this early decision.

items.subtitle: A man travelling with warrants to arrest Christians is blinded by a light and arrives as one of them.
items.reveal: According to the New Testament Book of Acts, a devout Jewish Pharisee named Saul, traveling to Damascus specifically to arrest local Christians, was suddenly struck blind by a brilliant light and heard the voice of Jesus speaking directly to him. He arrived in Damascus not as a persecutor of Christians, but as a newly convinced follower of the very faith he had set out to suppress, and he took the name Paul. Historians date this dramatic conversion event by working backward from a separate, independently confirmed historical fact: an inscription confirms that a Roman official named Gallio served as proconsul of Achaia in AD 51 to 52, which anchors the timing of Paul's later stay in the city of Corinth, and everything in his life leading up to that point.

items.subtitle: Four accounts set down a generation or two after the events, as the people who remembered them began to die.

place.label: The eastern empire; Antioch as the likeliest single centre

items.reveal: The four New Testament Gospels, describing the life and teachings of Jesus, were written down roughly a generation or two after the events they describe took place, around the time when the last living eyewitnesses who personally remembered those events were beginning to die out. Most scholars generally place the Gospel of Mark as having been written first, around AD 70, and the Gospel of John as the latest, sometime around AD 90 to 100. More conservative scholars argue for dates roughly a decade or two earlier than this for all four Gospels, partly because none of the four accounts explicitly mentions the significant historical destruction of Jerusalem's temple in AD 70 as having already happened by the time of writing.

items.subtitle: A tentmaker, a Pharisee, and a Roman citizen, who spent thirty years walking and sailing between cities and writing letters to the ones he had left.
items.reveal: Paul was a Jewish Pharisee, a skilled tentmaker by trade, and also a Roman citizen, who after his dramatic conversion to Christianity spent roughly thirty years traveling by foot and by ship between cities across the eastern Mediterranean world, spreading the new Christian faith and writing letters back to the very communities he had left behind. His Roman citizenship is the specific reason tradition holds he was executed by beheading rather than by the far more painful and humiliating method of crucifixion. Paul's surviving letters are actually the earliest Christian documents historians possess, having been written even before any of the four Gospels themselves were composed.

items.subtitle: A young mother of good family, arrested with her slave, who kept a diary in prison until the day she died in the arena.
items.reveal: Perpetua was a young Roman mother from a respectable family, arrested in Carthage along with her own enslaved servant for practicing the then-illegal religion of Christianity. While imprisoned and awaiting her execution in the arena, she kept a personal written diary describing her experiences and her faith, right up until the day she was killed. Her prison account survives today as one of the earliest known surviving texts written by a Christian woman anywhere, and it is also among the very earliest surviving texts written in Latin by any woman at all, of any religion.

items.subtitle: From a few dozen people in one province to perhaps a tenth of the empire, carried along Roman roads by ordinary travellers.
items.reveal: Christianity began as a small movement of just a few dozen followers concentrated in one Roman province, but by the time it was formally legalized across the empire, it had grown to make up perhaps a full tenth of the entire Roman Empire's total population, spreading largely along Roman roads carried by ordinary travelers, merchants, and soldiers rather than through any organized missionary campaign. The new religion spread especially quickly in cities and among women in particular. Remarkably, Christianity had already reached as far as Armenia and Ethiopia, regions entirely outside the borders of the Roman Empire itself, even before it was formally made legal within the empire's own borders.

items.subtitle: Within a lifetime of being illegal, it is the only religion the empire permits — and the old temples close.

time.label: From the Edict of Thessalonica to the ban on pagan sacrifice

items.reveal: Within about a single lifetime of being an illegal, persecuted religion, Christianity became the only religion the Roman Empire officially permitted, as emperors ordered pagan temples closed and banned traditional sacrifices to the old gods. The emperor Theodosius I closed the famous oracle at Delphi and ended the ancient Olympic Games, both traditions that had continued for well over a thousand years by that point. Only about eighty years separate the last official Roman persecution of Christians from the first instances of Christians themselves using state power to persecute pagans and other religious minorities.

items.subtitle: An emperor attacks without waiting for the western army, and two thirds of the eastern field force dies with him.
items.reveal: At the Battle of Adrianople, the Roman emperor Valens attacked a Gothic army without waiting for reinforcements from the western Roman army to arrive, and roughly two-thirds of his eastern field army, along with Valens himself, was killed in the resulting defeat. The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, writing not long afterward, called it the worst Roman military defeat since the Battle of Cannae, nearly 600 years earlier. After this catastrophic loss, Rome never again attempted to destroy a Germanic people that had already settled within its imperial frontier by force, and had to negotiate and make political arrangements with such groups instead.

items.prompt: The final division of the empire
items.subtitle: Theodosius leaves the east to one son and the west to the other, and the two halves never share a ruler again.
items.reveal: When the Roman emperor Theodosius I died, he left the eastern half of the empire to one of his sons and the western half to the other, and the two halves of the Roman Empire would never again be reunited under a single ruler afterward. His sons, Arcadius and Honorius, were only seventeen and ten years old respectively when they inherited their portions of the empire. The wealthier, more urbanized eastern half, with its shorter and more defensible frontier, would go on to survive for another thousand years, while the western half had only about eighty more years left before it collapsed entirely.

items.subtitle: Farmers and warriors beyond the Rhine and Danube, whom Rome fought, hired, traded with, and eventually could not do without.

place.label: Beyond the Rhine and Danube frontiers

items.reveal: The Germanic peoples were farming and warrior societies living beyond Rome's Rhine and Danube river frontiers, whom Rome fought as enemies, hired as soldiers, traded with extensively, and eventually came to depend on so heavily that the empire genuinely could not function without them. By the fourth century AD, a very large proportion of the actual soldiers serving in the Roman army were themselves ethnically Germanic. As a result, by this late period, the practical distinction between a foreign "barbarian invasion" and an internal Roman army "mutiny" had become genuinely difficult for contemporaries to draw clearly.

items.subtitle: A whole people asks for asylum, is admitted, is then starved and cheated by the officials meant to feed them — and takes up arms.
items.reveal: A large Gothic population, fleeing invading Huns from further east, requested and were granted formal asylum to cross the Danube River and settle peacefully within Roman imperial territory. Roman officials assigned to feed and resettle them instead exploited and cheated the refugees, deliberately starving many of them, which eventually drove the desperate Goths to take up arms in open revolt against Rome. The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, writing close to these events, places the blame for the resulting revolt squarely on Roman official corruption and mistreatment, rather than on any inherent Gothic treachery; historians generally consider this crisis the true beginning of the long process that eventually led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

items.subtitle: Seventy-three miles of stone across the narrowest part of the island, with a fort every Roman mile.

time.label: From construction to the withdrawal from Britain

items.reveal: Hadrian's Wall was a fortified stone barrier stretching seventy-three miles across the narrowest part of the island of Britain, built with a small fort positioned roughly every Roman mile along its entire length. Historians think it likely functioned as much as a controlled customs checkpoint and a visible political statement of Roman power as it did as a strict military defensive barrier. A remarkable cache of preserved wooden writing tablets found at Vindolanda, a fort located just behind the wall, includes a personal birthday party invitation written by one Roman woman to another, considered the earliest known piece of writing in Latin composed by a woman.

items.subtitle: Horse archers out of the eastern steppe who beat everyone they met, and pushed whole nations west ahead of them.

place.label: The steppe north of the Black Sea

time.label: Their appearance on the Roman horizon

items.reveal: The Huns were formidable horse-riding archers who emerged suddenly out of the eastern steppes north of the Black Sea, decisively defeating essentially every people they encountered as they expanded westward. Their arrival triggered a chain reaction, pushing entire other peoples and nations violently westward ahead of them, out of their own traditional homelands, in a desperate search for safety. The wider domino effect the Huns set in motion across Europe ultimately matters more to history than the Huns themselves did directly, since it was pressure from the Huns that specifically drove the Goths to the Danube frontier seeking Roman protection in the first place.

items.subtitle: On the last night of the year, Vandals, Alans, and Sueves cross the frozen river into Gaul, and the frontier is simply gone.
items.reveal: On the last night of a particular year, several large Germanic groups, including the Vandals, Alans, and Sueves, crossed the frozen Rhine River together into Roman Gaul, effectively erasing what had long been one of Rome's most important and heavily defended frontier lines almost overnight. The Roman military garrison originally responsible for defending this stretch of frontier proved unable to stop the crossing. In the resulting emergency, Roman troops were hastily withdrawn from Britain to help defend Gaul instead, and Britain itself was never fully regarrisoned by Roman forces again afterward.

items.subtitle: The last man to rule the whole Roman world, who did public penance when a bishop shut him out of church.
items.reveal: Theodosius I was the final Roman emperor to rule the entire unified Roman world, both east and west, under one single authority before it was permanently divided between his two sons. In a remarkable episode, the powerful bishop Ambrose of Milan once barred Theodosius from receiving Christian communion after Theodosius's soldiers had carried out a brutal massacre at Thessalonica, and the emperor publicly submitted to this religious punishment. This marked the first time in Roman history that an emperor had openly accepted that a church leader possessed genuine moral authority to judge and discipline even the emperor himself.

items.subtitle: Crossed a continent, crossed the sea, took the richest province in the west, and built a fleet.

place.label: From the Rhine through Spain to Carthage

time.label: From the Rhine crossing to the Byzantine reconquest (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: The Vandals were a Germanic people who migrated an enormous distance across the European continent, eventually crossing the sea into North Africa, where they conquered Carthage, one of the wealthiest and most valuable provinces remaining in the western Roman Empire, and went on to build a formidable naval fleet of their own. Capturing Carthage in AD 439 cut off a critical source of grain shipments that had long helped feed the city of Rome itself. The modern English word "vandalism," meaning senseless destruction, only dates back to the 1790s, and most historians today consider it a fairly unfair label, since the Vandals themselves were not noticeably more destructive than most other conquering peoples of their era.

items.subtitle: A Gothic king who had served in the Roman army and spent his life asking for land and a title, and took Rome when refused.
items.reveal: Alaric was a Gothic king who had actually served for a time as an officer within the Roman army himself, and who spent much of his career formally requesting land for his people to settle and an official Roman military title in recognition of his service. When Roman authorities repeatedly refused these requests, he eventually led his forces to besiege and sack the city of Rome itself. He died of a sudden fever only months after the sack of Rome, and his body was reportedly buried beneath a riverbed that his followers deliberately diverted for the purpose, afterward killing the enslaved workers who had done the digging so that the exact burial location would remain a permanent secret.

items.subtitle: The scourge of God — who ate off wooden plates while his guests ate off gold, and took tribute from both empires at once.

place.label: The Hunnic heartland on the Hungarian plain

items.reveal: Attila the Hun, sometimes called "the scourge of God" by frightened contemporaries, ruled a powerful Hunnic empire, and was known for his own personal simplicity even while famously entertaining important guests off gold dinnerware, apparently eating himself off plain wooden plates as a display of stern personal discipline. He extracted regular tribute payments from both the eastern and western halves of the Roman Empire simultaneously. He had his own brother and co-ruler murdered in AD 445 to secure sole control of the Hunnic empire; that empire, however, was held together mainly through fear of Attila's own personal reputation, and it collapsed into rival pieces within just a year of his death.
