items.subtitle: The pope rides north to meet him on a riverbank, they talk, and the Huns go home.
items.reveal: As Attila the Hun's army advanced toward the city of Rome itself, Pope Leo I rode north to meet him personally on a riverbank near Mantua, and following their conversation, Attila unexpectedly turned his army around and withdrew from Italy without attacking Rome. Christian tradition afterward gave Pope Leo full credit for personally persuading Attila to spare the city. Modern historians think other, more practical factors were probably at least as important in Attila's decision, including an outbreak of plague within his own army's camp, a failing harvest that threatened to leave his forces without adequate food, and a separate eastern Roman army actively raiding his own homeland while he was away; both explanations, the miraculous and the practical, actually circulated at the time.

items.prompt: The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
items.subtitle: A Roman general and a Visigothic king fight side by side against the Huns — and it is the only battle Attila does not win.
items.reveal: At the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, the Roman general Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric fought together, side by side, as allies against the invading army of Attila the Hun, marking the only battle Attila is known to have failed to win outright. Notably, the bulk of the soldiers in what is described as "Aetius's Roman army" were not actually ethnically Roman themselves, but were largely made up of allied Germanic troops instead. The battle's exact physical location has never been definitively identified by archaeologists, and the casualty figures given in surviving ancient sources are generally considered wildly unreliable; despite this defeat, Attila withdrew his forces and simply invaded Italy directly the very next year instead.

items.subtitle: He dies on his wedding night of a nosebleed, having drunk too much, and is found in the morning by his bride.
items.reveal: Attila the Hun died suddenly on his own wedding night, apparently from a severe nosebleed after drinking heavily at the wedding celebration, and his new bride reportedly discovered his body the following morning. The Roman diplomat Priscus, who had personally visited Attila's own camp on an earlier embassy, is the main ancient source reporting this account of a simple nosebleed as the cause of death, though other contemporaries suspected his new bride herself may have actually been responsible. Following his death, Attila's own sons divided his empire between themselves, quickly fell into bitter quarreling, and lost control of the entire Hunnic empire within only about twenty years.

items.subtitle: Accused of plotting to put his own son on the throne, he refuses to let his troops fight for him and walks out to the sword.
items.reveal: Stilicho, the powerful Roman general effectively holding the crumbling western Roman Empire together, was accused of secretly plotting to place his own son on the imperial throne. Rather than allow his loyal troops to fight on his behalf against these charges, he chose to refuse their support and walked out to accept his own execution by sword. In the aftermath, the imperial court then massacred the family members of many of Stilicho's Gothic soldiers still serving Rome, prompting some thirty thousand of those soldiers to defect immediately to the Gothic king Alaric instead; Rome itself was sacked by Alaric's forces only two years later.

items.subtitle: An emperor's sister, confined for an affair, smuggles her ring to Attila asking for rescue — and he reads it as an engagement, with half the empire as dowry.

place.label: Ravenna, with the message carried east

items.reveal: Honoria, sister of the western Roman emperor, was confined by her family after having an affair, and in response she secretly smuggled her personal ring to Attila the Hun, apparently asking him to rescue her from her confinement. Attila chose to interpret this message as a formal marriage proposal instead, and demanded half of the western Roman Empire as an appropriate dowry befitting his new bride. Whether Honoria genuinely intended her message as an actual marriage proposal remains impossible to know for certain, but Attila found the message a useful pretext either way, later specifically citing it as his official justification for invading Roman Gaul.

items.subtitle: Three days of plunder in a city no foreign enemy had entered for eight hundred years.
items.reveal: The Visigoths, led by their king Alaric, sacked the city of Rome over three days of looting and plunder, the first time any foreign enemy army had actually managed to enter and pillage the city in some eight hundred years. Militarily, the event actually changed relatively little in practical terms, since Rome had already stopped being the empire's functioning political capital more than a century earlier. Psychologically, however, the shock across the Roman world was enormous: the Christian scholar Jerome wrote in anguish that the city which had once captured the whole world had itself now been captured, and Augustine began writing his major work The City of God specifically in response to the crisis of confidence this event caused.

items.subtitle: Half-Vandal, married into the imperial family, and for thirteen years the only thing holding the western empire together.

place.label: Italy, ruling from Milan and Ravenna

items.reveal: Stilicho was a Roman general of half-Vandal ancestry who married into the imperial family, and for roughly thirteen critical years, he was effectively the single most important figure holding the crumbling western Roman Empire together as its de facto leader. He spent his career defending Rome against various invading Germanic peoples despite being himself of Germanic ancestry. This situation, a "barbarian" general personally defending Rome against other "barbarians," captures in a single man the whole complicated shape of the entire fifth-century western Roman world.

items.subtitle: Twice cornered and twice beaten, the Gothic king twice gets away with his army intact.

time.label: The Greek campaign and the battles of Pollentia and Verona

items.reveal: On two separate occasions, the Roman general Stilicho successfully cornered and militarily defeated the Gothic king Alaric's army, first in Greece and later in northern Italy. Both times, however, Alaric and his army managed to escape afterward with their forces still largely intact, rather than being fully destroyed or captured. Some contemporaries suspected and openly accused Stilicho of deliberately allowing Alaric to escape both times, believing Stilicho wanted to keep the ongoing Gothic threat alive specifically to keep himself politically indispensable and irreplaceable to Rome.

items.subtitle: Theodosius dies leaving a ten-year-old emperor in the west, and names his general to look after him.
items.reveal: When the emperor Theodosius I died, he left behind a ten-year-old son, Honorius, as emperor of the western Roman Empire, and named his trusted general Stilicho to serve as the young emperor's guardian and effective regent. Stilicho claimed Theodosius had actually named him guardian of both of his young sons, the western and eastern emperors alike, a claim the eastern imperial court in Constantinople firmly denied and rejected. As a direct result of this dispute, the eastern and western halves of the Roman Empire spent much of the following decade actively working against each other's interests rather than cooperating.

items.subtitle: The half that did not fall, still calling itself Roman, still speaking Greek, and still there a thousand years later.

place.label: Anatolia, the Balkans, and the eastern provinces

time.label: The eastern empire as a separate state, from the division of 395. It lasted to 1453 — see reveal.

items.reveal: The Eastern Roman Empire was the half of the Roman world that did not collapse in the fifth century, continuing to call itself "Roman," continuing to speak primarily Greek rather than Latin, and remaining a functioning state for another full thousand years after the western half fell. Its people never actually called themselves "Byzantines" during their own lifetimes; that particular label was only coined much later, in 1557, by a German scholar studying their history. To themselves, and to their neighbors at the time, they were simply Romans; the sixth-century emperor Justinian briefly succeeded in reconquering Italy and North Africa, temporarily restoring at least part of the old unified Roman territory.

items.prompt: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
items.subtitle: The last emperor is pensioned off to a villa on the Bay of Naples, and nobody replaces him.
items.reveal: The Western Roman Empire is traditionally considered to have ended when its last emperor, a young boy named Romulus Augustulus, was quietly deposed and pensioned off to live out his life at a comfortable villa on the Bay of Naples, with no new western emperor ever appointed to replace him. Remarkably, almost nobody living at the actual time seems to have specifically noticed or recorded this particular year as marking any especially significant turning point in history. The precise date of AD 476 is really a convenient marker chosen later by historians looking back, illustrating a useful general lesson: historical "periods" and their supposed turning points are usually constructed afterward by the people writing about the past, rather than being consciously experienced that way by the people actually living through them.

items.subtitle: A Germanic officer who took the crown off a child, declined to wear it, and sent the imperial regalia east.
items.reveal: Odoacer was a Germanic military officer serving in the Roman army who removed the crown from a child emperor, Romulus Augustulus, but then declined to claim the imperial title or crown for himself, instead sending Rome's official imperial regalia east to Constantinople as a symbolic gesture. He informed the eastern Roman court that the west no longer required its own separate emperor at all. Despite this dramatic political change, Odoacer kept much of Rome's traditional civil government running largely intact, including the Senate, the annually elected consuls, and the ordinary collection of taxes.

items.subtitle: Once a secretary at Attila's court, he ends up commanding the Roman army and putting his own small son on the throne.
items.reveal: Orestes had once served as a secretary at the court of Attila the Hun earlier in his career, before he eventually rose to command the Roman army in Italy and arranged to place his own young son, Romulus Augustulus, on the imperial throne as a puppet emperor. When his own Germanic soldiers demanded land grants in Italy as payment for their service, Orestes refused their demand, and his own troops subsequently killed him for this refusal. The very last western Roman emperor was thus effectively created, and shortly afterward removed, over what was fundamentally a dispute about soldiers' pay and land grants rather than any grand political principle.

items.subtitle: The western capital for the last seventy years — chosen because it sat behind marshes and had a harbour for escape.

time.label: As capital of the western empire

items.reveal: Ravenna served as the capital of the Western Roman Empire for its final roughly seventy years, deliberately chosen because it was protected by surrounding marshland, making it difficult for an attacking army to reach, and because it had direct access to a harbor that would allow the imperial court to escape by sea if necessary. This choice of a defensible, escape-ready capital, rather than the traditional city of Rome itself, reveals just how precarious the imperial government's own situation had become by this point. Because Ravenna largely stopped mattering politically after the western empire fell, and was never significantly rebuilt over in later centuries, its fifth- and sixth-century mosaic artwork survives today in better condition than anywhere else from this period.

items.subtitle: The last emperor in the west: a boy of about fifteen, whose two names were those of Rome's founder and its first emperor.
items.reveal: Romulus Augustus was the very last emperor to rule the Western Roman Empire, a boy of only about fifteen years old when he was placed on the throne by his own father. His two given names happened to combine the name of Rome's legendary founder, Romulus, with the name of Rome's very first emperor, Augustus, an almost too-perfect historical coincidence for the empire's final ruler. Contemporaries at the time mockingly nicknamed him "Augustulus," meaning roughly "little Augustus," reflecting how minor and powerless he actually was compared to his famous namesake.

items.subtitle: Raised as a hostage in Constantinople, sent west to remove Odoacer, and ruler of an Italy that kept working for thirty years.

time.label: King of Italy (scored to the AD 500 timeline limit)

items.reveal: Theodoric the Great was raised as a young hostage at the imperial court in Constantinople before later being sent west specifically to remove the Italian ruler Odoacer from power. He personally killed Odoacer at a banquet that had actually been arranged to formally settle the differences between them. Theodoric then ruled Italy successfully for roughly thirty years, during which traditional Roman law, Roman government offices, and even Roman aqueducts all continued functioning largely as before, offering a useful correction to the popular idea that Roman civilization simply switched off entirely the moment the last western emperor was deposed in AD 476.

items.subtitle: Fourteen days of methodical stripping — the pope negotiates that there will be no killing, and there is not much.
items.reveal: The Vandals, under their king Genseric, sacked the city of Rome over fourteen days of thorough, methodical looting, having negotiated in advance with the pope that the city's population would not be killed or harmed in the process, and largely they were not. Their sack was actually considerably more extensive and thorough than the more famous earlier sack by the Visigoths under Alaric, even though it is far less well remembered today. Among the treasures the Vandals stripped from the city were the gilded bronze roof tiles from the temple of Jupiter, along with the sacred temple vessels that the Roman general Titus had originally carried off from Jerusalem's temple four centuries earlier.
